sourceFormat: Each option is preserved as the original six-field JSON row; normalized fields are indexing aids only. Inferred value kinds are deliberately conservative; consult syntaxDescription and description for exact constraints.

options.syntaxDescription: default, screen, film (default default) - screen enables palette and block copy; film signals film grain but synthesises none on its own
options.description:
Tells the encoder what kind of material it is looking at so it can enable tools suited to it. screen turns on palette mode and intra block copy, which code large flat colour areas and repeated UI elements far more cheaply than ordinary prediction - the difference on a desktop capture or a slide deck is dramatic.

film is not a grain-preservation setting, and it is not grain synthesis either, though it is widely described as both. Measured against aomenc 3.8.2: an encode with nothing but --tune-content=film comes out carrying film grain parameters that are entirely zero - the signalling is switched on and there is no grain in it. What actually measures and describes the source's grain is --denoise-noise-level, which the Video tab's Grain Synthesis row owns, and setting that is what makes this row's film mode mean anything.

It does change the picture beside that: with a denoise level set as well, the output's grain table differs from the same encode without it, the tune having moved the quantisation the noise model is fitted against.
options.listedValuesDescription:
default|Ordinary live action and animation.
screen|Desktop capture, slides and UI recordings.
film|Grainy film - pair it with the Grain Synthesis row, which supplies the grain itself.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 variance, 2 complexity, 3 cyclic refresh; 1 favours flat skies
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame. Mode 1 distributes by variance, taking bits from busy areas where error is masked and giving them to flat ones where banding shows. Mode 2 works from a complexity estimate instead. Mode 3 is cyclic refresh, which refreshes part of each frame in turn and is aimed at low-bitrate streaming rather than file encoding.

libaom leaves this off by default because its other tools already handle much of the same problem, and the modes can hurt as often as they help on ordinary content.

Worth trying on sources that band, and worth measuring rather than assuming.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Variance-based, the usual choice if flat areas band.
2|Complexity-based distribution.
3|Cyclic refresh, for low-bitrate streaming.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Quantisation matrices; often improves detail retention at low bitrates, tuned via qm-min and qm-max
options.description:
Quantisation matrices weight quantisation by frequency rather than applying one step size across the whole transform block, so high-frequency coefficients - fine texture and grain - can be kept or discarded independently of the low-frequency structure.

Turning them on generally helps retain texture at a given bitrate and is a common recommendation for grainy or detailed sources. It pairs with the qm-min and qm-max range settings that control how aggressive the shaping is.

It is off by default and costs essentially nothing to try.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; uniform quantisation.
1|Enables the matrices; commonly a gain on detailed or grainy sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Adaptive use of the quantize_b path; small efficiency gain for a little extra encode time
options.description:
Selects adaptively between the two entropy coding paths AV1 provides for transform coefficients, choosing per situation rather than using one throughout. The gain is small and comes entirely from more accurate coefficient coding, not from any change in what is encoded.

It costs a little encoding time and is off by default. On slow, quality-focused encodes it is a cheap fraction of a percent.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Adaptive selection, a small gain on slow encodes.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr, ssim, iq, ssimulacra2 (default psnr) - Which metric the encoder optimises for
options.description:
Selects the distortion metric the encoder's decisions are scored against, which changes where bits go rather than just what gets reported. psnr minimises squared error, ssim weights by structural similarity, iq is a perceptual image-quality model, and ssimulacra2 optimises against the SSIMULACRA2 perceptual metric.

ssim generally produces a picture people prefer over psnr. ssimulacra2 optimises directly for a metric the Sample Encodes utility can also score an encode against, which is useful if you are being measured on it and questionable if you are not - tuning for a metric tends to exploit it.

The bundled aomenc offers ten tunes in its --help and can do only these four. vmaf, vmaf_neg, vmaf_with_preprocessing, vmaf_without_preprocessing and butteraugli are compile-time options this build was not built with, and libaom refuses an unusable tune outright rather than warning, so each of them is a failed encode rather than a setting that quietly does nothing. vmaf_saliency_map is the exception, and is worse: it is accepted and gives output byte-identical to psnr.
options.listedValuesDescription:
psnr|The default; minimises squared error.
ssim|Structure-weighted decisions; usually the better-looking choice.
iq|A perceptual image-quality model, aimed at how the picture looks rather than at a score.
ssimulacra2|Optimises against the SSIMULACRA2 perceptual metric.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 8) - Lowest quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1 to have any effect
options.description:
With quantisation matrices enabled, the encoder picks a matrix per frame from a range of flatness levels. This sets the lowest level it may choose, where lower numbers mean a more aggressively shaped matrix that treats high frequencies differently from low ones.

A shaped matrix keeps more of the fine texture that flat quantisation rounds away, which is why enabling matrices is a common recommendation for grainy and detailed sources.

It does nothing unless enable-qm is set to 1, and it must not exceed qm-max.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default.
5|Allows more aggressive shaping, retaining more fine texture.
0|The flattest-shaped extreme of the range.
10|A narrow, conservative range near the top.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 15) - Highest quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1 to have any effect
options.description:
The upper end of the quantisation matrix range the encoder may select from. Level 15 is effectively unshaped, treating all frequencies alike, so leaving the maximum here lets the encoder fall back to ordinary flat quantisation when shaping would not help.

Lowering it forces shaping to be applied even where the encoder would rather not, which retains texture more consistently and costs efficiency.

Like qm-min it requires enable-qm 1, and it must not fall below qm-min.
options.listedValuesDescription:
15|The default; the encoder may use an unshaped matrix.
12|Forces at least mild shaping throughout.
10|Consistent shaping, at a cost in efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-7 (default 0) - Biases transform coefficient decisions towards sharpness at a cost in measured error
options.description:
Biases the rate-distortion decisions made about transform coefficients towards keeping the ones that carry sharpness, rather than dropping them because they are expensive relative to the error they remove.

Higher values retain more fine detail and edge definition, and cost both bitrate and measured quality, since the encoder is deliberately choosing something a plain error metric scores lower.

It is a milder tool than the psychovisual settings in x264 and x265, and it is worth a try on detailed sources that come out looking soft.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no bias.
2|A mild sharpness bias for detailed live action.
4|Noticeably sharper, at a real bitrate cost.
7|The maximum.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 1) - Varies the quantiser within a frame; 3 and 4 target visual rather than metric quality
options.description:
Allows the quantiser to vary across a frame rather than staying fixed, so bits can follow what matters within the picture. Mode 1 optimises for an objective metric, mode 3 targets keyframe visual quality, and mode 4 uses a user-rating-derived visual model.

The objective default improves measured scores. The visual modes deliberately spend bits where people look rather than where error is largest, which is usually the better choice for material anyone will actually watch.

It depends on the temporal dependency model, which is enabled by default outside realtime mode. Note also that HDR sources are already given a delta quantiser mode automatically, so a value set here replaces that rather than adding to it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; objective optimisation.
0|Off; a fixed quantiser across the frame.
3|Targets keyframe visual quality.
4|Visual quality from a user-rating model.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 1) - CDEF deringing filter: 0 off, 1 on, 2 skip non-ref frames, 3 by qindex; off preserves fine grain
options.description:
The constrained directional enhancement filter is an in-loop deblocking and deringing stage that follows edge directions, so it cleans up ringing around edges without smearing the edge itself.

It is on by default and generally worth leaving on: without it, ringing artefacts around high-contrast edges persist into the reference frames and propagate.

Grain-preservation setups sometimes disable it because it removes fine noise along with the ringing, but that only makes sense at bitrates high enough that there is no ringing to remove.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Grain preservation at high bitrates, accepting some ringing.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 7) - Frames the alt-ref temporal filter may use; fewer suits high motion, more smooths noisy sources
options.description:
How many neighbouring frames the alternate-reference filter may blend together when it builds an alt-ref frame. The alt-ref is a synthetic, denoised frame that other frames predict from, and averaging several frames is what removes the noise.

More frames means a cleaner alt-ref and better prediction for the frames referring to it, which saves bits - but also means grain and fine motion detail are averaged away more thoroughly.

Grain-preserving setups lower this, sometimes to 0, accepting the bitrate cost to keep noise intact.
options.listedValuesDescription:
7|The default.
3|Reduced blending, keeping more grain and fine motion.
0|Disables the temporal filter entirely, for maximum grain retention.
15|The maximum; cleanest alt-ref, at the cost of fine detail.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 5) - Strength of the alt-ref temporal filter; lower preserves grain, higher cleans up noisy sources
options.description:
How aggressively the alternate-reference filter blends the frames it has gathered. Where arnr-maxframes decides how many frames are involved, this decides how much of each survives.

Higher values give a smoother, cleaner reference that predicts well and saves bitrate, at the cost of grain and fine detail being averaged out of the reference and therefore out of everything predicting from it.

Lowering it to 1 or 2 is the usual move on grainy film; raising it helps genuinely noisy sources such as low-light video, where the noise is not something anyone wants to preserve.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default.
2|Grainy film, keeping noise and texture.
0|No filtering; maximum grain retention.
6|Noisy low-light footage where the noise is unwanted.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Temporal filtering on keyframes; 2 adds an overlay frame but can break seeking in some players
options.description:
Applies the same temporal filtering used for alt-ref frames to keyframes as well, so a keyframe is built from several source frames rather than from one. A cleaner keyframe predicts better for everything that follows it.

Mode 2 additionally codes an overlay frame to correct the difference between the filtered keyframe and the actual source frame, which fixes the mismatch the filtering introduces.

Mode 2 is not compatible with all downstream pipelines and is best avoided unless you have reason to want it; grain-preserving encodes often set 0 for the same reasons they lower arnr strength.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; filtered keyframes.
0|Unfiltered keyframes, for grain retention.
2|Filtering with a correcting overlay frame.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1 outside realtime) - The loop restoration filter, which repairs coding artefacts after deblocking
options.description:
Loop restoration is a filter that runs after deblocking and CDEF, fitting a correction to each region to bring the reconstructed picture back towards the source. It repairs ringing and general coding error that the earlier filters leave behind.

It is on by default for non-realtime encoding and is generally worth keeping, because the repaired frame is what later frames predict from, so the benefit compounds.

Grain-preserving setups sometimes disable it, since like CDEF it cannot distinguish fine noise from the artefacts it is removing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default outside realtime; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Off, for grain retention at high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-48 (default 35) - Lookahead for alt-ref placement and bitrate allocation; lower cuts memory use and latency
options.description:
How many frames the encoder buffers before making decisions, which sets how far ahead it can see. Lookahead drives alt-ref placement, frame type decisions and bit allocation across a scene.

Alt-ref frames in particular depend on it: the encoder needs frames in hand to build one and to decide where it belongs. Lowering this below about 20 measurably costs compression, and 0 disables lookahead entirely for low-delay use.

The cost is memory and latency, not encoding speed.
options.listedValuesDescription:
19|The default.
35|The maximum; the most lookahead for offline encoding.
25|A common setting balancing memory against compression.
0|Low delay, at a substantial compression cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Motion vector cost updates: 0 per superblock, 1 per SB row, 2 per tile, 3 off; higher is faster
options.description:
How often the encoder recalculates the cost tables it uses to price motion vectors during the search. Recomputing them often keeps the prices accurate as the statistics change through a frame; recomputing them rarely saves time.

Higher values update less often and encode faster, at a small cost in decision quality because the search is choosing vectors against slightly stale prices.

It is purely a speed dial and does not change what the format can express.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|Most frequent updates; the most accurate decisions.
1|Update per SB row, a reasonable compromise.
2|Less frequent updates, noticeably faster.
3|Least frequent; fastest, with the roughest cost estimates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Forward reference keyframes, letting a keyframe also serve as a forward reference to save bits
options.description:
Allows forward keyframes, which are keyframes that can still be predicted from across, letting the encoder place a keyframe without fully resetting prediction at that point. Ordinary keyframes break the prediction chain entirely, which costs bits every time one appears.

Enabling this lets the encoder insert them more freely where a scene change makes one useful, without paying the full cost.

It changes the stream's random-access structure, so it is not appropriate where every keyframe must be a clean seek point.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; conventional keyframes only.
1|Allows forward keyframes, cheaper at scene changes.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 0) - The best quantiser allowed; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, capping how many bits any one frame may be given. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode may get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody would notice, which frees bits for difficult material in a rate-targeted encode and simply shrinks the file in constant quality mode.

It must not exceed max-q, and in constant quality encoding it does nothing unless the target sits below it.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
15|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
20|A firmer cap for bitrate-constrained delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 63) - The worst quantiser allowed; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality may fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocking and smearing difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer meet its bitrate target there and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

It must not fall below min-q.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
63|The default; no ceiling.
50|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
40|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far under the target rate a section may run
options.description:
How far below the target bitrate the encoder may let a section fall, as a percentage. It is permission to spend less than the target where the content does not need it.

Raising it lets easy passages come in well under target, which suits varied material where some scenes genuinely need very little. Lowering it forces the encoder to keep pace with the target even when there is nothing worth spending on, which mostly wastes bits.

Values above 100 are rejected.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Lets easy scenes save considerably more.
100|Maximum freedom to undershoot.
0|Holds the rate at target regardless of content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far over the target rate a section may run
options.description:
How far above the target bitrate the encoder may let a section run, as a percentage. It is the permission a difficult scene needs in order to spend beyond its share rather than degrade.

Raising it protects hard scenes at the cost of a less predictable size and a higher peak rate, which matters when the result has to fit a buffer or a delivery constraint. Lowering it holds the rate down and lets quality drop exactly where bits are most needed.

Values above 100 are rejected.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Gives difficult scenes more room to spend.
0|Holds hard to the target, at a visible cost on hard scenes.
100|Maximum freedom to overshoot.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-5 (default 1) - What it optimises for; 0 visual quality, 1 PSNR, 2 SSIM, 3 image quality, 4 MS-SSIM, 5 film grain
options.description:
Tune picks the quality model the encoder optimises its internal decisions against, which changes rate-distortion choices, filtering and where bits land rather than just which score gets reported. 0 is visual quality, 1 PSNR, 2 SSIM, 3 still-image quality, 4 MS-SSIM, and 5 is a film grain bundle that internally runs tune 0 with temporal filtering, restoration and CDEF off, --tx-bias 1 and --ac-bias 4.00.

Tune 1 is the metric-safe default. Tune 0 gives a sharper, more detailed picture for lower scores and more artefacts. Tune 5 holds onto grain aggressively and costs bitrate and encoding time; it is aimed at CRF 20 to 40 on a slow preset.

Tunes 2, 3 and 4 run only under CRF rate control, and tunes 0 and 5 fall back to 1 in low-delay. Tune 3 is not recommended outside all-intra encoding.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default, optimising for PSNR and the safe choice for general video.
0|Live action or animation where visible detail matters more than metric scores.
5|Heavily grained film scans, at CRF 20 to 40 and a slow preset.
3|Still images and all-intra encodes, paired with --avif 1.
2|SSIM-driven decisions, and the only tune --alt-ssim-tuning works with.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-8.0 (default 1.0) - Psychovisual rate distortion biasing towards texture; raise for grainy, heavily detailed film
options.description:
Adds an energy-preserving term to the encoder's rate-distortion decisions. It compares the visual energy of the source block against the encoded block, so flattening texture is charged as a real cost instead of being rewarded as a reduction in error. This is the same idea as psy-rd in x264 and x265.

The higher the value, the more bits go to grain, noise and fine texture that a plain error metric would happily throw away. Around 1.0 to 1.5 keeps texture and motion acuity intact; 4.0 to 6.0 preserves grain and noise dramatically better, but costs a lot of bitrate and sinks metric scores.

--sharp-tx is enabled by default specifically to reinforce ac-bias, so if you set this to 0 you should set --sharp-tx 0 as well.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.0|The default, retaining texture sharpness across general content.
1.5|Detailed live action and scenes with complex motion, a mild step up.
4.00|Grain retention on film scans, best alongside --enable-tf 0 and --enable-cdef 0.
6.00|The practical ceiling for grain and noise preservation, at a heavy bitrate cost.
0.0|Disables the metric entirely; pair it with --sharp-tx 0.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Biases transform search towards sharpness; 1 full, 2 size only, 3 interpolation, can add blocking
options.description:
Raises the measured cost of the prediction and transform choices that tend to produce a soft picture. Full mode penalises the blurry intra modes, DC and the smooth predictors, along with averaged compound inter modes, and it strongly penalises 64x64 intra blocks. Mode 2 keeps only the block-size part of that; mode 3 restricts the bias to interpolation filter selection.

You get more sharpness and detail retention, and more blocking and banding, because the encoder is pushed away from exactly the smooth predictors that hide those. It suits grainy, textured live action and works against clean gradients, skies and flat animation.

Tune 5 already sets mode 1. Part of mode 1's intra prediction bias only engages when --ac-bias is 0; the size and compound-mode biases apply either way.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default, applying no bias at all.
1|Full bias, for grainy or heavily textured live action.
2|Transform size only, a safer step that still avoids blurry 64x64 intra blocks.
3|Interpolation filter only, the lightest of the three modes.

options.syntaxDescription: -7 to 7 (default 1) - Deblocking sharpness bias, also affecting rate distortion; raise to keep fine detail
options.description:
Sharpness does two things at once. It sets the deblocking loop filter's sharpness level, so the filter smooths less across block edges, and it feeds the coefficient optimisation stage, where a higher value shrinks the rate term and leaves the encoder less willing to zero out small transform coefficients purely to save bits.

Higher values keep fine detail and grain that would otherwise be filtered or quantised away, in exchange for bits and for more visible blocking and ringing where the deblocker no longer cleans up after the quantiser. Lower values give a cleaner, softer picture. Raise it for detailed live action and stills, lower it for animation, flat gradients or low bitrates.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build, a mild bias towards sharpness.
0|Mainline's neutral behaviour, for animation or low-bitrate encodes that need the deblocker.
3|Detailed live action where deblocking is visibly softening texture.
7|Maximum detail retention, mostly worthwhile on stills and very high fidelity encodes.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1 in this build) - Sharper transform decisions that back up ac-bias; turn off if ac-bias is 0
options.description:
Changes how aggressively the encoder throws away transform coefficients. The coefficient optimisation pass normally weighs each surviving coefficient against the bits it costs and drops the marginal ones; with this enabled that rate term is removed from the luma decision, so coefficients carrying fine detail survive instead of being rounded to zero.

The result is a cleaner, more detailed picture for more bits and a slightly higher chance of artefacting. It exists to reinforce --ac-bias, so leaving it on alongside the default --ac-bias 1.0 is the intended pairing. If you set --ac-bias 0, turn this off too, since you would otherwise keep the extra coefficients with nothing steering which of them matter.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build, and the intended partner for the default --ac-bias 1.0.
0|The recommended companion setting whenever --ac-bias is set to 0.

options.syntaxDescription: 32 or 64 (default 64) - Caps the largest transform size; 32 holds fine texture better but costs efficiency
options.description:
AV1's 64-point transform has its 32 highest-frequency coefficients zeroed out by design, so any block coded with one loses its finest detail before quantisation even starts. Setting 32 stops the encoder considering 64-point transforms at all, and those coefficients survive.

The cost is speed and some efficiency: more, smaller transforms mean more overhead, and on flat or smooth material the 64-point transform was the right call. The gain shows on camera noise, fine film grain and detailed stills, where PSNR and SSIM do not register the blurring being traded away.

Setting 32 also stops the encoder discarding sub-64x64 block depths, so 32x32 transforms are genuinely available to it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
64|The default, and the right call on flat or clean sources where efficiency matters more.
32|Camera noise and fine film grain that 64-point transforms visibly blur.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Alternative SSIM pathway with visual quality tweaks; only does anything when tune is 2
options.description:
Switches the SSIM rate-distortion path onto an alternative per-pixel variance function evaluated across 4x4, 8x8 and 16x16 blocks alongside the existing superblock-level SSIM tuning, and pulls in the visual quality optimisations that tune 0 uses.

The picture leans towards tune 0's sharper, more textured look while the decisions themselves stay SSIM-driven. Reach for it if you already encode with tune 2 and the output keeps coming back softer than you want, and leave it off on clean animation or gradients, where tune 0's extra sharpness tends to surface as artefacts.

It only operates with --tune 2. On any other tune, setting it has no effect at all.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default, leaving tune 2's standard SSIM behaviour in place.
1|Tune 2 encodes of detailed live action that come out softer than intended.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-4 (default 2) - How hard low-contrast superblocks are boosted; 1 for smooth animation, 3 for mixed contrast
options.description:
Variance boost lowers the quantiser on 64x64 superblocks that measure low variance, so flat and delicately textured regions such as skin, cloud, fog and night interiors receive bits a fixed quantiser would have spent on high-contrast edges. This value selects how large that boost grows as measured variance falls.

Stronger curves buy visible detail in those regions but inflate bitrate and can make film grain retention uneven across a shot. Strength 1 suits flat animation, 2 handles most live action, 3 helps sources that swing between very bright and very dark, and 4 is worth it only when low-contrast detail outranks file size.

It does nothing unless variance boost itself is enabled, and it augments adaptive quantisation modes 0 and 2.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|Flat cel animation or screen capture with little texture.
2|The default; live action and animation with detailed texture.
3|Horror and thriller material mixing very dark and very bright scenes.
4|Archival work where low-contrast detail outranks file size.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-8 (default 5) - How much of a superblock must be low-contrast to boost it; higher is stricter, 4-7 advised
options.description:
Where strength decides how hard a superblock is boosted, the octile decides how many superblocks qualify. Each 64x64 superblock is split into 8x8 subblocks, their variances are ranked, and this value picks the point in that ranking which judges the block. At 1 an eighth of the block being low-contrast is enough to boost it; at 8 essentially all of it must be.

Low values spill bits onto high-contrast areas that did not need them and inflate size. High values are stingier and can leave visibly poorer patches inside blocks that are only partly flat. Four to seven is the useful span: move down when detail is lost inside busy frames, up when bitrate climbs without a visible return.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|Busy or grainy footage where flat patches hide inside detailed blocks.
4|Slightly broader boosting than default for mixed-contrast live action.
5|The default; balanced selectivity for most sources.
7|Tighter selectivity when bitrate climbs without visible gain.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Boost curve shape; 1 alternative, 2 still image, 3 for PQ HDR and is forced on PQ sources
options.description:
Selects the formula that converts a superblock's measured variance into a quantiser offset. The curves differ in where boosting starts and how steeply the offset grows, so they change both how bits are distributed and how the result looks. Curves 0 and 1 treat variance below 256 as low; curve 2 raises that threshold to 1024 and so boosts a far larger share of the frame.

Curve 0 is the general-purpose choice and curve 1 shifts the tradeoff without changing the aim. Curve 2 is built for still images and spends noticeably more on flat regions. Curve 3 is shaped for the PQ transfer, where code values sit quite differently from SDR and the other curves misjudge what counts as low contrast.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; general-purpose curve for SDR video.
1|An alternative allocation when curve 0 looks too soft or too costly.
2|Still images and single-frame encodes.
3|HDR sources using the PQ transfer function.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-8.0 (default 1.0) - Evens quality across temporal layers; raise for consistency, over 3.0 is extreme
options.description:
Within a mini-GOP the encoder normally spreads quantisers widely across temporal layers, giving reference frames much lower quantisers than the frames that depend on them. This setting squeezes that spread, so quality varies less from keyframe to leaf frame.

Consistency is bought from average quality: with the layers pulled together, reference frames are relatively less clean and predict less well for their children, so mean scores usually fall even as frame-to-frame variation does. Raise it when pulsing between frame types is what you notice, and set 0.0 for mainline behaviour when chasing metric scores.

At very low CRF the compression can improve fidelity outright rather than trade it. Above 3.0 the encoder warns that the value sits outside the range found generally useful.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0.0|Mainline SVT-AV1 behaviour; maximises average metric scores.
1.0|The default; a consistency gain at almost no cost.
2.0|High-quality encodes where holding the layers together matters more.
3.0|Very low CRF or maximum-fidelity work, where it can also aid fidelity.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 0) - Shifts QP by average frame luminance, spending more bits on dark scenes prone to banding
options.description:
Shifts a frame's quantiser according to the average luma of that frame, so dark scenes are coded finer than their measured complexity alone would earn. Dark footage is cheap to code and cheap frames get starved, which is why banding and blocking surface first in night exteriors and shadowed interiors. This value scales how far that shift goes, and 0 disables it.

Bits moved into dark frames come out of the rest of the encode, so on mostly bright material the setting costs size for nothing. It earns its keep on sources with long dark stretches: night cinematography, horror, concert and stage footage, and anything heavily graded down.

The decision is made per frame from a whole-frame average, so a dark object inside a bright frame is not affected.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no luminance-based adjustment.
25|A light lift for material with occasional night scenes.
50|Sustained dark cinematography where shadows band.
100|Maximum bias for very dark sources where shadow detail is the priority.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 8 in this build) - Floor on chroma quantisation matrix flatness; raise to protect chroma when starved
options.description:
Quantisation matrices weight coefficients by frequency instead of quantising them all alike, and this sets the lowest, least flat level the encoder may pick for the chroma planes. Level 15 is fully flat, so lower numbers mean stronger shaping: more fine chroma detail is discarded and the encode gets smaller.

The encoder chooses a level per frame by mapping that frame's quantiser into the span between this floor and chroma-qm-max, so lowering the floor widens how aggressive it is allowed to become. Drop it when chroma consumes bitrate you would rather give to luma; raise it towards 15 on saturated or heavily graded material where colour smearing shows first.

It requires quantisation matrices enabled, and must not exceed chroma-qm-max.
options.listedValuesDescription:
4|Aggressive chroma shaping for bitrate-constrained streaming encodes.
8|The default; the chroma floor this build ships with.
10|Gentler shaping for saturated or heavily graded sources.
15|Pins chroma matrices fully flat, with no frequency shaping on colour.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 15) - Ceiling on chroma quantisation matrix flatness; 15 leaves chroma unshaped at high bitrates
options.description:
The ceiling of the same chroma range: the flattest matrix the encoder may pick. At the default of 15 it can fall back to a fully flat matrix, leaving chroma coefficients unweighted at that end of the range.

Pulling this down forces some frequency shaping on chroma at all times rather than merely permitting it, which trims bitrate but caps how much fine colour detail can survive anywhere in the encode. It is the blunter of the two controls, so reach for it when you want a guaranteed chroma saving instead of a wider span for the encoder to work within.

It requires quantisation matrices enabled, and must be at least chroma-qm-min.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|Forces shaping on chroma throughout for a firm bitrate saving.
10|A moderate ceiling that still leaves most chroma detail intact.
12|A light trim for sources with noisy or oversampled chroma.
15|The default; permits fully flat chroma matrices.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 0, follows the preset) - 1 runs mode decision fully at 10-bit, 2 hybrid; needs a 10-bit input
options.description:
Mode decision is where the encoder tries candidate partitions and predictions and scores them. This chooses the precision that search runs at: 0 leaves it to the preset, 1 runs it fully at 10-bit, and 2 uses a hybrid of 8-bit and 10-bit. Searching at 10-bit stops the scoring rounding away differences the final coding pass can represent.

The cost is speed. High bit depth mode decision also disables the lightweight decision paths that fast presets lean on, so it is a genuine slowdown exactly where the preset would otherwise have declined it. This build already runs 10-bit mode decision through preset 5 and tapers it off above, so forcing it mainly matters from preset 6 upward.

It only has an effect on a 10-bit encode; with 8-bit input the encoder ignores it and follows the preset.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the preset decides, which means full 10-bit through preset 5.
1|Full 10-bit mode decision, the useful setting on fast 10-bit presets.
2|Hybrid 8/10-bit, recovering part of the gain for less of the slowdown.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Quantisation matrices, which the qm-min, qm-max and chroma-qm settings all depend on
options.description:
Enables quantisation matrices, which weight quantisation by frequency instead of applying one step size across the whole transform block. That lets fine texture and grain be preserved or discarded independently of the underlying structure.

This is the switch the whole matrix family hangs off: qm-min, qm-max, chroma-qm-min and chroma-qm-max all have no effect while it is 0.

It is on by default in this build, so those settings work out of the box; turning it off reverts to uniform quantisation.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build; matrices enabled.
0|Uniform quantisation, disabling the qm-min, qm-max and chroma-qm settings.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 6) - Lowest luma quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1
options.description:
The lowest matrix flatness the encoder may select for luma, where lower numbers mean a more aggressively shaped matrix that treats high frequencies very differently from low ones.

Allowing a lower floor lets the encoder shape quantisation harder where that helps, keeping fine texture that flat quantisation would round away. It is the luma counterpart to chroma-qm-min, and it is the more impactful of the two, since luma carries most of the detail.

It requires enable-qm 1 and must not exceed qm-max.
options.listedValuesDescription:
6|The default in this build.
8|A narrower, more conservative range.
2|Allows aggressive shaping, retaining more fine texture.
0|The most aggressive shaping available.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 10) - Highest luma quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1
options.description:
The upper end of the luma matrix range. Level 15 is effectively unshaped, so a high maximum lets the encoder fall back to ordinary flat quantisation wherever shaping would not help.

Lowering it forces shaping to be applied more consistently, which holds onto texture across the whole encode at some cost in efficiency.

It requires enable-qm 1 and must not fall below qm-min.
options.listedValuesDescription:
10|The default in this build.
15|Allows a fully unshaped matrix, as mainline defaults to.
8|Forces consistent shaping, at a cost in efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 0) - The best quantiser allowed; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, capping how many bits any one frame may receive. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody would notice, which shrinks the file without touching the material that actually needs bits.

It must not exceed max-qp, and in constant quality encoding it only bites when the target sits below it.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
15|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
20|A firmer cap for constrained delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 63) - The worst quantiser allowed; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality may fall when the encoder runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the smearing and blocking difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates, at the cost of the encoder no longer being able to meet a bitrate target there - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

It must not fall below min-qp.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
63|The default; no ceiling.
50|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
40|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: -63 to 63 (default 0) - Shifts the quantiser for the opening GOP, before the usual per-picture derivation
options.description:
Adds an offset to the sequence quantiser for the start-up group of pictures, before the per-picture quantiser is worked out. It exists because the opening of a sequence has no history behind it, so the encoder's estimates there are at their least informed.

A negative offset spends extra bits at the start, which gives everything predicting from those first frames a cleaner foundation and avoids the softness some encodes show for the first second.

That matters more than usual when a video is cut into chunks, since every chunk has its own start-up.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no offset.
-4|Extra quality at the opening, for a cleaner foundation.
-8|A strong start-up boost.
4|Fewer bits at the start, if the opening is unimportant.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Deblocking loop filter; 2 is a slower, more accurate variant, 0 leaves block edges in place
options.description:
The deblocking loop filter smooths the edges between coded blocks before a frame is stored as a reference, so block boundaries do not persist and propagate into everything predicting from it. Mode 2 is a slower, more accurate variant of the same filter.

Leaving it on is right for almost all encoding. The artefact it removes is the most recognisable failure mode of a block-based codec, and because the filtered frame is what later frames predict from, the benefit compounds.

Grain-preservation setups occasionally turn it off at very high bitrates, where there is little blocking to remove and the filter costs fine detail.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; the standard filter.
2|The slower, more accurate variant for quality-focused encodes.
0|Off; only sensible at very high bitrates, for grain retention.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Temporal filtering of alt-ref frames; 2 varies it adaptively, 0 keeps grain and motion detail
options.description:
Temporal filtering builds alternate reference frames by blending several source frames together. The blend cancels noise, producing a clean frame that predicts unusually well, which is a substantial part of where AV1's efficiency comes from.

The cost is that grain and fine motion detail are averaged away in the reference, and everything predicting from it inherits the smoothing. Mode 2 varies the filtering adaptively rather than applying it uniformly.

Turning it off is a common move in grain-preserving setups, particularly alongside a raised ac-bias, and it costs bitrate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; standard temporal filtering.
2|Adaptive filtering, varying by content.
0|Off, for maximum grain and motion detail retention.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 1) - Temporal filtering strength; lower keeps grain and fine motion, higher denoises and saves bits
options.description:
How hard the temporal filter blends when it constructs an alternate reference. Where enable-tf decides whether filtering happens at all, this decides how much of each contributing frame survives.

Lower values keep grain and fine motion detail in the reference, at the cost of a noisier reference that predicts less efficiently. Higher values denoise more thoroughly and save bits, flattening texture as they go.

It is the finer control of the two, and worth reaching for before disabling temporal filtering outright.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build.
0|The weakest setting, keeping the most grain.
2|A middle ground between grain retention and efficiency.
4|The strongest denoising, for genuinely noisy sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 1, 4x weaker than mainline) - Temporal filtering on keyframes only; lower keeps keyframe grain
options.description:
The same temporal filtering strength control as tf-strength, applied only to keyframes. Keyframes are filtered separately because they anchor everything until the next one, so a clean keyframe pays off across the whole interval.

Because a keyframe is displayed as well as referenced, filtering it too hard is visible directly: the picture softens at the cut and then sharpens as later frames add detail back, which reads as a pulse at every keyframe.

This build already applies markedly weaker keyframe filtering than mainline, so the default is a conservative setting rather than a neutral one.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build, already gentler than mainline.
0|No keyframe filtering, for maximum grain retention at cuts.
2|Cleaner keyframes, at the cost of a visible softening at each one.
4|The strongest; only for noisy sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 2) - Backs CDEF and restoration off where the source is noisy; 3 CDEF only, 4 restoration only
options.description:
Measures how noisy the source is and backs off the in-loop filters where it finds grain, on the basis that CDEF and loop restoration cannot tell fine noise from the ringing they exist to remove.

Without it, a grainy source has its grain steadily filtered out of the reference frames, and the encode ends up smoother than intended no matter what the psychovisual settings ask for. Modes 3 and 4 apply the backing-off to CDEF or to restoration alone, rather than both.

It is enabled by default in this build and is one of the settings that makes grain retention practical without disabling the filters entirely.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default in this build.
0|Off; the filters run at full strength regardless of noise.
3|Applies only to CDEF, leaving restoration alone.
4|Applies only to loop restoration.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-30 (default 15, meaning 1x) - Scales CDEF strength; lower sharpens and keeps grain, higher smooths ringing
options.description:
Scales the strength CDEF applies. CDEF is the directional filter that removes ringing along edges by filtering along the edge direction rather than across it; the scale here multiplies how hard it works, with 15 meaning normal strength.

Lower values filter less, keeping grain and fine texture that CDEF would otherwise take with the ringing, and leaving more ringing behind. Higher values smooth harder, which helps at low bitrates where ringing is the dominant artefact.

Dropping it is a gentler alternative to turning CDEF off outright.
options.listedValuesDescription:
15|The default, meaning normal CDEF strength.
8|Roughly half strength, keeping more grain and texture.
1|The minimum; almost no CDEF, for high-bitrate grain retention.
30|Double strength, for low bitrates where ringing dominates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - The constrained directional enhancement filter, which removes ringing along edges
options.description:
CDEF is an in-loop filter that removes ringing by filtering along the direction of an edge rather than across it, so it cleans up the halo around high-contrast detail without smearing the edge itself.

Leaving it on is right for normal encoding: the filtered frame is what later frames predict from, so ringing left in place propagates.

Grain-preserving setups sometimes turn it off because it takes fine noise along with the ringing, but that only makes sense at bitrates high enough that there is little ringing to remove. cdef-scaling is the gentler alternative.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Off, for grain retention at high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - The loop restoration filter, which repairs coding error after deblocking and CDEF
options.description:
Loop restoration runs after deblocking and CDEF, fitting a correction per region to bring the reconstruction back towards the source. It repairs the general coding error the earlier filters leave behind.

It is on by default and worth keeping for normal encoding, since the repaired frame is what everything afterwards predicts from.

Like CDEF it cannot distinguish fine noise from artefacts, so grain-preserving setups sometimes disable it - and noise-adaptive-filtering exists precisely to back it off on noisy sources without turning it off outright.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Off, for maximum grain retention at high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-200 (default 0) - Synthesises grain at this strength, 50 is about film-grain 50; masks banding on flat gradients
options.description:
Synthesises film grain rather than coding it. Real grain is close to random, so it compresses appallingly badly - a grainy source can spend most of its bitrate reproducing noise. Instead the encoder writes a parameter set and the decoder generates matching grain at playback, for almost no bits at all.

The trade is that the grain is statistically similar rather than identical, and it is applied after decoding, so it is not part of the picture anything else can act on.

It is also a practical fix for banding: grain on a flat gradient dithers the steps and hides them.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no synthesis.
50|Moderate grain, comparable to a film-grain 50 setting.
25|A light texture, useful mainly to break up banding.
100|Heavy grain, for matching a visibly grainy film scan.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 200 (default -1) - Chroma grain strength; -1 tracks about 60% of --noise, set it directly for film scans
options.description:
The strength of synthesised grain in the colour planes, separate from the luma strength set by noise. Left at -1 it follows the luma setting at roughly sixty percent, which suits most material.

Real film grain is not evenly distributed between luma and chroma: colour negative stocks carry visible chroma grain, while digital noise is often mostly luma. Setting this directly is how you match a particular look rather than accepting the ratio.

Setting it to 0 gives grain in luma only, which reads as clean and slightly digital.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; tracks about 60% of the luma strength.
0|Luma grain only, for a cleaner digital look.
30|Explicit chroma grain, for matching a colour film scan.
50|Strong chroma grain, matching heavily grained stock.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Derives chroma grain from the luma plane, which also puts colour grain on greyscale shots
options.description:
Derives the chroma grain pattern from the luma plane rather than generating it independently, so the colour grain follows the same structure as the brightness grain.

That correlation is closer to how some film stocks behave and can look more natural on colour material.

It has one consequence worth knowing: because the chroma grain is derived from luma rather than from the chroma content, greyscale and desaturated shots get colour grain applied to them, which appears as faint coloured speckle in a picture that should have none.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; chroma grain generated independently.
1|Chroma derived from luma; more natural on colour, speckles greyscale shots.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 13 (default -1) - Grain particle size; -1 picks one from the resolution, higher looks coarser and softer
options.description:
The size of the synthesised grain particles. Grain size is a property of the film stock and the format it was shot on: 16mm grain is large and obvious, 35mm finer, and a digital sensor's noise finer still.

Left at -1 the encoder picks a size from the resolution, which is a reasonable guess and gets the scale roughly right for most material.

Larger values produce coarser, more visible grain that also reads as slightly softer, because bigger particles obscure more of the detail underneath. Setting it explicitly is how you match a specific source rather than accept the guess.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; size chosen from the resolution.
8|Fine grain, suiting 35mm and high resolution digital.
11|Coarser grain, closer to 16mm.
13|The maximum; large, very visible particles.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 1) - Lifts AC coefficients in finely textured areas; raise to hold onto grain and fine detail
options.description:
Lifts the AC transform coefficients in finely textured areas, countering the tendency of quantisation to round small coefficients to zero and flatten texture into patches.

Where grain synthesis replaces noise wholesale, this preserves the real texture that is already there, so the two solve related problems by opposite means and can be used together.

Raising it holds onto grain and fine detail at some bitrate cost. It is one of this build's own additions and has no mainline equivalent.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build.
0|Off; standard coefficient handling.
2|Stronger texture retention on detailed sources.
4|The maximum, for heavily grained film at a real bitrate cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Scales the grain synthesis block size with resolution; 0 pins it to 32x32 at every size
options.description:
Scales the block size that grain synthesis is applied over with the resolution of the video, so grain on a 4K encode is generated over larger blocks than on a 720p one and ends up looking like the same grain viewed at the same physical size.

Pinned off, synthesis always uses 32x32 blocks regardless of resolution, which makes the grain look progressively finer as resolution rises - the same pattern spread over more pixels.

It is on by default and is generally what you want unless you are matching a reference that was made without it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; block size scales with resolution.
0|Fixed 32x32 blocks at every resolution.

options.syntaxDescription: Path to a pre-generated film grain table applied instead of analysing the source for grain
options.description:
Applies a pre-generated film grain table instead of having the encoder analyse the source and derive grain parameters itself. The file describes the grain to synthesise, and can vary it over the course of the video rather than applying one description throughout.

Tables are produced by tools such as grav1synth, which analyses a source and writes out what it measured. That is the way to match the grain of a specific scan precisely, and to keep it consistent across an encode split into several parts.

The table replaces the noise settings rather than adding to them.
options.listedValuesDescription:
/path/to/grain.tbl|A table generated from the source by grav1synth.
C:\\encodes\\film_grain.tbl|A Windows path; quote it if it contains spaces.
/mnt/media/scan_grain.tbl|A table shared across parts of a split encode, for consistent grain.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 2) - Screen content detection level, enabling palette and intra block copy for synthetic material
options.description:
Controls the screen content coding tools - palette mode and intra block copy - which code large flat colour areas and repeated on-screen elements far more cheaply than ordinary prediction. The difference on a desktop capture, a slide deck or a game UI is large.

The default detects screen content and enables the tools when it finds it, which is usually right. Forcing them on helps when detection misses obviously synthetic material; forcing them off saves the analysis on footage that is plainly camera-shot.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default; detect screen content and enable the tools when found.
1|Force the tools on, for material detection is missing.
0|Force them off, for ordinary camera footage.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 0) - Avoids the tools that are most expensive to decode, for playback on weak hardware
options.description:
Steers the encoder away from the coding tools that cost a decoder the most, producing a stream that plays back on hardware which would otherwise stutter. AV1 software decoding is demanding, and this is the setting that makes the difference on older machines.

The cost is compression: the tools being avoided are there because they help, so the same quality takes more bits.

Only worth setting when you know the target struggles, since it gives up efficiency for a benefit nothing else will show.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no decoder-cost restrictions.
1|A moderate reduction in decoding cost.
2|The strongest reduction, at a real compression cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Inserts overlay pictures as extra references for base-layer frames
options.description:
Allows the encoder to insert overlay pictures, which act as additional reference frames for base layer pictures. They give the prediction stage another, better-matched frame to work from at the points where the reference structure is weakest.

The gain is a modest compression improvement on content with steady motion, and the cost is encoding time and a slightly more complex reference structure.

It is off by default and is one of the cheaper quality options to try on an offline encode.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Enables overlay pictures, a small gain on steady motion.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-120 (blank lets the encoder choose) - Frames looked ahead beyond the minigop, filtering and rate control
options.description:
How far ahead the encoder looks beyond what the mini-GOP structure, temporal filtering and rate control already require. Lookahead is what lets it place references well and distribute bits across a scene rather than reacting frame by frame.

Left blank the encoder picks a depth from the other settings, which is a sensible choice in most cases. Setting it explicitly is a way to buy better bit distribution at the cost of memory and latency, or to cut both for low-delay use.

Beyond the length of a typical shot there is nothing further to learn.

The encoder advertises -1 as the automatic setting in its own --help, and its own parser then refuses it, answering "Invalid parameter 'lookahead' with value '-1'" and writing no stream. Automatic is reached by leaving this row empty, never by typing -1. Measured, 0, 1, 60 and 120 all encode and 121 is correctly refused.
options.listedValuesDescription:
120|The maximum; the most information for rate control.
60|A generous fixed depth for offline encoding.
0|No additional lookahead, for low delay.

options.syntaxDescription: Path to a Dolby Vision RPU file to attach; needs a libdovi-enabled build and an RPU matching the source
options.description:
Points the encoder at a binary Dolby Vision RPU file. Its per-frame metadata is attached to each picture as an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU, carrying the shot-by-shot tone mapping into the AV1 bitstream, so a Dolby Vision display gets dynamic mapping rather than static HDR10 values.

The file is produced by dovi_tool extract-rpu from the original Dolby Vision HEVC source, which writes RPU.bin by default. Profile 7 dual-layer sources must be converted to single-layer profile 8.1 first with dovi_tool's -m 2, as AV1 carries only single-layer Dolby Vision.

Metadata is matched to pictures by position, so the RPU must cover exactly the frames being encoded, in order; a trim or frame rate change desynchronises it, and frames past its end get no metadata. The encoder must also be built with libdovi.
options.listedValuesDescription:
/path/to/RPU.bin|The default output name written by dovi_tool extract-rpu.
/media/uhd/movie/RPU_p81.bin|A profile 7 RPU already converted to single-layer 8.1 with dovi_tool -m 2.
C:\Encodes\show_s01e01_rpu.bin|A per-episode RPU extracted from and kept beside its own source file.

options.syntaxDescription: Path to an HDR10+ metadata JSON file to attach; needs a libhdr10plus-enabled build and per-frame metadata
options.description:
Points the encoder at an HDR10+ metadata JSON file. Each frame's dynamic tone-mapping window data is parsed out and attached to the matching picture as an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU, so displays get per-scene tone mapping layered on top of the static HDR10 mastering data.

The file comes from hdr10plus_tool extract run over the original HDR10+ source, and is plain JSON with one entry per frame, so it can be read and edited before encoding. It only means anything for a PQ HDR source that carried HDR10+ to begin with; it will not manufacture dynamic metadata for a plain HDR10 master.

The JSON is applied by frame position, so it has to line up with exactly the frames being encoded; trimming or changing the frame rate desynchronises it. The encoder must also be built with hdr10plus support.
options.listedValuesDescription:
/path/to/metadata.json|The conventional output name from hdr10plus_tool extract.
/media/uhd/movie/hdr10plus_metadata.json|Metadata extracted from the source and kept alongside it.
C:\Encodes\movie_hdr10plus_edited.json|An extracted JSON hand-edited to adjust its per-scene windows before encoding.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - The encoder's most expensive perceptual model, weighing detail the way an eye does rather than the way an error metric does
options.description:
Switches the encoder's human-visual-system model to its highest complexity setting. The model is what decides how much a given distortion actually matters to a viewer, so a more careful one spends bits nearer where they are seen and less where they are not - most visibly on texture and on the busy areas a plain error metric treats as cheap.

It costs encoding time and nothing else, and the gain is small and content-dependent, which is why it is off by default.

Tune 5 sets this to 1 for itself, and does so after the whole command line has been parsed, so a 0 typed here is overwritten rather than respected. That is the one case worth knowing about: it is not a collision the encoder reports anywhere you can see.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default, and the right answer unless encoding time is cheap.
1|Slow, high-fidelity encodes where the extra time is affordable. Tune 5 sets this anyway.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1 in this build) - The switch for the variance boost family; turn it off to encode flat and dark areas at the quantiser they were given
options.description:
Variance boost lowers the quantiser on low-variance blocks - flat gradients, skies, dark scenes - where banding and blocking show first and where a plain rate-distortion decision happily spends nothing. This is the switch for the whole mechanism; variance-boost-strength, variance-octile and variance-boost-curve shape it and do nothing at all with this off.

This build ships it on, where mainline SVT-AV1 defaults it off - so a preset or a parameter written for one is not describing the other.

Turning it off is a deliberate choice for content with no flat areas worth protecting, or for a comparison against an encoder that does not have it. For ordinary video, leaving it on is what keeps skies and fades clean.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default in this build, and what the three shaping parameters need to mean anything.
0|Disables the whole family, for comparisons or content with nothing flat to protect.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr or ssim (default psnr) - Metric the encoder optimises for; ssim scales RD per block and often looks better
options.description:
Selects the distortion metric the encoder optimises its decisions against. psnr minimises squared error; ssim weights decisions by structural similarity, which changes rate-distortion scaling per block.

ssim generally produces a picture people prefer, because it spends bits on structure rather than on wherever squared error happens to be largest, and it usually scores better on perceptual metrics too.

Neither is a psychovisual setting in the sense x264's psy-rd is; VP9 has no equivalent, which is part of why its output tends to look softer than a comparable x264 encode.
options.listedValuesDescription:
psnr|The default; minimises squared error.
ssim|Structure-weighted decisions; usually the better-looking choice.

options.syntaxDescription: default, screen or film (default default) - Content hint; screen suits desktop capture, film retains grain
options.description:
Tells the encoder what kind of material it is coding. screen enables tools for desktop capture and UI recordings, where large flat areas and repeated elements code far more cheaply with the right prediction modes.

film adjusts the encoder's behaviour to retain grain rather than filtering it away. Note this is not the same as the option of the same name in aomenc, which synthesises grain at the decoder - VP9 has no grain synthesis, so here it genuinely means keeping more of the noise that is there.

default suits ordinary camera footage.
options.listedValuesDescription:
default|Ordinary live action and animation.
screen|Desktop capture, slides and UI recordings.
film|Grainy sources, retaining noise rather than smoothing it.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-7 (default 0) - Keeps fine detail by curbing coefficient and skip optimisation, costing PSNR and bitrate
options.description:
Trades measurable accuracy for a sharper-looking picture by curbing the optimisations that quietly smooth the result - the coefficient decisions and skip choices that drop small amounts of detail because they are cheap to lose.

Higher values keep more of that fine detail and cost both PSNR and bitrate. The effect is subtle compared with the equivalent controls in x264 and x265.

It also feeds the loop filter level, so raising it reduces deblocking as well.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no bias.
2|A mild sharpening for detailed live action.
5|Strong detail retention, at a real bitrate cost.
7|The maximum.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or higher (default 0 off) - Codes low-motion blocks as skip below this distortion; speeds up real-time
options.description:
Sets a distortion threshold below which a block is simply coded as skipped rather than searched and coded properly. Anything changing less than the threshold between frames is treated as not changing at all.

The point is speed, and the setting is aimed at real-time encoding of largely static content such as screen sharing, where most of the frame genuinely is identical.

Above 0 it will discard real low-amplitude change, including film grain and subtle gradients in motion, so it is a poor fit for offline quality encoding.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off, and the right setting for quality encoding.
100|Light skipping for real-time screen content.
1000|Aggressive skipping; visible on anything but static material.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Allows periodic frame-level Q boosts, spending bits where they help most on calm content
options.description:
Allows the rate controller to periodically raise the quality of individual frames, spending extra bits where doing so improves the frames that predict from them.

The gain comes from better references rather than from the boosted frames themselves, so it shows up most on calm content with long stretches of similar material.

It is off by default and interacts with the rate control mode in use.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Enables periodic frame boosts, useful on calm content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 0, off) - Temporal denoising before encoding, given as the number of frames blurred together
options.description:
Applies a temporal denoiser ahead of encoding, blending across the number of frames given. Noise is close to random and therefore very expensive to code, so removing it before the encoder sees it can save a great deal of bitrate on a noisy source.

The filter cannot tell sensor noise from fine texture or slight motion, so it removes both, and blending across more frames risks ghosting where anything moves.

Only worth using on genuinely noisy footage such as low-light video. For film grain you want to keep, leave it off.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no denoising.
1|The lightest setting, blending a single frame.
3|Moderate denoising for noisy low-light footage.
6|The maximum; strong, with a real risk of ghosting.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 1) - Alt reference frames; 2 and above enables multi-layer ARF, usually a quality gain
options.description:
Alternate reference frames are synthetic frames the encoder builds by filtering several source frames together. They are never displayed; other frames predict from them, and because they are denoised they predict very well, which is one of VP9's larger compression wins.

Values above 1 enable multi-layer alt-refs, letting the encoder maintain several at different temporal distances so both slow and fast motion have a good reference available.

More layers need lag-in-frames to hold enough frames to build them, so raising this without lookahead achieves nothing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; a single alt-ref layer.
6|The maximum; multi-layer, the usual choice for offline quality.
4|Multi-layer with less encoding cost than the maximum.
0|Disabled; a clear compression loss.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-25 (default 25) - Lookahead depth; more improves alt-ref placement, 0 gives low delay at a quality cost
options.description:
How many frames the encoder buffers before committing decisions, which sets how far ahead it can see. Lookahead is what makes alt-ref frames possible - the encoder needs the frames in hand to filter them together - and it also drives frame type and bit allocation choices.

Lowering it costs compression directly, and dropping it far enough disables alt-refs, taking one of VP9's main advantages with them.

Set it to 0 only for genuinely low-delay use; the cost is memory and latency, not encoding speed.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default and the maximum; the right setting for offline encoding.
16|Reduced buffering where memory is constrained.
0|Low delay, giving up alt-ref frames and a lot of efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 7) - Frames blended by the alt-ref temporal filter; lower keeps grain, higher denoises more
options.description:
How many neighbouring frames the alt-ref filter blends together when constructing an alternate reference. The blending is what removes noise and makes the alt-ref such a good prediction source.

More frames give a cleaner reference and better compression, and average away more grain and fine motion detail in the process. Fewer keep the noise but predict less well.

Grain-preserving setups lower this; noisy sources benefit from raising it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
7|The default.
3|Keeps more grain and fine motion detail.
0|Disables the filtering entirely.
15|The maximum; cleanest references, softest detail.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 5) - Alt-ref filter strength; drop to 1-2 to preserve film grain, raise for noisy sources
options.description:
How aggressively the alt-ref filter blends the frames it has gathered. Where arnr-maxframes sets how many frames take part, this sets how much of each survives the blend.

Dropping it to 1 or 2 is the usual move on grainy film, keeping noise that would otherwise be averaged out of the reference and therefore out of everything predicting from it. Raising it suits genuinely noisy footage, where the noise is not worth preserving and removing it saves bits.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default.
2|Grainy film, preserving noise and texture.
0|No filtering; maximum grain retention.
6|The maximum, for noisy low-light footage.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Extra adaptive quantisation on alt-ref frames; skipped at low bitrates where it costs more
options.description:
Applies additional adaptive quantisation specifically to alternate reference frames, spending extra bits on the parts of an alt-ref that other frames will lean on most.

Because everything predicting from an alt-ref inherits its quality, improving one frame can improve many. The catch is that alt-refs are already given a quality boost, and at low bitrates the extra spending comes straight out of the displayed frames.

Worth trying at higher bitrates; likely a loss at low ones.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Extra AQ on alt-ref frames, best at generous bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Frame parallel decodability; 0 allows backward probability updates and compresses better
options.description:
Controls whether the stream is coded so a decoder can work on several frames at once. Frame-parallel mode requires disabling backward probability updates, where the encoder refines its entropy model using statistics gathered from the frame it just coded.

Those backward updates are worth a small but real amount of compression, so turning frame-parallel decoding off makes the file smaller at the same quality.

Leave it on only if the target decoder needs the parallelism; for file encoding, 0 is the better setting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; parallel-decodable, slightly larger files.
0|Allows backward probability updates; better compression.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 0 off) - Adaptive quantisation: 1 variance, 2 complexity, 3 cyclic refresh, 4 equator360
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation redistributes bits within a frame. Mode 1 distributes by variance, moving bits from busy areas where error is masked to flat ones where banding shows. Mode 2 works from complexity. Mode 3 is cyclic refresh, which refreshes part of each frame in turn and targets low-bitrate streaming. Mode 4 is tuned for equirectangular 360 video, where the poles are massively oversampled and do not deserve equal bits.

It is off by default. Mode 1 is the one to try on sources that band; the others are situational.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Variance-based, the usual choice if flat areas band.
2|Complexity-based distribution.
3|Cyclic refresh, for low-bitrate streaming.
4|Equirectangular 360 video.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 0) - Best quantiser allowed; raise it to stop easy scenes from soaking up bitrate
options.description:
The best quantiser the rate controller may choose, which is a floor on how many bits it will spend on any one frame. A lower number means higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes soaking up bitrate they do not need - a static shot encoded at a very low quantiser can consume a surprising share of a target - which leaves more for the difficult material in a rate-targeted encode.

In constant-quality encoding it does nothing unless the target sits below it.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
15|Stops easy scenes from spending more than they need.
20|A tighter floor for bitrate-constrained delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 63) - Worst quantiser allowed; lower it to keep hard scenes from collapsing in VBR encodes
options.description:
The worst quantiser the rate controller may choose, bounding how far quality may fall on difficult material. A higher number is lower quality.

Lowering it stops hard scenes collapsing into blocking when the rate controller runs short of bits. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer meet its bitrate target on those scenes and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

Set it when a minimum acceptable quality matters more than hitting the target exactly.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
63|The default; no ceiling on quantiser.
50|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
40|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Temporal dependency model; improves bit allocation between frames, disable only to save time
options.description:
The temporal dependency model looks ahead to work out which blocks later frames will predict from, then spends bits on those blocks in proportion to how much depends on them. A block that fifty later frames refer to is worth more than one that is never referenced again.

This is one of the larger quality-per-bit wins available in VP9 and it is on by default. Disabling it only makes sense to save encoding time.

It needs lookahead to work, so lowering lag-in-frames weakens it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on.
0|Disables the model to save encoding time, at a real quality cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-10000 (default 0 off) - Corpus VBR complexity midpoint; holds quality steady across a library of clips
options.description:
Sets a fixed complexity midpoint for corpus VBR, a rate control mode intended for encoding a whole library of clips to a consistent quality rather than each clip to its own target.

Normally the encoder judges difficulty relative to the clip in front of it, so an easy clip and a hard one both end up looking average. Giving a shared midpoint across the library means an easy clip is allowed to come out small and good, and a hard one to spend more.

Only meaningful when the same value is used across a set; 0 disables it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; ordinary per-clip rate control.
1000|A shared midpoint across a library of mostly easy content.
3000|A higher midpoint for a more demanding corpus.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far under target rate a section may run; higher lets easy scenes save more bits
options.description:
How far below the target rate the encoder is allowed to run over a section, as a percentage. It gives the rate controller permission to spend less than the target where the content does not need it.

Raising it lets easy passages come in well under target and bank the difference, which suits a varied source where some scenes genuinely need very little.
