Lowering it forces the encoder to keep pace with the target even when there is nothing to spend bits on, which mostly wastes them.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Lets easy scenes save considerably more.
100|Maximum freedom to undershoot.
0|Holds the rate at target regardless of content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far over target rate a section may run; higher lets hard scenes spend more bits
options.description:
How far above the target rate the encoder is allowed to run over a section, as a percentage. It is the permission a difficult scene needs to spend beyond its share rather than degrade.

Raising it protects hard scenes at the cost of a less predictable size and a higher peak rate, which matters if the result has to fit a buffer or a delivery constraint.

Lowering it holds the rate down and lets quality drop on the material that most needs bits.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Gives difficult scenes more room to spend.
0|Holds hard to the target, at a visible cost on hard scenes.
100|Maximum freedom to overshoot.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 50) - Where rate control sits between constant bitrate at 0 and full variable bitrate at 100
options.description:
Positions the rate controller between constant and variable bitrate behaviour. At 0 it holds the rate steady regardless of what the content needs, which is what a fixed-bandwidth channel requires. At 100 it lets the rate follow the difficulty of the material freely.

Higher values give hard scenes the bits they need and let easy ones come in small, which is what you want for a file. Lower values keep the rate predictable, which is what you want for a live stream.

It applies to rate-targeted encoding rather than constant quality.
options.listedValuesDescription:
50|The default; a balance between the two.
100|Full variable bitrate; quality-led, size follows content.
0|Constant bitrate behaviour, for fixed-bandwidth delivery.
75|Leans towards variable while keeping some restraint.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 0) - Floor on what a GOP may spend, as a percentage of the target rate
options.description:
Sets the least a group of pictures may be given, expressed as a percentage of the target bitrate. It stops the rate controller starving a stretch of video that it judges easy.

Raising it guarantees a minimum spend everywhere, which helps when the controller is being too pessimistic about apparently simple content - flat animation and slow scenes are often judged easier than they look.

It works with maxsection-pct to bracket how far the rate may swing between sections.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
40|Guarantees each section a reasonable minimum spend.
60|A tight floor, keeping the rate more even.

options.syntaxDescription: Percentage of target, 0 for unlimited (default 2000) - Ceiling on what a GOP may spend
options.description:
Sets the most a group of pictures may be given, as a percentage of the target bitrate. It caps how far a difficult stretch may run above its share.

Lowering it holds the peak rate down, which matters for streaming and for hardware with a fixed input rate, at the cost of quality on exactly the scenes that most need bits. Raising it lets hard scenes spend freely and makes the local bitrate less predictable.

It works with minsection-pct to bracket the swing between sections.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2000|The default; a generous ceiling.
400|A firm cap, keeping the peak rate down for streaming.
800|A moderate cap.
0|Unlimited.

options.syntaxDescription: film, animation, grain, stillimage, psnr, ssim, fastdecode, zerolatency - Preset tweaks for a source or use
options.description:
Tune applies a set of adjustments on top of whatever preset is in use, aimed at a kind of source or a delivery constraint. film, animation, grain and stillimage move psy-rd, aq-strength, deblocking and the b-frame and reference counts to suit that material; grain in particular loosens deblocking and raises the psy settings so noise survives instead of being filtered into mush.

fastdecode drops tools that cost the decoder rather than the encoder - CABAC, the loop filter, weighted prediction - so weak hardware can keep up. zerolatency turns off lookahead and B-frames for live streaming.

psnr and ssim exist for benchmarking: they switch the psychovisual optimisations off, which raises those metric scores while making the picture look worse. Do not use them for anything anyone will watch.
options.listedValuesDescription:
film|Live action from a camera, the usual choice.
animation|Cel animation and 2D cartoons; adds B-frames and softens deblocking.
grain|Grainy film scans, preserving noise at a large bitrate cost.
zerolatency|Live streaming, where lookahead delay is unacceptable.
fastdecode|Playback on weak hardware, at some compression cost.

options.syntaxDescription: baseline, main, high, high10, high422 or high444 - Caps the tools used so limited decoders can play the file
options.description:
Restricts the encoder to the coding tools a given H.264 profile allows, so a decoder that only implements that profile can play the result. baseline drops CABAC and B-frames, main allows both at 8-bit 4:2:0, and high adds the 8x8 transform and is what essentially every current device decodes.

The high10, high422 and high444 profiles unlock higher bit depths and chroma subsampling, and are almost never played by hardware - they are for intermediate and mastering files, not delivery.

Setting this overrides any other setting that would exceed the profile, so a profile plus an incompatible option is resolved in the profile's favour rather than refused.
options.listedValuesDescription:
high|The normal choice for delivery; universally supported.
main|Older hardware and Blu-ray authoring.
baseline|Very old mobile decoders, at a real efficiency cost.
high10|10-bit output for archival or intermediate files, not for playback.

options.syntaxDescription: 1 to 6.2, including 1b (blank lets x264 derive it) - Decoder level written to the stream; x264 only warns, it clamps nothing
options.description:
The decoder level written into the stream header. Levels bound resolution, frame rate, bitrate and how many reference frames may be buffered, and hardware decoders advertise the highest level they implement.

x264 works out a suitable level on its own, so this is only worth setting when a target demands a specific one - Blu-ray at 4.1, or a device that refuses anything higher.

Be aware that x264 only warns when your other settings exceed the level you asked for; it does not reduce ref frames or anything else to fit. Getting a conformant stream means setting those yourself.
options.listedValuesDescription:
4.1|Blu-ray, and a very common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
3.0|Older mobile devices at standard definition.
4.0|Broad compatibility for 1080p without Blu-ray's constraints.

options.syntaxDescription: alpha:beta, each -6 to 6 (default 0:0) - Loop filter strength; negative keeps grain, positive hides blocking
options.description:
Offsets for the in-loop deblocking filter, which smooths the edges between coded blocks before the frame is used as a reference. The first number shifts the filter's strength and the second the threshold at which an edge is considered worth filtering.

Negative values filter less, so grain and fine texture survive the loop instead of being averaged away - at the cost of visible block edges if the bitrate is not there to support them. Positive values filter more, which hides blocking at low bitrates and costs detail.

tune film and tune grain already move these, so setting both means yours wins.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0:0|The default, neutral filtering.
-1:-1|A mild sharpening, common for detailed live action.
-3:-3|Strongly preserves grain; needs a generous bitrate or it blocks.
1:1|Smooths more, for low bitrate encodes where blocking shows.

options.syntaxDescription: flat or jvt (default flat) - Preset quantisation matrix; jvt weights high frequencies down, softening detail
options.description:
Selects the quantisation matrix, which weights how coarsely each transform frequency is quantised. flat treats every frequency alike. jvt uses the JVT matrix, which quantises high frequencies more heavily than low ones.

flat is the right choice for almost all modern encoding: it keeps fine detail rather than assuming the viewer will not miss it. jvt throws away high-frequency detail to save bits, which shows as softening, and it exists mainly for compatibility with older encoders and for matching a reference stream.

If you want frequency-dependent quantisation for quality reasons, aq-mode is the better tool.
options.listedValuesDescription:
flat|The default, and the right choice for essentially all encoding.
jvt|The JVT matrix; softer, for matching legacy encoder output.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-16 (default 3) - B-frames between I and P frames; more helps low-motion and animated sources, costs latency
options.description:
The longest run of consecutive B-frames the encoder may insert. B-frames predict from both earlier and later frames, which makes them by far the cheapest frames to code, so allowing longer runs lets static and slow material spend its bits where something is actually happening.

Returns fall off past five or so on live action, and beyond about eight almost nothing is gained on any source. Animation and static footage benefit the most because long stretches genuinely do not change.

Every B-frame adds encoding latency and a frame of decode delay, which is why streaming presets set this to 0.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default, a sound balance for live action.
0|Baseline profile output and low-latency streaming.
8|Animation and mostly static footage, where long runs pay off.
16|The maximum; realistically no better than 8.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - How B-frame placement is decided: 0 off, 1 fast, 2 optimal but slow with high bframes
options.description:
Decides where in the sequence B-frames actually go, up to the limit bframes sets. 0 skips the decision and always uses the maximum run, which is fast and usually wasteful. 1 is a quick heuristic. 2 runs a proper search over the possibilities and picks the best arrangement.

Mode 2 is the one worth having on anything not being encoded in real time, but its cost grows with the bframes setting, so pairing b-adapt 2 with a large bframes value is where slow presets spend a lot of their time.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default, a fast heuristic that is right most of the time.
2|Slower and better; the choice for offline encoding.
0|Fastest, always using the maximum run; for real-time only.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-16 (default 3) - Reference frames the motion search may use; more helps animation, costs speed and compatibility
options.description:
How many previously decoded frames the motion search may predict from. More references help whenever the same content reappears - repetitive motion, cuts back to an earlier shot, animation that reuses cels - because the encoder can point at the frame that actually matches.

Cost is roughly linear in encoding time, and returns fall off quickly on ordinary live action past about five.

Hardware decoders limit this through the level: at 1080p, level 4.1 allows only four. Going higher produces a file that a compliant decoder is entitled to refuse.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default, fine for general live action.
5|A good offline setting for detailed or repetitive material.
1|Fastest, and what some very limited decoders require.
16|The maximum; useful on animation, and out of spec for most hardware.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 2) - Weighted prediction for P-frames: 0 off, 1 weighted refs, 2 also duplicates; helps fades
options.description:
Weighted prediction lets a P-frame scale and offset the reference it predicts from, so a frame that is simply brighter or darker than the one before does not have to be re-coded from scratch. Fades, flashes and lighting changes are where it earns its keep.

Mode 1 applies the weighting; mode 2 also allows duplicate weighted references, which helps most on fades. Both are essentially free.

Some older decoders and Blu-ray authoring require this off, and it is one of the tools fastdecode disables.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default; the strongest form, and what you want for fades.
1|Weighted references without duplicates, for stricter compatibility.
0|Off, for Blu-ray authoring or very old decoders.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-250 (default 40) - Frames looked ahead when deciding frame types and mb-tree; higher paces bits better
options.description:
How many frames ahead the encoder looks before committing to a frame type and a quantiser. The lookahead drives both frame type decisions and mb-tree, which spends bits on blocks that later frames will keep referencing.

Longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and makes mb-tree's estimates more useful, at the cost of memory and encoding latency. Past roughly the length of a typical shot there is nothing left to learn.

Setting it to 0 disables mb-tree entirely, which is why low-latency presets look worse at the same bitrate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
40|The default, a good match for most content.
60|Longer scenes and offline encoding, giving mb-tree more to work with.
0|Disables lookahead and mb-tree, for minimum latency.
250|The maximum; memory-hungry with little to show for it.

options.syntaxDescription: dia, hex, umh, esa or tesa (default hex) - Integer pixel motion search; umh and up pay off on high-motion HD
options.description:
The integer-pixel motion search pattern. dia checks a tiny diamond around the predicted vector, hex a hexagon, and umh runs an uneven multi-hexagon search that is far more likely to find large or unusual motion. esa and tesa search the whole merange exhaustively.

hex is the sensible default. umh is the one upgrade worth paying for, and it matters most at high resolution and on fast motion, where the right vector can be a long way from the prediction.

esa and tesa are exhaustive rather than clever: they cost enormously and almost never beat umh by enough to notice.
options.listedValuesDescription:
hex|The default, and a good speed to quality balance.
umh|High resolution or fast motion; the worthwhile upgrade.
dia|Fastest, for real-time encoding.
tesa|Exhaustive and extremely slow, for benchmarking rather than delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-11 (default 7) - Subpixel motion estimation and mode decision quality; the main quality-versus-speed dial
options.description:
Controls how hard the encoder refines a motion vector below whole-pixel precision, and how carefully it decides between modes. This is the single most effective quality-versus-speed dial x264 has.

The scale changes behaviour as it climbs: from 6 upward, rate-distortion optimisation is used for P and B frames, which is also the point at which psy-rd starts doing anything. From 8 upward, motion vectors and intra modes get an RD refinement pass. 10 and 11 additionally require trellis 2.

Below 6 the encoder is making mode decisions on a rough estimate rather than on actual coding cost, which shows.
options.listedValuesDescription:
7|The default, and already past the point where psy-rd works.
10|Slow presets; RD refinement on vectors and intra modes.
11|The maximum, for the last fraction of a percent.
2|Real-time encoding, where mode decisions have to be cheap.

options.syntaxDescription: 4-1024 (default 16) - Largest motion vector search range; only exceeds 16 with me umh, esa or tesa
options.description:
The radius, in pixels, of the integer motion search. It bounds how far from the predicted position the encoder is willing to look for a match.

Raising it only does anything with a search pattern that can use the room: dia and hex have fixed shapes and ignore it, so it applies to umh, esa and tesa. With those, a larger range catches fast pans and whip motion at high resolution that would otherwise be coded as expensive intra blocks.

Cost grows quickly, and on ordinary content the extra range simply goes unused.
options.listedValuesDescription:
16|The default, enough for typical motion at up to 1080p.
24|Fast motion at 1080p and above, paired with me umh.
32|Whip pans and sports at 4K.
64|Rarely justified; the search cost is substantial.

options.syntaxDescription: spatial, temporal, auto or none (default spatial) - How B-frames derive motion vectors they do not code
options.description:
Direct mode lets a B-frame infer its motion vectors from neighbouring blocks instead of coding them, which is a large part of why B-frames are cheap. This chooses how that inference works: spatial predicts from neighbouring blocks in the same frame, temporal from the co-located block in a reference.

auto alternates between the two and picks whichever performed better, which costs a little analysis and is generally the best setting for offline encoding.

none disables direct mode entirely and forces every vector to be coded, which is a straightforward loss.
options.listedValuesDescription:
spatial|The default; predicts from spatial neighbours.
auto|Alternates and picks the better of the two; the best offline setting.
temporal|Predicts from the co-located block in a reference.
none|Disables direct mode; costs bitrate for no benefit.

options.syntaxDescription: p8x8, b8x8, i8x8, i4x4, p4x4, all or none (default varies by preset) - Which macroblock splits may be tried
options.description:
H.264 can split a macroblock into smaller partitions so that motion is described at a finer scale. This lists which of those splits the encoder is allowed to consider, given as a comma-separated set.

Allowing more partitions lets the encoder describe complex motion and fine detail more accurately, at a cost in analysis time roughly proportional to how many it must test. Restricting them is a speed measure and shows up as blockier motion around detailed edges.

The preset already sets a sensible list, so this is worth touching mainly to force all on a fast preset, or to cut the list on a slow one.
options.listedValuesDescription:
all|Every partition type; the most thorough analysis.
p8x8,b8x8,i8x8,i4x4|The common set used by the medium and slower presets.
none|No sub-macroblock partitions; fastest and visibly blockier.

options.syntaxDescription: none, strict or normal (default normal) - Whether B-frames may themselves be used as references
options.description:
Normally B-frames are never referenced by anything, so they are disposable. B-pyramid allows some of them to act as references for other B-frames, which builds a hierarchy and improves compression noticeably on material with long B-frame runs.

normal is the default and allows the full arrangement. strict limits the structure to what the Blu-ray specification permits, which is what to use for disc authoring.

none disables it. That costs efficiency, and is only needed for decoders that cannot cope with referenced B-frames.
options.listedValuesDescription:
normal|The default; full hierarchical B-frames.
strict|The restricted form Blu-ray authoring requires.
none|No referenced B-frames, for limited decoders.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 1) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 variance, 2 auto-variance, 3 with dark-scene bias
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error hides and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking are obvious. Without it, dark and smooth regions are where an encode visibly falls apart first.

Mode 1 distributes by variance. Mode 2 adjusts the strength per frame using the frame's own content, which spreads bits more evenly across a varied sequence. Mode 3 adds a bias towards dark regions, which is where banding is most visible.

Turning it off raises PSNR and makes the result look worse, which is why psnr and ssim tunes do exactly that.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default variance-based distribution.
2|Auto-variance, adapting per frame; a good offline choice.
3|Auto-variance with a dark-scene bias, for night and shadow detail.
0|Off; higher metric scores, visibly worse picture.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-3.0 (default 1.0) - Strength of adaptive quantisation; raise to cut blocking in flat areas, lower for grain
options.description:
How far adaptive quantisation is allowed to shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values take more bits out of detailed areas and put more into flat ones.

Raise it when flat regions - skies, walls, gradients, fades to black - show banding or blocking. Lower it when the source is grainy or heavily textured, because there the bits are better left where the detail is, and a strong setting will smooth the grain the rest of your settings are trying to keep.

tune grain and tune film already move this, so an explicit value overrides theirs.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.0|The default, suitable for most live action.
0.6|Grainy or heavily textured sources, keeping bits on detail.
1.3|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
0.0|Disables the strength entirely, equivalent to turning AQ off.

options.syntaxDescription: rd:trellis, each 0.0-10.0 (default 1.0:0.0) - Keeps detail over PSNR; rd needs subme 6+, trellis needs trellis on
options.description:
Psychovisual rate-distortion, given as two numbers. The first biases mode decisions towards keeping the same amount of visual energy as the source rather than towards the lowest measurable error, so the encoder stops preferring a smooth block over a detailed one that is slightly wrong. The second applies the same idea inside trellis quantisation.

This is what stops x264 output looking soft, and it is exactly why it costs PSNR and SSIM: it is deliberately choosing something those metrics score lower.

The first value needs subme 6 or higher to do anything, and the second needs trellis enabled. tune grain and tune film raise these; psnr and ssim zero them.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.0:0.0|The default; psy-rd on, psy-trellis off.
1.0:0.15|A mild trellis component, for detailed live action.
1.5:0.0|Stronger detail retention on grainy sources.
0.0:0.0|Off, for metric benchmarking only.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Trellis rate-distortion quantisation: 0 off, 1 on the final macroblock encode, 2 on all decisions
options.description:
Trellis quantisation chooses which transform coefficients to keep by weighing what each one costs in bits against what it contributes, rather than rounding each in isolation. It recovers a useful amount of quality for the bitrate.

Mode 1 applies it only to the final encode of each macroblock. Mode 2 applies it during mode decision as well, so the choice between modes is made on the cost they will actually have - better, and slower.

subme 10 and 11 require mode 2. Trellis also has to be on for the second half of psy-rd to do anything.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; trellis on the final macroblock encode.
2|On all mode decisions; the offline choice and required by subme 10+.
0|Off, for real-time encoding.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-1.0 (default 0.60) - QP curve compression; 0.0 acts like constant bitrate, 1.0 like constant QP
options.description:
Compresses the curve that maps frame complexity to quantiser, deciding how bitrate is shared between easy and hard scenes. At 0.0 every frame is pushed to the same size, which is constant bitrate behaviour and makes complex scenes fall apart. At 1.0 every frame gets the same quantiser, which is constant quality and lets file size follow the content.

The default sits between the two, giving hard scenes more bits than constant quality would while still holding overall size near the target.

It interacts with mb-tree, which uses this value in its own calculations, so large changes affect more than the scene-to-scene split.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0.60|The default, a sound balance for VBR.
0.75|Closer to constant quality; better on content with a wide difficulty range.
0.50|Tighter size control, at the cost of the hardest scenes.
1.00|Constant quantiser behaviour.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the chroma quantiser relative to luma; negative spends more bits on colour
options.description:
Offsets the quantiser used for the chroma planes from the one used for luma. Negative values quantise chroma more finely, spending more bits on colour; positive values coarsen it to spend more on brightness detail.

x264 already quantises chroma more finely than luma at high QPs, on the basis that the eye tolerates colour error better than brightness error. This adjusts that relationship.

Negative values are worth trying on saturated, colour-critical material, and on animation where flat colour areas show chroma banding. Positive values are a way to buy luma detail on a tight bitrate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Extra bits on colour; useful for animation and saturated sources.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100000 (default 0, off) - In-encoder noise reduction; removes fine noise before it is coded, at a cost in detail
options.description:
Applies noise reduction inside the encoder, removing low-amplitude detail before it is coded. Noise is close to random and therefore expensive, so removing it can save a substantial amount of bitrate on a noisy source.

The cost is that it cannot distinguish sensor noise from fine texture, so it removes both. Values are on a wide scale and the effect climbs quickly; a few hundred is a mild clean-up, several thousand is visibly smoothing.

For film grain you almost always want to keep, prefer psy-rd and a negative deblock over this.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no noise reduction.
100|A mild clean-up for lightly noisy digital footage.
500|Noticeable smoothing, saving real bitrate on noisy sources.
1000|Strong; removes fine texture along with the noise.

options.syntaxDescription: kbit/s (default 0, off) - Ceiling on local bitrate; set with vbv-bufsize for streaming or hardware decoders
options.description:
Caps the bitrate over any window the buffer covers, rather than over the file as a whole. Without it, a constant-quality encode is free to spend whatever a difficult scene needs, which is fine for a local file and fatal for a stream or a hardware decoder with a fixed input rate.

It only takes effect alongside vbv-bufsize; a maxrate with no buffer size does nothing.

Constraining the rate necessarily costs quality exactly where the content is hardest, so set it to what the target actually requires and no lower.
options.listedValuesDescription:
6000|Roughly a 1080p streaming ceiling.
3000|A conservative cap for constrained connections.
40000|Blu-ray's video ceiling.
0|The default; no cap.

options.syntaxDescription: kbit (default 0, off) - Size of the VBV buffer; smaller windows hold the maxrate ceiling more tightly
options.description:
The size of the notional buffer the maxrate is enforced over, in kilobits. Together the two say how much the bitrate may vary and over what period.

A buffer equal to the maxrate allows one second of variation, which is the usual streaming arrangement. Smaller buffers hold the ceiling more tightly and hurt quality on hard scenes; larger ones let the encoder spend where it needs to at the cost of a longer startup delay and more risk of underrun.

Like maxrate, this does nothing on its own.
options.listedValuesDescription:
6000|One second of buffer against a 6000 kbit/s ceiling.
12000|Two seconds; gentler on difficult scenes, slower to start.
30000|Blu-ray's buffer size.
0|The default; no buffer constraint.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-81 (default 0) - The best quantiser rate control may use; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, which is a ceiling on how many bits any one frame may be given. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody will notice. In a bitrate-targeted encode that frees bits for the difficult material; in CRF it simply caps quality on the easy parts and shrinks the file.

Values above about 10 start to be visible on flat content, so this is a fine adjustment rather than a blunt one.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
10|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
15|A firmer cap, noticeably smaller files on easy content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-81 (default 81) - The worst quantiser rate control may use; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality is allowed to fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocky collapse that difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer hit its bitrate target on those scenes and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

The default is effectively no limit, so this only matters in bitrate-targeted encoding where the target is tight.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
81|The default; effectively unlimited.
40|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
35|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-81 (default 4) - The largest quantiser change allowed between consecutive frames
options.description:
Limits how far the quantiser may move from one frame to the next. It exists to stop the rate controller reacting so sharply to a change in difficulty that quality visibly pulses.

Raising it lets rate control respond faster to a sudden change in scene complexity, which helps it hold a bitrate target through hard cuts, at the risk of visible quality steps.

Lowering it makes quality smoother over time and leaves the controller slower to react, which can overshoot the target when a difficult scene arrives abruptly.
options.listedValuesDescription:
4|The default.
2|Smoother quality over time; slower to react to scene changes.
8|Faster reaction, better target tracking, more visible steps.

options.syntaxDescription: Float above 1.0 (default 1.40) - How much finer I-frames are quantised than P-frames
options.description:
The quantiser ratio between I-frames and P-frames. I-frames are coded without reference to anything else and everything after them predicts from them, so spending extra bits there pays off across the whole GOP.

Raising it gives keyframes more bits, which helps when scene changes look soft for a moment before recovering. Lowering it evens the frames out, which can reduce the visible pulse some content shows at each keyframe.

Changes here interact with qcomp, since both shape how bits are distributed across frame types.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.40|The default.
1.30|Flatter distribution; less visible pulsing at keyframes.
1.50|More bits on keyframes, sharpening scene starts.

options.syntaxDescription: Float above 1.0 (default 1.30) - How much coarser B-frames are quantised than P-frames
options.description:
The quantiser ratio between P-frames and B-frames. B-frames are usually not referenced by anything, so quantising them more coarsely is nearly free - the error does not propagate.

Raising it takes more bits out of B-frames and gives them to the P-frames that everything predicts from. Lowering it evens the two out, which is worth doing when b-pyramid is on, because then some B-frames are references and their errors do propagate.

tune animation lowers this for exactly that reason.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.30|The default.
1.20|Evens out B-frames; sensible with b-pyramid enabled.
1.40|More bits diverted to P-frames.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-51.0 (blank leaves it off) - With CRF and VBV together, the worst rate factor the encoder may fall back to
options.description:
When CRF is combined with a VBV constraint, the encoder will raise its rate factor - lowering quality - as far as it needs to in order to respect the bitrate ceiling. This caps how far it may go.

Reaching that cap means the encoder can no longer satisfy VBV, so it will exceed the ceiling rather than degrade further. That is the trade: a guaranteed minimum quality in exchange for a bitrate that may breach the constraint on the hardest material.

It does nothing without vbv-maxrate and vbv-bufsize set.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|A firm quality floor for constrained streaming.
30|A looser floor, breaching the ceiling less often.
20|A high floor; expect the bitrate cap to be exceeded on hard scenes.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr, ssim, grain, zero-latency, fast-decode, animation (blank applies no tune) - grain keeps film noise, animation cel art
options.description:
Tune adjusts the preset's settings towards a kind of source or a delivery constraint. grain raises the psy settings and loosens deblocking and adaptive quantisation so film noise survives rather than being smoothed into patches. animation goes the other way, suiting flat cel artwork with strong AQ and more B-frames.

fast-decode removes tools that cost the decoder, for weak playback hardware. zero-latency disables lookahead and frame reordering for live use.

psnr and ssim disable the psychovisual optimisations, which raises those scores and makes the picture look worse. They are benchmarking aids, not delivery settings.
options.listedValuesDescription:
grain|Grainy film scans; the most commonly used tune in x265.
animation|Cel animation and flat 2D artwork.
zero-latency|Live streaming, at a compression cost.
fast-decode|Playback on weak hardware.
ssim|Metric benchmarking only; visibly softer output.

options.syntaxDescription: main, main10, main444-10, main12, the -intra variants and more - Caps tools so a target decoder accepts the stream
options.description:
Restricts the encoder to the coding tools and bit depths a given HEVC profile permits, so a decoder implementing only that profile can play the result. main is 8-bit 4:2:0, main10 is 10-bit 4:2:0, and the 444 and 12-bit variants cover higher chroma and precision.

main10 is worth knowing about: 10-bit encoding reduces banding and usually compresses slightly better even from an 8-bit source, and unlike H.264 it is widely supported by hardware.

The -intra variants code every frame as a keyframe, for editing and mastering rather than delivery.
options.listedValuesDescription:
main|8-bit 4:2:0; the broadest hardware compatibility.
main10|10-bit 4:2:0; better gradients and widely supported.
main444-10|10-bit 4:4:4 for mastering or screen content.
main-intra|All-intra output for editing workflows.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 for auto or a level like 4.1 or 51 (default 0) - Constrains the stream for hardware, forces VBV in CRF
options.description:
The HEVC level written into the stream, bounding resolution, frame rate, bitrate and buffering so a decoder can tell in advance whether it can cope. Written either as a level number like 4.1 or as the integer form, 41.

Leave it at 0 and x265 works out a level from the encode. Set it when a specific hardware target demands one.

Setting it has a side effect worth knowing: it enables VBV in CRF mode, applying that level's rate and buffer limits. That constrains the bitrate on difficult scenes in a way plain CRF does not, so the file will no longer be constant quality.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; x265 derives the level from the encode.
4.1|A common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
5.0|4K30 within tighter limits than 5.1.

options.syntaxDescription: tC:Beta offsets, each -6 to 6 (default 0:0) - Deblocking strength; raise to hide blocking, lower to keep detail
options.description:
Offsets for the in-loop deblocking filter, which smooths coded block edges before the frame is reused as a reference. The first number shifts the filter's strength, the second the threshold for treating an edge as worth filtering.

Negative values filter less, so grain and fine detail survive the loop rather than being averaged away, at the cost of visible block edges when the bitrate is short. Positive values smooth harder, which hides blocking at low rates and costs texture.

tune grain already loosens these, so an explicit setting replaces its choice.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0:0|The default, neutral filtering.
-1:-1|A mild sharpening for detailed live action.
-3:-3|Strong grain retention; needs bitrate behind it.
1:1|More smoothing, for low bitrate encodes that block.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 0) - Limits which slice types the sample adaptive offset filter runs on
options.description:
The sample adaptive offset filter corrects reconstructed samples against the source, cleaning up ringing and banding. It is effective at low bitrates and notorious for smoothing fine texture and grain at high ones.

This limits which slice types it runs on rather than turning it off wholesale: the levels progressively enable it for more slice types, so you can keep it where it helps most and leave the rest untouched.

It is the middle ground between leaving the filter on everywhere and disabling it, which grain-preserving setups often do.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the filter follows the preset's own setting.
1|Enabled for I-slices only, where ringing is most visible.
2|I and P slices.
4|All slice types.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-16 (default 4) - Longest run of consecutive B-frames; raise for static scenes, 0 for low-latency output
options.description:
The longest run of consecutive B-frames allowed. B-frames predict from both directions and are much cheaper to code than P-frames, so longer runs let static material spend its bits on the parts of the sequence that actually change.

Static scenes and animation gain the most. On busy live action the returns fall away past five or six, and no source gains much beyond eight.

Each B-frame adds reordering delay, so live and low-latency encoding sets this to 0 and accepts the efficiency loss.
options.listedValuesDescription:
4|The default, a sound balance.
8|Animation and static footage, where long runs pay.
0|Low-latency streaming; P and I frames only.
16|The maximum; realistically no better than 8.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-8 (default 3) - L0 reference frames the search may use; more helps repetitive motion, and 9 or more will not open
options.description:
How many L0 reference frames the motion search may predict from. More references help when content recurs - repetitive motion, cuts returning to an earlier shot, animation reusing artwork - because the encoder can point at a frame that genuinely matches.

Encoding time grows with each one and the gains fall off quickly on ordinary live action.

Compatibility is the real limit, and it is enforced rather than warned about: HEVC levels bound the decoded picture buffer, and x265 refuses to open the encoder at all once the level it derived cannot hold the count asked for. Measured on this build, 8 opens and 9 does not, at every frame size tried - the run dies with x265_encoder_open() failed and writes nothing. Naming a high --level-idc does let it open, but x265 then lowers the count to 7, so it is not a way to reach more references than leaving the level alone.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default, fine for general content.
5|Detailed or repetitive material, encoded offline.
1|Fastest, and the safest for constrained decoders.
8|The most this build will open; 9 and up refuse to start.

options.syntaxDescription: Above bframes, up to 250 (default 20) - Frames looked ahead for slice types; longer sharpens scenecuts and cutree
options.description:
How many frames the encoder examines before fixing slice types and quantisers. The lookahead drives slice type decisions, scenecut detection and cutree, which spends bits on blocks that later frames will keep referring to.

A longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and sharpens cuts, because the encoder can see a scene change coming rather than reacting after it. It costs memory and latency.

It must be larger than bframes to be useful, and past the length of a typical shot there is nothing further to learn.
options.listedValuesDescription:
20|The default.
40|Offline encoding, giving cutree more to work with.
60|Long takes and slow scenes.
10|Lower latency, at some rate control quality.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-7 (default 2) - Subpixel refinement passes in the motion search; higher costs speed but helps fine or fast motion
options.description:
How hard the encoder refines motion vectors below whole-pixel precision, and how many candidates it tests while doing so. Higher values run more refinement passes and evaluate more positions.

The gain shows up on fine detail and fast motion, where a vector that is half a pixel out leaves a visible residual that has to be coded. On flat or slow content the extra passes find little.

It is one of the main speed dials the presets move, and the cost is roughly linear in the value.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default, matching the medium preset.
4|Slower presets; a good offline compromise.
7|The maximum, for the last of the quality at a steep price.
0|Fastest, for real-time encoding.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-32767 (default 57) - Motion search range in pixels; raise past 57 only for fast pans at high resolution
options.description:
The radius in pixels of the motion search. It bounds how far from the predicted position the encoder will look for a match, so it decides whether fast motion is found or coded expensively as intra blocks.

The default is generous for 1080p. Raising it helps whip pans, sports and high resolution material where genuine displacement between frames is large; on ordinary content the extra range goes unused and only costs time.

Values are capped below 32768, and search cost grows quickly, so large ranges are rarely worth it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
57|The default, ample for typical motion at 1080p.
92|Fast pans and sports at 4K.
32|Faster, adequate for slow or low resolution content.
16|Real-time encoding where search cost dominates.

options.syntaxDescription: dia, hex, umh, star, sea or full (default hex) - Motion search pattern; umh and above find large motion
options.description:
The pattern the encoder follows when searching for a matching block in a reference frame. dia checks a small diamond, hex a hexagon, umh an uneven multi-hexagon that is far better at finding large or unusual motion, and star a different wide pattern. sea and full search exhaustively.

hex is fine for ordinary content. umh is the upgrade that matters, and it matters most at high resolution and on fast motion, where the correct vector can sit a long way from the prediction.

sea and full cost enormously and rarely beat umh by a visible margin.
options.listedValuesDescription:
hex|The default; a good speed to quality balance.
umh|Fast motion or high resolution; the worthwhile upgrade.
star|A wide search, between umh and exhaustive in cost.
dia|Fastest, for real-time encoding.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-5 (default 2) - How many merge candidates a block may consider before coding its own motion vector
options.description:
HEVC lets a block inherit motion from a neighbour instead of coding its own vector, which is very cheap. This sets how many candidate neighbours the encoder evaluates before giving up and coding a vector.

More candidates means more chances to find an inheritable match, so fewer vectors need coding. The cost is analysis time roughly proportional to the number tested.

Raising it helps most where motion is coherent across large areas - pans, static scenes with a moving subject - and the slower presets already do so.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default.
3|A modest step up, used by the slower presets.
5|The maximum; the most thorough merge analysis.
1|Fastest; nearly every block codes its own vector.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 3) - How aggressively the encoder prunes which references it fully searches
options.description:
Reference frames cost search time roughly in proportion to how many are checked for every block. This lets the encoder skip references that analysis of the parent block suggests are not worth checking.

Mode 1 prunes using the results at the previous depth, mode 2 using the current block's own analysis, and mode 3 uses both. Higher values are faster and risk missing a reference that would have matched.

Set it to 0 when you have raised ref and want every reference genuinely searched, since otherwise the extra references may be skipped before they are tried.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default; both pruning methods, the fastest option.
0|No pruning; every reference is searched, which is what a high ref count assumes.
1|Prunes from the previous depth only.
2|Prunes from the current block's analysis only.

options.syntaxDescription: -90 to 100 (default 0) - Nudges the lookahead towards or away from choosing B-frames
options.description:
Biases the decision the lookahead makes about whether a frame should be a B-frame. Positive values make B-frames more likely, negative values less.

B-frames are cheap, so leaning towards them saves bitrate - but on high-motion content a B-frame that should have been a P-frame predicts badly and costs more than it saves. The lookahead usually judges this well.

Worth nudging positive on static or animated content where you can see B-frames are being underused, and negative on fast motion where quality dips between P-frames.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the lookahead decides unaided.
20|Leans towards B-frames; suits static or animated content.
-20|Leans away from them, for high-motion footage.
50|A strong bias; expect the maximum B-frame run most of the time.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 2) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 plain, 2 auto-variance, 3 dark-scene bias, 4 edge aware
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation redistributes bits within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error is masked and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking show. Dark and smooth regions are where an HEVC encode visibly breaks down first, and this is the main defence.

Mode 1 distributes by block variance. Mode 2 adapts the strength using the frame's own content. Mode 3 adds a bias towards dark areas, and mode 4 weights by edge density, which helps keep flat regions next to sharp edges clean.

Switching it off raises metric scores and looks worse.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default, auto-variance.
3|Dark and night scenes prone to banding.
4|Edge-aware; useful on animation and mixed content.
0|Off; better numbers, worse picture.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-3.0 (default 1.0) - How strongly adaptive quantisation shifts QP; raise for flat gradients, lower if rates swing
options.description:
How far adaptive quantisation may shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values move more bits out of detailed areas and into flat ones.

Raise it when gradients, skies and fades show banding. Lower it on grainy or heavily textured sources, where a strong setting spends bits flattening the very noise the psy settings are trying to keep, and where it can make the bitrate swing between shots.

tune grain lowers this, so setting it explicitly replaces that choice.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.0|The default, suitable for most content.
0.5|Grainy film, keeping bits on detail and steadying the rate.
1.3|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
0.0|Disables the redistribution.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-5.0 (default 2.0) - Preserves the source's energy in the reconstruction; needs rd 3 or above, costs PSNR and SSIM
options.description:
Psychovisual rate-distortion biases mode decisions towards preserving the source's energy rather than minimising measurable error, so the encoder stops preferring a smooth block over a detailed one that is slightly wrong. Without it x265 output tends to look plasticky, especially on faces and grain.

It costs PSNR and SSIM by design - it is choosing what those metrics score lower - which is why the psnr and ssim tunes set it to 0.

It needs rd 3 or higher to have any effect, since below that the encoder is not doing the rate-distortion analysis this modifies.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2.0|The default, and a good general setting.
1.0|Gentler, for clean digital sources.
4.0|Strong detail retention on grainy film.
0.0|Off, for metric benchmarking only.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-50.0 (default 0.0, 1.0 on slow presets) - Favours higher energy through quantisation; needs rdoq-level 1 or 2
options.description:
The quantisation-stage counterpart to psy-rd. Where psy-rd influences which mode is chosen, this biases which transform coefficients survive quantisation, favouring those that carry the source's high-frequency energy.

It is the more effective of the two for keeping film grain alive, and correspondingly the more expensive in bitrate. Values well above the default are normal on grain-heavy material.

It requires rdoq-level 1 or 2, which the faster presets do not enable, so on those it silently does nothing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.0|The slow-preset default; a reasonable starting point.
2.0|Noticeably stronger grain and texture retention.
10.0|Aggressive; used in grain-preservation setups at high bitrates.
0.0|Off, the default on faster presets.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-6 (default 3) - Rate-distortion optimisation level; higher looks harder and shrinks output, 4 aliases 3
options.description:
How thoroughly the encoder analyses each block before committing to a coding decision. Higher levels test more possibilities with a fuller cost model instead of estimating, which shrinks the output at the same quality.

The scale is not fully granular: 4 behaves as 3 and 6 behaves as 5, so the meaningful steps are 1, 2, 3 and 5. Level 3 is where full rate-distortion optimisation begins, and it is also the point below which psy-rd stops working.

Cost rises sharply at 5, which is why only the slowest presets use it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default, and the minimum for psy-rd to function.
5|Slow presets; the last real quality step.
2|Faster, for time-constrained encodes.
1|Fastest, with visibly worse decisions.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.5-1.0 (default 0.6) - Quantiser curve compression; 1.0 behaves like constant QP, raise to favour busy scenes
options.description:
Compresses the curve mapping frame complexity to quantiser, setting how bitrate is shared between easy and hard scenes. At 1.0 every frame gets the same quantiser, which is constant quality and lets size follow content. Lower values push frames towards equal size, giving complex scenes less than they need.

The default leans towards size predictability. Raising it gives busy scenes more bits and improves how the encode holds up on the hardest material, at the cost of a less predictable file size.

cutree uses this value too, so changes affect more than the scene-to-scene split.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0.6|The default.
0.7|A common adjustment for grain and detailed content.
0.8|Closer to constant quality across a wide difficulty range.
1.0|Constant quantiser behaviour.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default follows rd; on at rd 4-6) - Rate-distortion optimised quantisation, which psy-rdoq requires
options.description:
Decides how coefficients are quantised. Level 0 rounds each one in isolation. Level 1 optimises which coefficients survive by weighing the bits each costs against what it contributes. Level 2 additionally optimises the coding decisions around them.

This is the setting psy-rdoq depends on: at level 0 there is no rate-distortion quantisation for it to bias, so psy-rdoq does nothing at all regardless of its value.

x265 enables it implicitly at rd 4 and above, which means on faster presets it is off and psy-rdoq is silently inert. Setting it explicitly is how you get psychovisual quantisation on a quicker preset.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|Rate-distortion optimised quantisation; enough for psy-rdoq to work.
2|Also optimises the surrounding coding decisions; slower.
0|Off, and psy-rdoq has no effect.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cb chroma quantiser relative to luma; negative spends more bits on blue-yellow
options.description:
Offsets the quantiser used for the Cb chroma plane from the luma quantiser. Negative values quantise it more finely and spend more bits on that colour difference channel; positive values coarsen it.

Chroma is already subsampled in 4:2:0, so colour detail is the first thing to break down on saturated material - flat colour areas band, and strong reds and blues smear. A negative offset is the direct remedy.

Set it alongside crqpoffs, since adjusting one channel and not the other shifts the colour balance of the artefacts.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Extra bits on chroma; useful for animation and saturated sources.
-4|A strong chroma bias for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cr chroma quantiser relative to luma; negative spends more bits on red-green
options.description:
Offsets the quantiser used for the Cr chroma plane from the luma quantiser, the counterpart to cbqpoffs.

Red detail is where 4:2:0 chroma subsampling is most visible, because red carries a lot of the perceived colour energy and very little of the luma. Saturated reds smearing or blocking is the usual symptom, and a negative offset here is what fixes it.

Normally set to the same value as cbqpoffs unless you are correcting a specific channel.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Extra bits on red-green detail; pairs with cbqpoffs -2.
-4|A strong bias, for saturated red-heavy material.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 64, 32 or 16 (default 64) - The largest coding unit size; smaller helps fine detail at low resolution
options.description:
The size of the largest block the encoder may code as a unit. HEVC subdivides these down to the minimum size as the content demands, so this sets the top of that tree rather than a fixed block size.

Large units code flat areas very cheaply, which is why 64 is the default and why HEVC beats H.264 most clearly at high resolution. At low resolutions, or on very detailed content, a 64x64 unit rarely covers anything uniform and the encoder spends its time subdividing.

Dropping to 32 speeds up encoding and can help below 720p; it costs efficiency at 1080p and above.
options.listedValuesDescription:
64|The default; the right choice at 1080p and above.
32|Faster, and sometimes better below 720p.
16|Rarely useful; a substantial efficiency loss.

options.syntaxDescription: 8, 16 or 32 (default 8) - The smallest coding unit; raising it is a speed measure that costs fine detail
options.description:
The smallest block the encoder is allowed to subdivide down to. Small units describe fine detail and complex motion accurately; large ones cannot, but are much faster to search.

The default of 8 lets the encoder go as fine as HEVC allows. Raising it prunes the bottom of the analysis tree, which saves a great deal of time and shows up as softness and blockiness wherever detail is finer than the limit.

This is a speed setting. There is no quality reason to raise it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default; full subdivision.
16|Noticeably faster, at a visible cost in fine detail.
32|Fastest, and clearly blocky on detailed content.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-4 (default 1) - How far transform units may subdivide inside an intra block
options.description:
Transform units are the blocks the actual frequency transform is applied to, and they subdivide separately from coding units. This sets how many levels of subdivision are allowed inside an intra-predicted block.

Deeper subdivision lets the transform follow detail more closely, so intra blocks - keyframes especially, and any area the encoder cannot predict - hold fine texture better. Each extra level multiplies the analysis work.

Raising it is one of the more effective quality steps on detailed and high-resolution material, and the slower presets already do.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default.
2|A worthwhile step on detailed material; used by slower presets.
3|Deeper analysis, with diminishing returns.
4|The maximum; very slow.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-4 (default 1) - How far transform units may subdivide inside an inter block
options.description:
The same transform subdivision control as tu-intra-depth, applied to inter-predicted blocks - those predicted from other frames, which is most of the picture in most sequences.

Deeper subdivision lets the transform match the shape of the residual left after prediction, which matters where motion is complex and prediction leaves fine, uneven error behind.

Because inter blocks dominate the frame count, raising this costs more encoding time than the intra equivalent for a similar gain.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default.
2|A worthwhile step on complex motion; used by slower presets.
3|Deeper analysis, with diminishing returns.
4|The maximum; very slow.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 0) - Discourages 32x32 intra transform units, which can look blocky
options.description:
Applies a cost penalty to 32x32 transform units in intra-predicted blocks. Mode 1 makes them more expensive so the encoder picks them less often; mode 2 disables them outright.

Large intra transforms spread quantisation error across a wide area, which reads as visible blocking on detailed content even when the measured error is low. Penalising them pushes the encoder towards smaller transforms that keep the error local.

It costs bitrate, since the large transform is genuinely cheaper when it fits, so this is a picture-quality adjustment rather than an efficiency one.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no penalty.
1|Makes 32x32 intra transforms more expensive.
2|Disables them entirely; the strongest anti-blocking setting.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-69 (default 0) - The best quantiser rate control may use; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, which caps how many bits any one frame may receive. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode may get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody would notice, which in a bitrate-targeted encode leaves more for the difficult material and in CRF simply shrinks the file.

Values much above 10 begin to show on flat content, so treat it as a fine adjustment.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
10|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
15|A firmer cap, giving noticeably smaller files.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-69 (default 69) - The worst quantiser rate control may use; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality may fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocky collapse difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer meet its bitrate target there and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

The default is effectively unlimited, so this only bites in bitrate-targeted encoding with a tight target.

In a target quality mode the quantiser is chosen by a search, and this bound applies to it as well. Setting it tightly can stop that search reaching the quality target, since the encoder is no longer allowed to go where the search wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
69|The default; effectively unlimited.
45|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
40|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: Float above 1.0 (default 1.4) - How much finer I-frames are quantised than P-frames
options.description:
The quantiser ratio between I-frames and P-frames. An I-frame is coded without reference to anything else and everything after it predicts from it, so bits spent there pay off across the whole interval.

Raising it gives keyframes more bits, which helps when scene starts look soft for a moment before sharpening. Lowering it evens the frame types out and can reduce the visible pulse some content shows at every keyframe.

It interacts with qcomp, which also shapes how bits are spread.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.4|The default.
1.3|Flatter distribution; less pulsing at keyframes.
1.5|More bits on keyframes, sharpening scene starts.

options.syntaxDescription: Float above 1.0 (default 1.3) - How much coarser B-frames are quantised than P-frames
options.description:
The quantiser ratio between P-frames and B-frames. B-frames that nothing references can be quantised more coarsely almost for free, since their error does not propagate.

Raising it moves bits out of B-frames and into the P-frames everything predicts from. Lowering it evens them out, which is the right move when B-frames are being used as references, because then their error does propagate.

tune animation lowers this, since animation leans heavily on long B-frame runs.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1.3|The default.
1.2|Evens out B-frames; sensible when they act as references.
1.4|More bits diverted to P-frames.

options.syntaxDescription: G(x,y)B(x,y)R(x,y)WP(x,y)L(max,min) in SMPTE ST 2086 units, no default - Signals HDR10 mastering display volume
options.description:
Signals the mastering display's colour volume for HDR10, in SMPTE ST 2086 form: the chromaticity of the green, blue and red primaries and the white point, then the display's maximum and minimum luminance. Coordinates are in units of 0.00002, and luminance in units of 0.0001 cd/m2.

This is metadata only. It does not change a single coded pixel - it tells the display what the content was graded on so it can tone-map sensibly to its own capabilities.

Take the values from the source's own metadata rather than inventing them; a wrong volume produces worse tone mapping than none.

options.syntaxDescription: MaxCLL,MaxFALL in cd/m2, e.g. 1000,400, no default - Signals HDR10 content and frame-average light levels to displays
options.description:
Two HDR10 light-level figures: the maximum content light level, which is the brightest single pixel anywhere in the video, and the maximum frame-average light level, the brightest frame taken as a whole. Both are in cd/m2.

Like master-display this is metadata and changes no pixels. Displays use it to decide how much tone mapping a title needs before it starts, rather than adapting scene by scene.

The values should be measured from the actual content - ffmpeg and mkvinfo can read them off a graded master - since guessed figures make displays tone-map for brightness that is not there.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1000,400|A typical 1000 cd/m2 grade.
4000,1000|A 4000 cd/m2 master.
0,0|Explicitly signals that the levels are unknown.

options.syntaxDescription: hq, ll, ull or lossless (default hq) - What the encoder is tuned for; the tab already sets lossless at quality 0
options.description:
Picks what NVENC is tuned for, which moves the rate control and the buffering underneath whatever preset is in use. hq is the ordinary offline choice and the default. ll and ull trade compression for latency, cutting the encoder's reordering and buffering so a frame comes out almost as soon as it goes in - which is what a live stream wants and what a file does not.

lossless encodes the source exactly. It produces very large files, and the encoder switches itself into constant-QP mode for it whatever rate control was asked for.

This is the one row that can name an option the tab sets itself: with the quality value at 0 the tab emits -tune lossless. The grid's rows go on the command line after the rate control, so a tune set here wins - which also makes hq the way to take an encode back off lossless without touching the quality box.
options.listedValuesDescription:
hq|The default, and the right choice for encoding a file.
ll|Low latency, for live streaming rather than files.
ull|Ultra low latency; the strongest form and the largest quality cost.
lossless|Mathematically lossless output, at an enormous bitrate.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation within a frame; moves bits to the flat areas that band first
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error hides and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking are obvious. Without it, dark and smooth regions are where an encode visibly falls apart first.

NVENC's version is a plain on/off rather than the choice of modes a software encoder offers, with aq-strength beside it deciding how far the quantiser may shift. It is off by default, which is a large part of why a hardware encode can look worse than a software one at the same bitrate.

There is no real speed cost - the analysis is work the hardware does anyway - so this is close to free quality on anything with skies, gradients, fades or large flat surfaces.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|On; what almost any offline encode wants.
0|The default, off.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation across frames; needs lookahead, and a GPU that implements it
options.description:
Where spatial AQ redistributes bits inside one frame, temporal AQ redistributes them between frames, spending more on the parts of the picture that later frames will keep referencing. It is the same idea as a software encoder's macroblock tree.

It needs lookahead frames to work with, so it does nothing unless rc-lookahead is also set. It is the one AQ setting the hardware can refuse outright: ffmpeg's own check prints "Temporal AQ not supported" and carries on without it, which older GPUs will do.

Worth having on material with sustained motion over a background worth protecting. On a fast, cut-heavy source there is much less for it to find.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|On; pair it with rc-lookahead or it does nothing.
0|The default, off.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-15 (default 8) - How far spatial AQ may shift the quantiser; raise for flat sources, lower for grain
options.description:
How far adaptive quantisation is allowed to shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values take more bits out of detailed areas and put more into flat ones. It does nothing at all unless spatial-aq is on - ffmpeg's own description of this option says so.

Raise it when flat regions - skies, walls, gradients, fades to black - show banding or blocking. Lower it when the source is grainy or heavily textured, because there the bits are better left where the detail is, and a strong setting will smooth the grain the rest of your settings are trying to keep.

The scale runs 1 to 15 with 8 in the middle, so this is a coarser control than a software encoder's fractional strength and one step is a real change.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default, the middle of the range.
5|Grainy or heavily textured sources, keeping bits on detail.
12|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
15|The maximum; strong redistribution, and visible smoothing of texture.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 auto, 0 off or 4 on (default -1) - NVENC's temporal filter; needs bf 4 or more and a recent GPU
options.description:
NVENC's own temporal filter, which averages across neighbouring frames before encoding to take out noise that would otherwise be expensive to code. It is a hardware feature of the newer encoder generations, and ffmpeg prints "Temporal filtering not supported by the device" and carries on without it where the GPU has no such block.

It has a hard requirement beside it: ffmpeg refuses the combination unless there are at least four B-frames, saying "Temporal filtering needs at least 4 B-Frames (-bf 4)". So this row and the bf row are set together or not at all.

Only -1, 0 and 4 mean anything - those are the levels NVENC defines, and the encoder answers anything else with "Invalid temporal filtering level". ffmpeg's own range check on this option is much wider than that and will happily let a 2 or a 7 through to be refused later on.

Like any denoiser it cannot tell sensor noise from fine texture, so on a grainy film scan it takes the grain with it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the encoder decides.
4|Temporal filtering on, which needs bf set to 4 or more.
0|Explicitly off, overriding whatever the preset would pick.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 unset, 0-3, or auto (default -1) - How hard the lookahead analyses; needs rc-lookahead set first
options.description:
How much work the lookahead does with the frames it has been given. Higher levels analyse more and may place frame types and quantisers better, at a cost in encoder throughput - which is what ffmpeg's own description of the option says.

It is meaningless on its own: with rc-lookahead at 0 there are no lookahead frames to analyse. Set that row first.

The named auto constant is 15, and it is not the same thing as the default of -1. -1 leaves the field unset so the driver's own behaviour applies; auto asks the driver to pick a level. The GPU can also cap what it will take, which ffmpeg reports as "Lookahead level not supported" along with the maximum.

Measured against this build the option refuses anything above 15.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the field is left unset.
auto|Asks the driver to pick a level; the constant behind it is 15.
1|A light analysis pass over the lookahead frames.
3|The deepest defined level, and the slowest.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cb chroma quantiser from luma; negative spends more bits on colour
options.description:
Offsets the quantiser used for the Cb chroma plane from the one used for luma. Negative values quantise chroma more finely, spending more bits on colour; positive values coarsen it to spend more on brightness detail.

NVENC splits this into two rows where a software encoder has one, so a shift meant for chroma as a whole means setting qp_cr_offset to match. Setting only one of the two tints where the error lands rather than balancing it, which is occasionally what you want and usually not.

Negative values are worth trying on saturated, colour-critical material, and on animation where flat colour areas show chroma banding. Positive values are a way to buy luma detail on a tight bitrate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Extra bits on colour; useful for animation and saturated sources.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cr chroma quantiser from luma; the red-difference half of qp_cb_offset
options.description:
The same control as qp_cb_offset applied to the Cr plane. Negative values quantise the red-difference chroma more finely and positive ones more coarsely.

The two are separate options, so a plain "spend more on chroma" means giving both the same value. Left unequal they weight one chroma plane against the other, which moves where colour error shows rather than how much of it there is.

Chroma is subsampled in the formats this encoder is usually given, so it starts from a quarter of the samples luma has - which is why a small negative offset here can be worth more than the same bits spent on luma detail.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Matches a qp_cb_offset of -2 for an even chroma bias.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: constqp, vbr or cbr (default -1, whatever the preset implies) - Overrides the rate control mode the tab has already set
options.description:
Which rate control mode NVENC runs. Left alone the value is -1, and the mode follows from the preset and from the bitrate or quality arguments the tab has already put on the command line.

That is the thing to be careful about here. The tab emits its own rate control - a bitrate with a minimum, maximum and buffer size for a bitrate target, or -b:v 0 -cq N for a quality target - and this row overrides the mode underneath it. Asking for constqp under a bitrate target, or cbr under a quality target, produces a command whose two halves disagree, and the encoder resolves that rather than refusing it.

Set it when you know which mode you want and the preset is picking the other one. Leave it alone otherwise.

Older NVENC builds had vbr_hq, cbr_hq and cbr_ld_hq beside these three. Measured against this build they are gone - only constqp, vbr and cbr parse - and the quality half of what they used to mean now lives in the preset and multipass settings.
options.listedValuesDescription:
vbr|Variable bitrate; the mode a quality or average-bitrate target wants.
cbr|Constant bitrate, for streaming and fixed-rate delivery.
constqp|A fixed quantiser, ignoring any bitrate target.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or more frames (default 0, off) - Frames analysed ahead of the encode; off by default, and four other rows need it
options.description:
How many frames ahead the encoder looks before committing to a frame type and a quantiser. A longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and lets the encoder put its I-frames where the cuts actually are, at the cost of memory and of that many frames of latency.

It is off by default on NVENC, and that matters more than the number itself: temporal-aq, b_adapt, no-scenecut and lookahead_level all describe what the lookahead should do, and all of them are inert while there is no lookahead to do it. This row is what switches that whole group on.

The encoder also needs enough buffered frames to hold the window. ffmpeg says "Lookahead not enabled. Increase buffer delay (-delay)" where it cannot, and a GPU with no lookahead block at all gets "RC lookahead not supported".

Past roughly the length of a typical shot there is nothing left for it to learn.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no lookahead, and the rows depending on it do nothing.
32|A sound general setting, about a second at 30 fps.
60|Longer scenes and offline encoding.
250|Deep lookahead; memory-hungry with little more to show for it.

options.syntaxDescription: disabled, qres or fullres (default disabled) - NVENC's own two passes, inside a single ffmpeg pass
options.description:
NVENC can run two passes over each frame inside one encode: a first that measures how difficult the frame is and a second that codes it with that knowledge. qres does the first pass at quarter resolution, fullres at full.

This is not ffmpeg's two-pass, which runs the whole file twice. Nothing here writes a stats file and the encode stays a single run, so it is the way to get better bit distribution out of a hardware encoder without doubling the wall clock.

qres is close to free and is where to start. fullres measures more accurately and costs real throughput, which on a hardware encoder is most of the reason you chose it.

It earns the most under a bitrate target, where the first pass tells the rate controller what it is about to spend. Under a fixed quality target there is much less for it to do.
options.listedValuesDescription:
disabled|The default; a single pass.
qres|Quarter-resolution first pass; the usual choice, and nearly free.
fullres|Full-resolution first pass; the most accurate and the slowest.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, no floor) - The best quantiser rate control may use; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, which is a ceiling on how many bits any one frame may be given. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody will notice, which under a bitrate target frees those bits for the difficult material.

This is NVENC's own option rather than ffmpeg's generic qmin, and the two have different ranges. Measured against this build, a value of 55 is refused as out of range [-1 - 51], so it is the encoder's own bounds that apply here.

Under the quality target the tab emits, a tight floor can stop the encoder reaching the quality asked for, since it is no longer allowed to go where the target wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; no floor.
10|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
15|A firmer cap, noticeably smaller files on easy content.
20|A hard cap, for size-critical work on clean sources.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, no ceiling) - The worst quantiser rate control may use; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality is allowed to fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocky collapse that difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer hit its bitrate target on those scenes and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

The default of -1 is no limit, so this only matters where the bitrate target is tight. Like qmin it is NVENC's own option rather than ffmpeg's generic one, and it stops at 51.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; no ceiling.
40|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
35|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.
51|The maximum, which is the same as no ceiling at all.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for I-frames; a seed for the rate controller, not a bound
options.description:
The quantiser the rate controller starts I-frames at, before it has learnt anything about the source. It is a seed rather than a bound - once the encode is running the controller moves away from it - so the effect is concentrated in the opening seconds.

That is exactly where a bitrate-targeted encode looks worst. With nothing measured yet the controller guesses, and a bad guess shows as a soft or blocky first shot before it settles. Setting the three init_qp rows near where you know the encode will end up removes that.

Under rc constqp they are not a starting point at all: nothing adapts, so the initial values are the values used throughout.
