options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
20|A high-quality start, for a generous bitrate.
26|A middling start for ordinary delivery bitrates.
32|A conservative start, for a tight bitrate.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for P-frames; normally a step or two above init_qpI
options.description:
The P-frame half of init_qpI. P-frames predict from what came before, so they carry less new information and are conventionally coded a little coarser than the I-frames they hang off - a step or two above the I-frame value is the usual arrangement.

Set it alongside init_qpI and init_qpB rather than on its own. The three together describe the shape of the GOP's bit distribution, and moving one without the others simply shifts where the error lands.

Under rc constqp this is not a starting point but the quantiser P-frames are actually coded at.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
22|About two steps above an init_qpI of 20, the conventional spacing.
28|A tighter budget, with I-frames around 26.
20|Equal to the I-frame value; spends more on P-frames than usual.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for B-frames; conventionally the coarsest of the three
options.description:
The B-frame half of init_qpI. B-frames predict from both directions and nothing refers to them unless b_ref_mode says otherwise, so they are conventionally the coarsest of the three - a couple of steps above the P-frame value.

It does nothing where there are no B-frames, and NVENC produces none by default. The bf row is what creates them.

Where b_ref_mode is on, some B-frames are references after all, and coarsening those costs more than it saves - which is an argument for closing the gap to init_qpP rather than widening it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
25|About three steps above an init_qpI of 20, the conventional spacing.
22|A narrow spread, for use with b_ref_mode each or middle.
30|Cheap B-frames, buying quality for the frames referencing them.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Holds the bitrate steady from GOP to GOP rather than letting it follow the content
options.description:
Minimises the variation in size between one GOP and the next. Normally a rate controller lets a difficult stretch take more bits and pays it back over an easy one, which is most of what gives a variable bitrate encode its quality. This constrains that.

It exists for delivery paths that cannot absorb the variation - a fixed-rate transport, a hardware player with a small buffer - and it costs quality on exactly the scenes that needed the extra bits.

Do not set it for an ordinary file. It is a transport constraint dressed up as a quality setting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the rate controller spends where the content needs it.
1|Even GOP sizes, for a constrained delivery path.

options.syntaxDescription: Frames between keyframes (default 12) - ffmpeg's GOP size; the tab sets none for NVENC, so its default applies
options.description:
How many frames may pass before the encoder must start a new GOP with a keyframe. This is ffmpeg's own option rather than one of NVENC's, and it is the only way to reach the keyframe interval from this tab: the tab does not emit a -g for NVENC as it does for the software encoders, so what runs is ffmpeg's own default of 12.

Twelve frames is very short - half a second at 25 fps - and a keyframe is the most expensive frame there is. Raising it is one of the larger size savings available from this tab, and it costs nothing but seek granularity.

Set it against how the file will be used. A couple of seconds is normal for delivery, a segmented stream wants the segment length, and an editing intermediate wants it low or at 1 for all-intra.

A scene cut can still force a keyframe of its own where the lookahead is running and no-scenecut is not set, so this is a ceiling on the spacing rather than a fixed grid.
options.listedValuesDescription:
12|ffmpeg's default, and what runs if this row is left blank.
250|Ten seconds at 25 fps; a sound choice for a delivery file.
50|Two seconds at 25 fps, for tighter seeking and streaming.
1|Every frame a keyframe, for an editing intermediate.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or more, -1 for automatic (default 0) - B-frames between reference frames; NVENC makes none unless asked
options.description:
The longest run of consecutive B-frames the encoder may insert. B-frames predict from both earlier and later frames, which makes them by far the cheapest frames to code, so allowing them lets static and slow material spend its bits where something is actually happening.

This is ffmpeg's own option and its default is 0, so an NVENC encode produces no B-frames at all unless this row is filled in. That is a real compression difference on its own, and it is also what leaves b_adapt, b_ref_mode, init_qpB and tf_level doing nothing on an otherwise default command line.

The driver clamps the run to what the GPU implements and ffmpeg reports it, saying "B-frames=N is not supported by this GPU, switched to M". A GPU with no B-frame support at all gets "The current GPU in use does not support H.264 B-frame encoding".

Every B-frame adds encoding latency and a frame of decode delay, which is why a low-latency tune wants this at 0.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|ffmpeg's default; no B-frames at all.
3|A sound general setting for live action.
4|The minimum tf_level requires, and where most GPUs top out.
-1|Automatic; leaves the choice to the encoder.

options.syntaxDescription: 1 or more (default 1) - Reference frames the motion search may use; more helps repetitive material
options.description:
How many previously decoded frames the motion search may predict from. More references help whenever the same content reappears - repetitive motion, cuts back to an earlier shot, animation that reuses cels - because the encoder can point at the frame that actually matches.

This is ffmpeg's own option, and its default of 1 is far lower than a software encoder's. Raising it is cheap on hardware, where the search is fixed-function rather than something paid for in encoding time.

The GPU decides whether it can oblige: ffmpeg prints "Multiple reference frames are not supported by the device" and carries on with one where it cannot.

Hardware decoders limit this through the level as well. At 1080p, level 4.1 allows only four, and going past that produces a file a compliant decoder is entitled to refuse.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|ffmpeg's default; a single reference.
2|A cheap improvement wherever the GPU supports it.
4|The most level 4.1 allows at 1080p.
8|Repetitive or animated material, at some compatibility risk.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Whether B-frame placement is decided per scene; only does anything with rc-lookahead set
options.description:
Decides where in the sequence B-frames actually go, up to the limit bf sets. On, the encoder uses the lookahead to place them where they pay; off, it simply always uses the maximum run.

ffmpeg's own description of this option is explicit that it applies when lookahead is enabled, so with rc-lookahead at 0 the setting is inert whichever way it is left.

Turning it off is a latency and determinism choice rather than a quality one: it removes a decision that depends on frames the encoder has not yet delivered. For a file there is no reason to.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; B-frames placed where the lookahead says they pay.
0|A fixed maximum run, for deterministic low-latency output.

options.syntaxDescription: disabled, each or middle (default -1, left to the driver) - Whether B-frames may themselves be used as references
options.description:
Normally B-frames are never referenced by anything, so they are disposable. This allows some of them to act as references for other frames, which builds a hierarchy and improves compression noticeably on material with long B-frame runs.

each makes every B-frame a reference. middle promotes only the middle of each run, which is the arrangement a software encoder's B-pyramid produces and the cheaper of the two. disabled states the conventional behaviour outright, rather than leaving the field unset the way the default does.

It is a feature of the later NVENC generations on H.264, and ffmpeg names which part is missing rather than failing: "Each B frame reference mode is not supported", or the same for middle.

It needs B-frames to exist, so the bf row comes first. And a referenced B-frame is no longer disposable, which is an argument against coarsening it with init_qpB.
options.listedValuesDescription:
middle|Promotes the middle B-frame of each run; the usual choice.
each|Every B-frame a reference; the strongest form.
disabled|Conventional disposable B-frames, stated explicitly.
-1|The default; the field is left unset for the driver to decide.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Set to 1 to stop the lookahead inserting an I-frame at a scene cut
options.description:
With the lookahead running, NVENC inserts an I-frame where it detects a cut, because a cut is the one place a keyframe is nearly free and predicting across it is nearly useless. This turns that off.

ffmpeg's own description says it applies when lookahead is enabled, so like b_adapt it does nothing while rc-lookahead is 0.

The reason to set it is a fixed keyframe grid - segmented streaming, or a workflow that cuts on a known frame count - where a keyframe arriving early is a problem rather than a saving. For an ordinary file leave it alone: adaptive I-frames are one of the larger wins the lookahead buys.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; a detected cut gets its own I-frame.
1|Keyframes only on the g interval, for a fixed segment grid.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Makes a forced keyframe an IDR, so it is a real seek point
options.description:
A keyframe is not automatically a point a decoder can start from. An I-frame refreshes the picture; an IDR additionally empties the reference list, so nothing after it may refer to anything before it. Only the IDR is a clean entry point.

This makes every keyframe forced from outside - by a -force_key_frames expression, or by a segmenting muxer asking for one - an IDR rather than a plain I-frame.

Set it whenever the output is going to be cut, segmented or seeked at those points. It costs a little compression, since the frames after an IDR lose access to references they could otherwise have used.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; forced keyframes are plain I-frames.
1|Forced keyframes become IDRs, for segmenting and clean seeking.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Lets the encoder mark some P-frames non-reference, so it can code them cheaply
options.description:
A P-frame is normally a reference, so its errors propagate to everything predicting from it and the encoder must spend accordingly. This lets it mark some of them as referenced by nothing, which means they can be coded cheaply without the cost carrying forward.

It is the B-frame trick applied to P-frames, and it is a way to get some of that benefit where B-frames are unavailable - a baseline profile stream, a GPU with no B-frame support, or a latency budget that cannot afford the reordering.

Insertion is automatic and there is no count to set. It helps most under a tight bitrate, where the saved bits go somewhere useful, and least where the bitrate is generous.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; every P-frame is a reference.
1|Automatic non-reference P-frames, for tight bitrates and low latency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Weighted prediction, letting a frame scale its reference; helps fades and flashes
options.description:
Weighted prediction lets a frame scale and offset the reference it predicts from, so a frame that is simply brighter or darker than the one before does not have to be re-coded from scratch. Fades, flashes and lighting changes are where it earns its keep.

NVENC's version is a plain on/off where a software encoder offers a choice of strengths, and the GPU may not implement it at all - which ffmpeg reports as "Weighted Prediction not supported" before carrying on without it.

It is not free of side effects on this encoder. ffmpeg also carries the message "Split encoding not supported with weighted prediction enabled", so on the multi-engine GPUs that split a frame between encoders, turning this on gives up that parallelism. On a source with no fades in it there is nothing to gain in exchange.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default, off.
1|On, for sources with fades, flashes or changing light.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Spreads the refresh across many frames instead of coding whole keyframes
options.description:
Instead of periodically coding an entire frame as intra, the encoder refreshes a moving band of each frame, so that over one refresh cycle every part of the picture has been renewed. There is no large keyframe anywhere in the output.

That evens the bitrate out completely, which is the point of it: a keyframe is a spike, and a fixed-rate transport or a small decoder buffer cannot take spikes. It is a streaming feature.

The cost for a file is severe and worth being plain about. With no IDR anywhere, seeking has nothing to land on and many players will only start from the beginning. Do not set it on something anyone will scrub through.

The GPU must implement it; ffmpeg says "Intra refresh not supported by the device" where it does not.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; ordinary periodic keyframes.
1|Rolling intra refresh, for constant-bitrate streaming only.

options.syntaxDescription: baseline, main, high, high10, high422 or high444p (default high) - Caps the tools used so limited decoders can play the file
options.description:
Restricts the encoder to the coding tools a given H.264 profile allows, so a decoder that only implements that profile can play the result. baseline drops CABAC and B-frames, main allows both at 8-bit 4:2:0, and high adds the 8x8 transform and is what essentially every current device decodes.

The high10, high422 and high444p profiles unlock higher bit depths and chroma subsampling, and are almost never played by hardware - they are for intermediate and mastering files, not delivery.

The profile and the pixel format have to agree, and the tab sets the pixel format itself. Asking for high444p over an 8-bit 4:2:0 format is a contradiction the driver resolves rather than a setting that takes effect, so change the colour format alongside it.

Two spellings to watch. NVENC calls the last profile high444p, and high444 - which is what a software encoder answers to - is refused outright. And the row is named profile:v rather than plain profile because ffmpeg has this option on audio encoders too: a bare -profile draws "Please use -profile:a or -profile:v, -profile is ambiguous" and is then applied to whatever streams will take it, which is not a thing to leave to chance in a command that also carries an audio encoder.
options.listedValuesDescription:
high|The normal choice for delivery; universally supported.
main|Older hardware and Blu-ray authoring.
baseline|Very old mobile decoders, at a real efficiency cost.
high444p|4:4:4 output for intermediates, with the colour format set to match.

options.syntaxDescription: auto, or 1 to 6.2 including 1b (default auto) - Decoder level written to the stream header
options.description:
The decoder level written into the stream header. Levels bound resolution, frame rate, bitrate and how many reference frames may be buffered, and hardware decoders advertise the highest level they implement.

The encoder works out a suitable level on its own, so this is only worth setting when a target demands a specific one - Blu-ray at 4.1, or a device that refuses anything higher.

Spell it exactly as the list has it. These names are constants, and a spelling that is not one of them is not rejected: it is evaluated as a plain number instead, so 6.3 quietly becomes level 6 and 7.0 becomes level 7. Measured against this build only a result outside 0 to 62 is refused, which means a typo here produces a stream tagged with a level nobody asked for.
options.listedValuesDescription:
auto|The default; the encoder picks a level to fit.
4.1|Blu-ray, and a very common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
4.0|Broad compatibility for 1080p without Blu-ray's constraints.

options.syntaxDescription: default, auto, cabac or cavlc (default 'default') - Entropy coder; cavlc decodes more cheaply and compresses worse
options.description:
The entropy coder that packs the encoded symbols into the bitstream. CABAC is arithmetic coding adapted to context and is what every current H.264 encode uses; CAVLC is the simpler variable-length alternative.

CABAC compresses better at every bitrate, by enough to matter, and costs the decoder more work in exchange. CAVLC exists for decoders that cannot keep up and for the baseline profile, which does not permit CABAC at all - so setting the profile to baseline settles this row along with it.

Leave it on default unless you have a particular decoder in mind. ac and vlc are accepted as aliases of cabac and cavlc, and auto asks the encoder to choose between them.
options.listedValuesDescription:
default|The default; the encoder's own choice.
cabac|Forces CABAC, which is what the main and high profiles want.
cavlc|Forces CAVLC, for very weak decoders and baseline output.
auto|Lets the encoder pick between the two.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Writes access unit delimiters, which some transport and broadcast chains require
options.description:
An access unit delimiter is a small NAL unit marking where each coded frame begins. It carries no picture data - it exists so a demuxer can find frame boundaries without parsing the slices.

Almost nothing needs it in a file. MPEG-TS and broadcast-style workflows are where it comes up, along with some hardware decoders and analysis tools that expect the boundary marked explicitly.

The cost is a handful of bytes per frame, so setting it where it is not needed is harmless but pointless.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no delimiters.
1|Writes them, for MPEG-TS and broadcast delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Applies the workarounds a Blu-ray authoring chain needs
options.description:
Turns on the constraints Blu-ray requires of an H.264 stream, which are things no other target cares about - the GOP structure, the placement of the parameter sets, and the arrangement of referenced B-frames chief among them.

It is only useful if you are actually authoring a disc, and it wants setting together with the rest of what that needs: level 4.1, a profile the specification allows, and a keyframe interval within its limit.

For anything else it is a compression cost with no benefit, the constraints existing to satisfy a decoder nothing else has.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no constraints applied.
1|Blu-ray authoring, alongside level 4.1 and a matching profile.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Carries A/53 closed captions from the source into the encoded stream
options.description:
Broadcast and capture sources carry closed captions inside the video itself, as A/53 caption data attached to the picture rather than as a subtitle track. This passes that data through into the encoded stream, and unusually for this list it is on by default.

The reason to know the row is here is the reverse case. A re-encode of a US broadcast capture keeps its captions through this option and nothing on the subtitle side is involved, which is how they survive a conversion that appears to carry no subtitle track at all.

Turn it off to strip them - for a clean master, or where something downstream trips over caption data it was not expecting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; captions in the source are carried through.
0|Strips the caption data from the output.

options.syntaxDescription: hq, uhq, ll, ull or lossless (default hq) - What the encoder is tuned for; the tab already sets lossless at quality 0
options.description:
Picks what NVENC is tuned for, which moves the rate control and the buffering underneath whatever preset is in use. hq is the ordinary offline choice and the default. uhq asks for more again, and it is one of the few things the HEVC encoder has that the H.264 one does not - ffmpeg's option list stops at lossless there and carries a fifth constant here. ll and ull trade compression for latency, cutting the encoder's reordering and buffering so a frame comes out almost as soon as it goes in - which is what a live stream wants and what a file does not.

lossless encodes the source exactly. It produces very large files, and the encoder switches itself into constant-QP mode for it whatever rate control was asked for.

This is the one row that can name an option the tab sets itself: with the quality value at 0 the tab emits -tune lossless. The grid's rows go on the command line after the rate control, so a tune set here wins - which also makes hq the way to take an encode back off lossless without touching the quality box.
options.listedValuesDescription:
hq|The default, and the right choice for encoding a file.
uhq|Ultra high quality; more analysis again, and HEVC-only among these two.
ll|Low latency, for live streaming rather than files.
ull|Ultra low latency; the strongest form and the largest quality cost.
lossless|Mathematically lossless output, at an enormous bitrate.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation within a frame; moves bits to the flat areas that band first
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error hides and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking are obvious. Without it, dark and smooth regions are where an encode visibly falls apart first.

NVENC's version is a plain on/off rather than the choice of modes a software encoder offers, with aq-strength beside it deciding how far the quantiser may shift. It is off by default, which is a large part of why a hardware encode can look worse than a software one at the same bitrate.

There is no real speed cost - the analysis is work the hardware does anyway - so this is close to free quality on anything with skies, gradients, fades or large flat surfaces.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|On; what almost any offline encode wants.
0|The default, off.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation across frames; needs lookahead, and a GPU that implements it
options.description:
Where spatial AQ redistributes bits inside one frame, temporal AQ redistributes them between frames, spending more on the parts of the picture that later frames will keep referencing. It is the same idea as a software encoder's macroblock tree.

It needs lookahead frames to work with, so it does nothing unless rc-lookahead is also set. It is the one AQ setting the hardware can refuse outright: ffmpeg's own check prints "Temporal AQ not supported" and carries on without it, which older GPUs will do.

Worth having on material with sustained motion over a background worth protecting. On a fast, cut-heavy source there is much less for it to find.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|On; pair it with rc-lookahead or it does nothing.
0|The default, off.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-15 (default 8) - How far spatial AQ may shift the quantiser; raise for flat sources, lower for grain
options.description:
How far adaptive quantisation is allowed to shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values take more bits out of detailed areas and put more into flat ones. It does nothing at all unless spatial-aq is on - ffmpeg's own description of this option says so.

Raise it when flat regions - skies, walls, gradients, fades to black - show banding or blocking. Lower it when the source is grainy or heavily textured, because there the bits are better left where the detail is, and a strong setting will smooth the grain the rest of your settings are trying to keep.

The scale runs 1 to 15 with 8 in the middle, so this is a coarser control than a software encoder's fractional strength and one step is a real change. 0 is not off - it is refused as out of range.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default, the middle of the range.
5|Grainy or heavily textured sources, keeping bits on detail.
12|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
15|The maximum; strong redistribution, and visible smoothing of texture.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 auto, 0 off or 4 on (default -1) - NVENC's temporal filter; needs bf 4 or more and a recent GPU
options.description:
NVENC's own temporal filter, which averages across neighbouring frames before encoding to take out noise that would otherwise be expensive to code. It is a hardware feature of the newer encoder generations, and ffmpeg prints "Temporal filtering not supported by the device" and carries on without it where the GPU has no such block.

It has a hard requirement beside it: ffmpeg refuses the combination unless there are at least four B-frames, saying "Temporal filtering needs at least 4 B-Frames (-bf 4)". So this row and the bf row are set together or not at all.

Only -1, 0 and 4 mean anything - those are the levels NVENC defines, and the encoder answers anything else with "Invalid temporal filtering level". ffmpeg's own range check on this option is much wider than that and will happily let a 2 or a 7 through to be refused later on.

Like any denoiser it cannot tell sensor noise from fine texture, so on a grainy film scan it takes the grain with it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the encoder decides.
4|Temporal filtering on, which needs bf set to 4 or more.
0|Explicitly off, overriding whatever the preset would pick.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 unset, 0-3, or auto (default -1) - How hard the lookahead analyses; needs rc-lookahead set first
options.description:
How much work the lookahead does with the frames it has been given. Higher levels analyse more and may place frame types and quantisers better, at a cost in encoder throughput - which is what ffmpeg's own description of the option says.

It is meaningless on its own: with rc-lookahead at 0 there are no lookahead frames to analyse. Set that row first.

The named auto constant is 15, and it is not the same thing as the default of -1. -1 leaves the field unset so the driver's own behaviour applies; auto asks the driver to pick a level. The GPU can also cap what it will take, which ffmpeg reports as "Lookahead level not supported" along with the maximum.

Measured against this build the option refuses anything above 15.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the field is left unset.
auto|Asks the driver to pick a level; the constant behind it is 15.
1|A light analysis pass over the lookahead frames.
3|The deepest defined level, and the slowest.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cb chroma quantiser from luma; negative spends more bits on colour
options.description:
Offsets the quantiser used for the Cb chroma plane from the one used for luma. Negative values quantise chroma more finely, spending more bits on colour; positive values coarsen it to spend more on brightness detail.

NVENC splits this into two rows where a software encoder has one, so a shift meant for chroma as a whole means setting qp_cr_offset to match. Setting only one of the two tints where the error lands rather than balancing it, which is occasionally what you want and usually not.

Negative values are worth trying on saturated, colour-critical material, and on animation where flat colour areas show chroma banding. Positive values are a way to buy luma detail on a tight bitrate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Extra bits on colour; useful for animation and saturated sources.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: -12 to 12 (default 0) - Shifts the Cr chroma quantiser from luma; the red-difference half of qp_cb_offset
options.description:
The same control as qp_cb_offset applied to the Cr plane. Negative values quantise the red-difference chroma more finely and positive ones more coarsely.

The two are separate options, so a plain "spend more on chroma" means giving both the same value. Left unequal they weight one chroma plane against the other, which moves where colour error shows rather than how much of it there is.

Chroma is subsampled in the formats this encoder is usually given, so it starts from a quarter of the samples luma has - which is why a small negative offset here can be worth more than the same bits spent on luma detail.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default.
-2|Matches a qp_cb_offset of -2 for an even chroma bias.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Encodes at ten bits from an eight-bit source, which bands far less
options.description:
Ten-bit encoding does not need a ten-bit source. The extra precision is used inside the encoder, where it carries less rounding error through prediction and the transform, and what comes out has visibly finer gradients - skies, fades to black, studio walls - than the same encode at eight bits. It usually compresses a shade better as well.

This is not the colour format, which the tab sets itself and which decides what the encoder is handed. This decides what the encoder writes. Choosing a ten-bit colour format makes the output ten-bit on its own, so this row is for the case where the source is eight-bit and you want ten-bit output anyway.

Set the profile row to main10 alongside it, that being the profile a ten-bit HEVC stream belongs to. The GPU has to have a ten-bit encoder, and ffmpeg says "10 bit encode not supported" where it does not.

The compatibility cost is much smaller than the same move in H.264: main10 is what HDR and most streaming HEVC already use, so current hardware decodes it, where H.264's high10 was never played by anything.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the output bit depth follows the colour format.
1|Ten-bit output from an eight-bit source; set profile:v main10 too.

options.syntaxDescription: auto, forced, 2, 3, 4 or disabled (default auto) - Splits a frame across several NVENC engines on the cards that have them
options.description:
The workstation and datacentre cards carry more than one NVENC engine. Split encoding cuts each frame into horizontal strips and gives them to different engines, so one stream is encoded by several at once - which is throughput a single engine cannot reach and most of the reason those cards have more than one.

The constants are worth reading carefully, because 0 is auto and not off: disabled is 15. auto leaves it to the preset and the tuning info, forced turns it on with the driver choosing how many strips, and 2, 3 and 4 force that many - each doing nothing unless the card actually has that many encoders.

It is not free. A strip boundary is a place the encoder cannot predict across, so the frame is coded in pieces that know nothing about each other, and the compression cost grows with the number of strips. On any single-NVENC card, which is most GeForce hardware, there is nothing to split across and the setting changes nothing either way.

weighted_pred rules it out - ffmpeg carries the message "Split encoding not supported with weighted prediction enabled" - so those two rows are a choice between them. The option is HEVC-only here; the H.264 encoder does not offer it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
auto|The default; the preset and the tuning info decide.
forced|On, with the driver choosing how many strips.
2|Two strips, on a card with at least two encoders.
disabled|Off for every configuration; the constant behind it is 15.

options.syntaxDescription: constqp, vbr or cbr (default -1, whatever the preset implies) - Overrides the rate control mode the tab has already set
options.description:
Which rate control mode NVENC runs. Left alone the value is -1, and the mode follows from the preset and from the bitrate or quality arguments the tab has already put on the command line.

That is the thing to be careful about here. The tab emits its own rate control - a bitrate with a minimum, maximum and buffer size for a bitrate target, or -b:v 0 -cq N for a quality target - and this row overrides the mode underneath it. Asking for constqp under a bitrate target, or cbr under a quality target, produces a command whose two halves disagree, and the encoder resolves that rather than refusing it.

Set it when you know which mode you want and the preset is picking the other one. Leave it alone otherwise.

Older NVENC builds had vbr_hq, cbr_hq and cbr_ld_hq beside these three. Measured against this build they are gone - only constqp, vbr and cbr parse - and the quality half of what they used to mean now lives in the preset and multipass settings.
options.listedValuesDescription:
vbr|Variable bitrate; the mode a quality or average-bitrate target wants.
cbr|Constant bitrate, for streaming and fixed-rate delivery.
constqp|A fixed quantiser, ignoring any bitrate target.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or more frames (default 0, off) - Frames analysed ahead of the encode; off by default, and four other rows need it
options.description:
How many frames ahead the encoder looks before committing to a frame type and a quantiser. A longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and lets the encoder put its I-frames where the cuts actually are, at the cost of memory and of that many frames of latency.

It is off by default on NVENC, and that matters more than the number itself: temporal-aq, b_adapt, no-scenecut and lookahead_level all describe what the lookahead should do, and all of them are inert while there is no lookahead to do it. This row is what switches that whole group on.

The encoder also needs enough buffered frames to hold the window. ffmpeg says "Lookahead not enabled. Increase buffer delay (-delay)" where it cannot, and a GPU with no lookahead block at all gets "RC lookahead not supported".

Past roughly the length of a typical shot there is nothing left for it to learn.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no lookahead, and the rows depending on it do nothing.
32|A sound general setting, about a second at 30 fps.
60|Longer scenes and offline encoding.
250|Deep lookahead; memory-hungry with little more to show for it.

options.syntaxDescription: disabled, qres or fullres (default disabled) - NVENC's own two passes, inside a single ffmpeg pass
options.description:
NVENC can run two passes over each frame inside one encode: a first that measures how difficult the frame is and a second that codes it with that knowledge. qres does the first pass at quarter resolution, fullres at full.

This is not ffmpeg's two-pass, which runs the whole file twice. Nothing here writes a stats file and the encode stays a single run, so it is the way to get better bit distribution out of a hardware encoder without doubling the wall clock.

qres is close to free and is where to start. fullres measures more accurately and costs real throughput, which on a hardware encoder is most of the reason you chose it.

It earns the most under a bitrate target, where the first pass tells the rate controller what it is about to spend. Under a fixed quality target there is much less for it to do.
options.listedValuesDescription:
disabled|The default; a single pass.
qres|Quarter-resolution first pass; the usual choice, and nearly free.
fullres|Full-resolution first pass; the most accurate and the slowest.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, no floor) - The best quantiser rate control may use; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, which is a ceiling on how many bits any one frame may be given. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody will notice, which under a bitrate target frees those bits for the difficult material.

This is NVENC's own option rather than ffmpeg's generic qmin, and the two have different ranges. Measured against this build, a value of 55 is refused as out of range [-1 - 51], so it is the encoder's own bounds that apply here.

Under the quality target the tab emits, a tight floor can stop the encoder reaching the quality asked for, since it is no longer allowed to go where the target wants to take it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; no floor.
10|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
15|A firmer cap, noticeably smaller files on easy content.
20|A hard cap, for size-critical work on clean sources.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, no ceiling) - The worst quantiser rate control may use; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality is allowed to fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocky collapse that difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer hit its bitrate target on those scenes and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

The default of -1 is no limit, so this only matters where the bitrate target is tight. Like qmin it is NVENC's own option rather than ffmpeg's generic one, and it stops at 51.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; no ceiling.
40|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
35|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.
51|The maximum, which is the same as no ceiling at all.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for I-frames; a seed for the rate controller, not a bound
options.description:
The quantiser the rate controller starts I-frames at, before it has learnt anything about the source. It is a seed rather than a bound - once the encode is running the controller moves away from it - so the effect is concentrated in the opening seconds.

That is exactly where a bitrate-targeted encode looks worst. With nothing measured yet the controller guesses, and a bad guess shows as a soft or blocky first shot before it settles. Setting the three init_qp rows near where you know the encode will end up removes that.

Under rc constqp they are not a starting point at all: nothing adapts, so the initial values are the values used throughout.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
20|A high-quality start, for a generous bitrate.
26|A middling start for ordinary delivery bitrates.
32|A conservative start, for a tight bitrate.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for P-frames; normally a step or two above init_qpI
options.description:
The P-frame half of init_qpI. P-frames predict from what came before, so they carry less new information and are conventionally coded a little coarser than the I-frames they hang off - a step or two above the I-frame value is the usual arrangement.

Set it alongside init_qpI and init_qpB rather than on its own. The three together describe the shape of the GOP's bit distribution, and moving one without the others simply shifts where the error lands.

Under rc constqp this is not a starting point but the quantiser P-frames are actually coded at.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
22|About two steps above an init_qpI of 20, the conventional spacing.
28|A tighter budget, with I-frames around 26.
20|Equal to the I-frame value; spends more on P-frames than usual.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 51 (default -1, automatic) - Starting quantiser for B-frames; conventionally the coarsest of the three
options.description:
The B-frame half of init_qpI. B-frames predict from both directions and nothing refers to them unless b_ref_mode says otherwise, so they are conventionally the coarsest of the three - a couple of steps above the P-frame value.

It does nothing where there are no B-frames, and NVENC produces none by default. The bf row is what creates them.

Where b_ref_mode is on, some B-frames are references after all, and coarsening those costs more than it saves - which is an argument for closing the gap to init_qpP rather than widening it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the driver picks.
25|About three steps above an init_qpI of 20, the conventional spacing.
22|A narrow spread, for use with b_ref_mode each or middle.
30|Cheap B-frames, buying quality for the frames referencing them.

options.syntaxDescription: Frames between keyframes (default 12) - ffmpeg's GOP size; the tab sets none for NVENC, so its default applies
options.description:
How many frames may pass before the encoder must start a new GOP with a keyframe. This is ffmpeg's own option rather than one of NVENC's, and it is the only way to reach the keyframe interval from this tab: the tab does not emit a -g for NVENC as it does for the software encoders, so what runs is ffmpeg's own default of 12.

Twelve frames is very short - half a second at 25 fps - and a keyframe is the most expensive frame there is. Raising it is one of the larger size savings available from this tab, and it costs nothing but seek granularity.

Set it against how the file will be used. A couple of seconds is normal for delivery, a segmented stream wants the segment length, and an editing intermediate wants it low or at 1 for all-intra.

A scene cut can still force a keyframe of its own where the lookahead is running and no-scenecut is not set, so this is a ceiling on the spacing rather than a fixed grid.
options.listedValuesDescription:
12|ffmpeg's default, and what runs if this row is left blank.
250|Ten seconds at 25 fps; a sound choice for a delivery file.
50|Two seconds at 25 fps, for tighter seeking and streaming.
1|Every frame a keyframe, for an editing intermediate.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or more, -1 for automatic (default 0) - B-frames between reference frames; NVENC makes none unless asked
options.description:
The longest run of consecutive B-frames the encoder may insert. B-frames predict from both earlier and later frames, which makes them by far the cheapest frames to code, so allowing them lets static and slow material spend its bits where something is actually happening.

This is ffmpeg's own option and its default is 0, so an NVENC encode produces no B-frames at all unless this row is filled in. That is a real compression difference on its own, and it is also what leaves b_adapt, b_ref_mode, init_qpB, unidir_b and tf_level doing nothing on an otherwise default command line.

The driver clamps the run to what the GPU implements and ffmpeg reports it, saying "B-frames=N is not supported by this GPU, switched to M". HEVC B-frames arrived on NVENC later than H.264's, so a card that produces them happily on the other encoder may produce none here.

Every B-frame adds encoding latency and a frame of decode delay, which is why a low-latency tune wants this at 0.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|ffmpeg's default; no B-frames at all.
3|A sound general setting for live action.
4|The minimum tf_level requires, and where most GPUs top out.
-1|Automatic; leaves the choice to the encoder.

options.syntaxDescription: 1 or more (default 1) - Reference frames the motion search may use; more helps repetitive material
options.description:
How many previously decoded frames the motion search may predict from. More references help whenever the same content reappears - repetitive motion, cuts back to an earlier shot, animation that reuses cels - because the encoder can point at the frame that actually matches.

This is ffmpeg's own option, and its default of 1 is far lower than a software encoder's. Raising it is cheap on hardware, where the search is fixed-function rather than something paid for in encoding time.

The GPU decides whether it can oblige: ffmpeg prints "Multiple reference frames are not supported by the device" and carries on with one where it cannot.

The level bounds it as well, through the size of the decoded picture buffer, and that bound tightens as the picture gets larger - so a count that is legal at 1080p need not be at 4K. Past it, the file no longer matches the level in its own header and a compliant decoder is entitled to refuse it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|ffmpeg's default; a single reference.
2|A cheap improvement wherever the GPU supports it.
4|A sound ceiling for delivery, well inside what the levels allow.
8|Repetitive or animated material, at some compatibility risk.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Whether B-frame placement is decided per scene; only does anything with rc-lookahead set
options.description:
Decides where in the sequence B-frames actually go, up to the limit bf sets. On, the encoder uses the lookahead to place them where they pay; off, it simply always uses the maximum run.

ffmpeg's own description of this option is explicit that it applies when lookahead is enabled, so with rc-lookahead at 0 the setting is inert whichever way it is left.

Turning it off is a latency and determinism choice rather than a quality one: it removes a decision that depends on frames the encoder has not yet delivered. For a file there is no reason to.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; B-frames placed where the lookahead says they pay.
0|A fixed maximum run, for deterministic low-latency output.

options.syntaxDescription: disabled, each or middle (default -1, left to the driver) - Whether B-frames may themselves be used as references
options.description:
Normally B-frames are never referenced by anything, so they are disposable. This allows some of them to act as references for other frames, which builds a hierarchy and improves compression noticeably on material with long B-frame runs.

each makes every B-frame a reference. middle promotes only the middle of each run, which is the arrangement a software encoder's B-pyramid produces and the cheaper of the two. disabled states the conventional behaviour outright, rather than leaving the field unset the way the default does.

It is a feature of the later NVENC generations, and ffmpeg names which part is missing rather than failing: "Each B frame reference mode is not supported", or "Middle B frame reference mode is not supported".

It needs B-frames to exist, so the bf row comes first. And a referenced B-frame is no longer disposable, which is an argument against coarsening it with init_qpB.
options.listedValuesDescription:
middle|Promotes the middle B-frame of each run; the usual choice.
each|Every B-frame a reference; the strongest form.
disabled|Conventional disposable B-frames, stated explicitly.
-1|The default; the field is left unset for the driver to decide.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Lets B-frames predict in one direction only, for latency rather than compression
options.description:
A B-frame normally predicts in both directions, from a frame before it and a frame after it, and that backward reference is most of why it codes so cheaply. This restricts them to looking backwards only, keeping the other half of what a B-frame is - that nothing refers to it, so it can be coded cheaply without the cost carrying forward.

What it buys is the reordering. A frame that predicts from something later cannot be coded until that later frame has arrived, which is the delay B-frames impose on a live encode; one that only looks back does not have to wait. It is a low-latency feature, and it belongs with tune ll or ull rather than with an offline encode.

For a file there is little reason to set it. Giving up the backward reference gives up most of the compression B-frames were there for, and an offline encode has no latency budget to spend the difference on.

It needs B-frames to exist at all, so the bf row comes first, and it needs a GPU that implements it - ffmpeg says "Unidirectional B-Frames not supported by the device" and carries on without it. The H.264 encoder has no such option; this is one of the three that are HEVC-only here.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; B-frames predict in both directions.
1|Unidirectional B-frames, for low-latency encoding.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Set to 1 to stop the lookahead inserting an I-frame at a scene cut
options.description:
With the lookahead running, NVENC inserts an I-frame where it detects a cut, because a cut is the one place a keyframe is nearly free and predicting across it is nearly useless. This turns that off.

ffmpeg's own description says it applies when lookahead is enabled, so like b_adapt it does nothing while rc-lookahead is 0.

The reason to set it is a fixed keyframe grid - segmented streaming, or a workflow that cuts on a known frame count - where a keyframe arriving early is a problem rather than a saving. For an ordinary file leave it alone: adaptive I-frames are one of the larger wins the lookahead buys.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; a detected cut gets its own I-frame.
1|Keyframes only on the g interval, for a fixed segment grid.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Makes a forced keyframe an IDR, so it is a real seek point
options.description:
A keyframe is not automatically a point a decoder can start from. An I-frame refreshes the picture; an IDR additionally empties the reference list, so nothing after it may refer to anything before it. Only the IDR is a clean entry point.

This makes every keyframe forced from outside - by a -force_key_frames expression, or by a segmenting muxer asking for one - an IDR rather than a plain I-frame.

Set it whenever the output is going to be cut, segmented or seeked at those points. It costs a little compression, since the frames after an IDR lose access to references they could otherwise have used.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; forced keyframes are plain I-frames.
1|Forced keyframes become IDRs, for segmenting and clean seeking.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Lets the encoder mark some P-frames non-reference, so it can code them cheaply
options.description:
A P-frame is normally a reference, so its errors propagate to everything predicting from it and the encoder must spend accordingly. This lets it mark some of them as referenced by nothing, which means they can be coded cheaply without the cost carrying forward.

It is the B-frame trick applied to P-frames, and it is a way to get some of that benefit where B-frames are unavailable - a GPU with no HEVC B-frame support, or a latency budget that cannot afford the reordering.

Insertion is automatic and there is no count to set. It helps most under a tight bitrate, where the saved bits go somewhere useful, and least where the bitrate is generous.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; every P-frame is a reference.
1|Automatic non-reference P-frames, for tight bitrates and low latency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Weighted prediction, letting a frame scale its reference; helps fades and flashes
options.description:
Weighted prediction lets a frame scale and offset the reference it predicts from, so a frame that is simply brighter or darker than the one before does not have to be re-coded from scratch. Fades, flashes and lighting changes are where it earns its keep.

NVENC's version is a plain on/off where a software encoder offers a choice of strengths, and the GPU may not implement it at all - which ffmpeg reports as "Weighted Prediction not supported" before carrying on without it.

It is not free of side effects on this encoder. ffmpeg also carries the message "Split encoding not supported with weighted prediction enabled", so on the multi-engine cards this gives up the parallelism the split_encode_mode row is about. On a source with no fades in it there is nothing to gain in exchange.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default, off.
1|On, for sources with fades, flashes or changing light.

options.syntaxDescription: main, main10, rext or mv (default main) - Caps the tools used so limited decoders can play the file
options.description:
Restricts the encoder to the coding tools and bit depths a given HEVC profile permits, so a decoder implementing only that profile can play the result. main is 8-bit 4:2:0 and is the default here; main10 is 10-bit 4:2:0; rext is the Range Extensions profile, which is where 4:4:4 chroma lives.

main10 is the one worth knowing about. Ten-bit HEVC bands far less than eight-bit and usually compresses a little better, and unlike H.264's high10 it is what streaming services and HDR already use, so current hardware decodes it. The bit depth itself comes from the colour format the tab sets, or from the highbitdepth row; this names the profile the stream is tagged with, and the two have to agree.

That is the trap. The profile and the colour format are set in different places, and asking for main here over a ten-bit colour format is a contradiction the driver resolves rather than a setting that takes effect. Change them together.

mv is Multiview HEVC, for a stereoscopic stream carrying two views. It is not a way to encode an ordinary file - ffmpeg carries both "Multiview not supported by the device" and "Multiview encoding only works for Main profile content", and nothing on this tab produces a second view to put in it. And the row is named profile:v rather than plain profile because ffmpeg has this option on audio encoders too: a bare -profile draws "Please use -profile:a or -profile:v, -profile is ambiguous" and is then applied to whatever streams will take it, which is not a thing to leave to chance in a command that also carries an audio encoder.
options.listedValuesDescription:
main|The default; 8-bit 4:2:0 and the broadest compatibility.
main10|10-bit 4:2:0; better gradients, and widely supported by hardware.
rext|Range Extensions, for a 4:4:4 colour format.
mv|Multiview HEVC; a stereoscopic profile, not an ordinary one.

options.syntaxDescription: main or high (default main) - The HEVC tier, which raises the bitrate and buffer limits the level allows
options.description:
HEVC splits every level into two tiers. Main tier is sized for consumer delivery; high tier raises the bitrate and buffer ceilings that same level permits, several times over, for contribution and mastering work. It exists so that a level number does not have to mean one bitrate for a Blu-ray and for a studio master alike.

It changes no coding decision on its own. What it changes is what the stream's own header says it is allowed to do, and therefore which decoders will accept it - a decoder that claims main tier at your level is entitled to refuse a file tagged high tier, so setting it for no reason is a way to have a file rejected that would otherwise have played.

It only means anything alongside the level row, since a tier qualifies a level, and high tier is defined from level 4 upwards. Set it where a genuinely high bitrate would otherwise exceed what your level permits, and leave it alone otherwise.

This is one of the three options the HEVC encoder has and the H.264 one does not - H.264 has no tiers at all.
options.listedValuesDescription:
main|The default; consumer delivery, and what hardware decoders expect.
high|Contribution and mastering bitrates, from level 4 upwards.

options.syntaxDescription: auto, or 1 to 6.2 (default auto) - Decoder level written to the stream header
options.description:
The decoder level written into the stream header. Levels bound resolution, frame rate, bitrate and how many pictures may be held in the decoded picture buffer, and hardware decoders advertise the highest level they implement.

The encoder works out a suitable level on its own, so this is only worth setting when a target demands a specific one - a television or a set-top box that refuses anything above 5.1, say. The tier row qualifies whatever is set here, main and high tier at the same level allowing very different bitrates.

Spell it exactly as the list has it. These names are constants, and a spelling that is not one of them is not rejected: it is evaluated as a plain number instead, and measured against this build only a result outside 0 to 186 is refused. So 6.3 is accepted and tags the stream with a level nobody asked for, while H.264's 1b - which is not an HEVC level - is refused outright.
options.listedValuesDescription:
auto|The default; the encoder picks a level to fit.
4.1|A common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
6.2|The highest defined; 8K and high frame rates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Writes access unit delimiters, which some transport and broadcast chains require
options.description:
An access unit delimiter is a small NAL unit marking where each coded frame begins. It carries no picture data - it exists so a demuxer can find frame boundaries without parsing the slices.

Almost nothing needs it in a file. MPEG-TS and broadcast-style workflows are where it comes up, along with some hardware decoders and analysis tools that expect the boundary marked explicitly.

The cost is a handful of bytes per frame, so setting it where it is not needed is harmless but pointless.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no delimiters.
1|Writes them, for MPEG-TS and broadcast delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Carries SMPTE 12M timecode from the source into the encoded stream
options.description:
SMPTE 12M timecode, written into the video as a time code SEI message beside the picture rather than as a track of its own. Where the source carries one - a camera original, a broadcast capture, anything that came off tape - this passes it through, and like a53cc beside it, it is on by default.

The reverse case is what makes the row worth knowing. A timecode that survives a re-encode is this option's doing and has nothing to do with any timecode the container carries, so a file that looks as though it has no metadata at all can still arrive with one embedded in the video, where an editor will find it and a player will not.

Turn it off for a clean master, or where something downstream reads the SEI and gets confused by timing from the original. It costs a few bytes a frame when there is a timecode to write and nothing at all when there is not.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; a timecode in the source is carried through.
0|Strips the timecode SEI from the output.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Carries A/53 closed captions from the source into the encoded stream
options.description:
Broadcast and capture sources carry closed captions inside the video itself, as A/53 caption data attached to the picture rather than as a subtitle track. This passes that data through into the encoded stream, and unusually for this list it is on by default.

The reason to know the row is here is the reverse case. A re-encode of a US broadcast capture keeps its captions through this option and nothing on the subtitle side is involved, which is how they survive a conversion that appears to carry no subtitle track at all.

Turn it off to strip them - for a clean master, or where something downstream trips over caption data it was not expecting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; captions in the source are carried through.
0|Strips the caption data from the output.

options.syntaxDescription: default, screen, film (default default) - screen enables palette and block copy; film synthesises grain at playback
options.description:
Tells the encoder what kind of material it is looking at so it can enable tools suited to it. screen turns on palette mode and intra block copy, which code large flat colour areas and repeated UI elements far more cheaply than ordinary prediction - the difference on a desktop capture or a slide deck is dramatic.

film is not a grain-preservation setting. It switches on AV1's film grain synthesis: the encoder denoises the picture, measures the grain it removed, and writes a parameter set so the decoder regenerates it at playback. That saves a great deal of bitrate, at the cost of grain that is statistically similar rather than identical.

default suits ordinary camera footage. Those three are the only spellings libaom takes here - anything else, animation included, is refused and the encode does not start.
options.listedValuesDescription:
default|Ordinary live action and animation.
screen|Desktop capture, slides and UI recordings.
film|Grainy film, with the grain synthesised at playback rather than coded.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr, ssim, ssimulacra2, iq, vmaf and its variants (default psnr) - Which metric the encoder optimises for
options.description:
Selects the distortion metric the encoder's decisions are scored against, which changes where bits go rather than just what gets reported. psnr minimises squared error, ssim weights by structural similarity, and ssimulacra2 and the vmaf variants optimise against perceptual models. iq is an image-quality tune aimed at stills and all-intra work.

ssim generally produces a picture people prefer over psnr. The vmaf modes optimise directly for a metric widely used to judge streaming quality, which is useful if you are being measured on it and questionable if you are not - tuning for a metric tends to exploit it.

Two cautions specific to this build. butteraugli is not compiled in and is refused outright, so it is not on the list above. And every vmaf mode wants a model file at libvmaf's own default path: without one the encoder prints a single "could not read model" line and carries on encoding anyway, so a vmaf tune can look like it ran when it did not.
options.listedValuesDescription:
psnr|The default; minimises squared error.
ssim|Structure-weighted decisions; usually the better-looking choice.
ssimulacra2|A perceptual model, and the one that needs no external files.
iq|Image-quality tuning, aimed at stills and all-intra material.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr, qm-psnr (default psnr) - Which distortion measure the mode search itself uses
options.description:
Chooses the distortion measure used inside the encoder's own rate-distortion search, which is a separate question from the tune above: tune sets the goal, this sets the yardstick the block-level decisions are made with.

qm-psnr weights the error by the quantisation matrix in force, so the search stops treating a high-frequency coefficient the matrix is about to throw away as though it mattered as much as a low-frequency one. That only means anything with enable-qm switched on.

It is cheap to try and its effect is confined to where bits land within a block, not to how many the frame gets.
options.listedValuesDescription:
psnr|The default; plain squared error in the search.
qm-psnr|Error weighted by the quantisation matrix; pair it with enable-qm 1.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 variance, 2 complexity, 3 cyclic refresh; 1 favours flat skies
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame. Mode 1 distributes by variance, taking bits from busy areas where error is masked and giving them to flat ones where banding shows. Mode 2 works from a complexity estimate instead. Mode 3 is cyclic refresh, which refreshes part of each frame in turn and is aimed at low-bitrate streaming rather than file encoding.

libaom leaves this off by default because its other tools already handle much of the same problem, and the modes can hurt as often as they help on ordinary content.

Worth trying on sources that band, and worth measuring rather than assuming.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Variance-based, the usual choice if flat areas band.
2|Complexity-based distribution.
3|Cyclic refresh, for low-bitrate streaming.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 1) - Varies the quantiser within a frame; 3 and 4 target visual rather than metric quality
options.description:
Allows the quantiser to vary across a frame rather than staying fixed, so bits can follow what matters within the picture. Mode 1 optimises for an objective metric, mode 3 targets keyframe visual quality, and mode 4 uses a user-rating-derived visual model. Modes 5 and 6 are further variants this build accepts.

The objective default improves measured scores. The visual modes deliberately spend bits where people look rather than where error is largest, which is usually the better choice for material anyone will actually watch.

It depends on the temporal dependency model, so setting enable-tpl-model to 0 takes most of it away. Note also that HDR sources are already given a delta quantiser mode automatically, so a value set here replaces that rather than adding to it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; objective optimisation.
0|Off; a fixed quantiser across the frame.
3|Targets keyframe visual quality.
4|Visual quality from a user-rating model.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Quantisation matrices; often improves detail retention at low bitrates, tuned via qm-min and qm-max
options.description:
Quantisation matrices weight quantisation by frequency rather than applying one step size across the whole transform block, so high-frequency coefficients - fine texture and grain - can be kept or discarded independently of the low-frequency structure.

Turning them on generally helps retain texture at a given bitrate and is a common recommendation for grainy or detailed sources. It pairs with the qm-min and qm-max range settings that control how aggressive the shaping is.

It is off by default and costs essentially nothing to try.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; uniform quantisation.
1|Enables the matrices; commonly a gain on detailed or grainy sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 5) - Lowest quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1 to have any effect
options.description:
With quantisation matrices enabled, the encoder picks a matrix per frame from a range of flatness levels. This sets the lowest level it may choose, where lower numbers mean a more aggressively shaped matrix that treats high frequencies differently from low ones.

A shaped matrix keeps more of the fine texture that flat quantisation rounds away, which is why enabling matrices is a common recommendation for grainy and detailed sources.

It does nothing unless enable-qm is set to 1, and it should not exceed qm-max. Note that nothing on this path range-checks the number the way the aomenc command line does, so a value outside 0-15 is accepted and then means nothing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default.
3|Allows more aggressive shaping, retaining more fine texture.
0|The most steeply shaped extreme of the range.
8|A narrower, more conservative floor.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 9) - Highest quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1 to have any effect
options.description:
The upper end of the quantisation matrix range the encoder may select from. Level 15 is effectively unshaped, treating all frequencies alike, so raising the maximum lets the encoder fall back to ordinary flat quantisation when shaping would not help.

Lowering it forces shaping to be applied even where the encoder would rather not, which retains texture more consistently and costs efficiency.

Like qm-min it requires enable-qm 1, it should not fall below qm-min, and it is not range-checked here.
options.listedValuesDescription:
9|The default.
15|Lets the encoder pick an effectively unshaped matrix.
12|A mild widening of the default range.
7|Forces shaping throughout, at a cost in efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-7 (default 0) - Biases transform coefficient decisions towards sharpness at a cost in measured error
options.description:
Biases the rate-distortion decisions made about transform coefficients towards keeping the ones that carry sharpness, rather than dropping them because they are expensive relative to the error they remove.

Higher values retain more fine detail and edge definition, and cost both bitrate and measured quality, since the encoder is deliberately choosing something a plain error metric scores lower.

It is a milder tool than the psychovisual settings in x264 and x265, and it is worth a try on detailed sources that come out looking soft.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no bias.
2|A mild sharpness bias for detailed live action.
4|Noticeably sharper, at a real bitrate cost.
7|The maximum.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Adaptive use of the quantize_b path; small efficiency gain for a little extra encode time
options.description:
Selects adaptively between the two entropy coding paths AV1 provides for transform coefficients, choosing per situation rather than using one throughout. The gain is small and comes entirely from more accurate coefficient coding, not from any change in what is encoded.

It costs a little encoding time and is off by default. On slow, quality-focused encodes it is a cheap fraction of a percent.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Adaptive selection, a small gain on slow encodes.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Lets the chroma planes take their own quantiser offset instead of following luma
options.description:
The delta quantiser machinery normally moves the quantiser for a block as a whole. This lets the chroma planes be offset separately, so colour can be given more or fewer bits than the luminance it sits under.

The case for it is material where the colour is doing the work and the usual luma-led allocation starves it - saturated animation, strongly graded footage, anything where chroma noise or blocking shows before luma detail does. On ordinary camera video the default allocation is already close to right and this changes little.

It is off by default and costs no meaningful encode time, so it is one to try and measure rather than to reason about.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; chroma follows the luma quantiser.
1|Chroma gets its own offset; worth trying on saturated or graded material.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 1) - CDEF deringing filter: 0 off, 1 on, 2 skip non-ref frames, 3 by qindex; off preserves fine grain
options.description:
The constrained directional enhancement filter is an in-loop deblocking and deringing stage that follows edge directions, so it cleans up ringing around edges without smearing the edge itself.

It is on by default and generally worth leaving on: without it, ringing artefacts around high-contrast edges persist into the reference frames and propagate.

Grain-preservation setups sometimes disable it because it removes fine noise along with the ringing, but that only makes sense at bitrates high enough that there is no ringing to remove.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Grain preservation at high bitrates, accepting some ringing.
2|Filters reference frames only, saving a little time.
3|Applied selectively by quantiser.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - The loop restoration filter, which repairs coding artefacts after deblocking
options.description:
Loop restoration is a filter that runs after deblocking and CDEF, fitting a correction to each region to bring the reconstructed picture back towards the source. It repairs ringing and general coding error that the earlier filters leave behind.

It is on by default and is generally worth keeping, because the repaired frame is what later frames predict from, so the benefit compounds.

Grain-preserving setups sometimes disable it, since like CDEF it cannot distinguish fine noise from the artefacts it is removing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for normal encoding.
0|Off, for grain retention at high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 1) - The deblocking filter: 0 off, 1 everywhere, 2 reference frames only, 3 by quantiser
options.description:
AV1's deblocking filter is the first of the three in-loop stages, smoothing the boundaries between transform blocks before CDEF and loop restoration run. This decides where it is applied rather than how hard - the strength is chosen by the encoder.

Modes 2 and 3 are speed settings dressed as quality ones: skipping non-reference frames, or skipping where the quantiser is low enough that there is nothing to deblock, saves time and leaves the frames that matter filtered. Mode 0 turns it off entirely, which is only defensible at bitrates high enough that no block edges are visible.

Turning it off does preserve fine grain, and it also lets block edges into every frame that predicts from the result, so it is the most expensive of the three filters to switch off.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; deblocking everywhere.
2|Reference frames only; a small speed gain.
3|Applied by quantiser, skipping frames that do not need it.
0|Off entirely, for grain retention at very high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Lets the deblocking filter strength vary within a frame rather than being set per frame
options.description:
With this on, the loop filter level is signalled per superblock instead of once for the whole frame, so a busy region and a flat one can be deblocked differently.

It pairs naturally with a delta quantiser mode, because once the quantiser varies across the frame a single filter strength is wrong somewhere by construction - too strong where the quantiser is low and too weak where it is high.

It costs a small amount of signalling and a little encode time, and it is off by default.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; one filter level per frame.
1|Per-superblock filter levels; a natural companion to a delta quantiser mode.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 7) - Frames the alt-ref temporal filter may use; fewer suits high motion, more smooths noisy sources
options.description:
How many neighbouring frames the alternate-reference filter may blend together when it builds an alt-ref frame. The alt-ref is a synthetic, denoised frame that other frames predict from, and averaging several frames is what removes the noise.

More frames means a cleaner alt-ref and better prediction for the frames referring to it, which saves bits - but also means grain and fine motion detail are averaged away more thoroughly.

Grain-preserving setups lower this, sometimes to 0, accepting the bitrate cost to keep noise intact.
options.listedValuesDescription:
7|The default.
3|Reduced blending, keeping more grain and fine motion.
0|Disables the temporal filter entirely, for maximum grain retention.
15|The maximum; cleanest alt-ref, at the cost of fine detail.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 5) - Strength of the alt-ref temporal filter; lower preserves grain, higher cleans up noisy sources
options.description:
How aggressively the alternate-reference filter blends the frames it has gathered. Where arnr-maxframes decides how many frames are involved, this decides how much of each survives.

Higher values give a smoother, cleaner reference that predicts well and saves bitrate, at the cost of grain and fine detail being averaged out of the reference and therefore out of everything predicting from it.

Lowering it to 1 or 2 is the usual move on grainy film. Raising it is the half with less to show for itself: measured against this build, 4, 5 and 6 all produce byte-identical output, so the useful range in practice runs downwards from the default rather than up.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default.
2|Grainy film, keeping noise and texture.
0|No filtering; maximum grain retention.
3|A mild reduction, still noticeably cleaner than 2.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Temporal filtering on keyframes; 2 adds an overlay frame but can break seeking in some players
options.description:
Applies the same temporal filtering used for alt-ref frames to keyframes as well, so a keyframe is built from several source frames rather than from one. A cleaner keyframe predicts better for everything that follows it.

Mode 2 additionally codes an overlay frame to correct the difference between the filtered keyframe and the actual source frame, which fixes the mismatch the filtering introduces.

Mode 2 is not compatible with all downstream pipelines and is best avoided unless you have reason to want it; grain-preserving encodes often set 0 for the same reasons they lower arnr strength.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; filtered keyframes.
0|Unfiltered keyframes, for grain retention.
2|Filtering with a correcting overlay frame.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 off, or a strength (default 0) - Denoises the picture by this much and has the decoder synthesise matching grain
options.description:
AV1's film grain synthesis. The encoder denoises the picture by the amount given, measures the grain it took out, and writes a parameter set the decoder uses to regenerate grain at playback - so the grain costs a few bytes of description instead of a large share of the bitrate. On grainy film that is the single largest saving libaom can make.

What comes back is statistically similar rather than identical, which is the trade. Values around 10 suit lightly grainy digital, 25 an ordinary film scan, and above 50 the denoising starts taking picture with it. 0, the default, leaves the source alone and codes whatever grain is in it.

The companion row below decides whether the denoised picture is the one that gets encoded. Both were measured against the bundled build: this parameter overrides the -denoise-noise-level 0 the tab sends for itself, so setting it here is what makes either row do anything.

The encoder may print "Solving latest noise equation system failed" on a source with no real grain in it, which is its noise model declining to fit rather than an error - the encode carries on.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|Off; the grain in the source is coded as picture.
10|Light denoising, for lightly grainy digital sources.
25|An ordinary 35mm scan.
50|Heavy grain, at the edge of what stays faithful.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Whether the grain-synthesis denoiser's clean picture is what actually gets encoded
options.description:
This is the second half of the noise level set on the Video tab. That setting measures the grain, denoises the picture and writes a grain parameter set for the decoder to regenerate at playback; this decides whether the denoised picture is the one handed to the encoder, or whether the grain table is written while the original frames are encoded as they are.

On by default, which is the arrangement that saves the bitrate: coding a clean picture is far cheaper than coding grain, and the decoder puts the grain back. Setting it to 0 keeps the real grain in the stream and writes the synthesis parameters alongside it, which is a great deal more expensive and preserves the actual noise rather than something statistically like it.

It does nothing at all unless a noise level is set, and the two are worth thinking about together - a high noise level with denoising off is asking to pay for the grain twice.
options.listedValuesDescription:
