1|The default; encode the denoised picture and resynthesise the grain.
0|Encode the grain as it is, with the synthesis parameters written alongside.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - The temporal dependency model, which spends bits on frames other frames will predict from
options.description:
Before encoding, libaom looks ahead and works out how much later frames depend on each earlier one, then lowers the quantiser on the frames that carry the most weight. A frame twenty others predict from is worth far more bits than one nothing refers to, and this is what discovers that.

It is the single biggest reason libaom's quality per bit holds up on long GOPs, and it is on by default. It is also what deltaq-mode leans on, so turning this off takes most of the delta quantiser modes away with it.

The only reason to disable it is speed, and it is an expensive way to buy speed compared with the encoder's own speed setting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on.
0|Off; faster, and measurably worse per bit.

options.syntaxDescription: 3-7 (default 7) - How many reference frames the encoder may choose between
options.description:
AV1 lets a block predict from any of up to seven reference frames, and this caps how many of them the encoder will consider. Every one it may use is another candidate the motion search has to try, so the setting is a direct trade of encoding time against prediction quality.

Cutting it to 4 or 5 is a genuine speed lever on slow presets and costs little on material where the recent past is all that is worth referring to. It costs more on content that repeats - a locked-off shot, a panning background that comes back - which is exactly what the further references are for.

The minimum this build accepts is 3.
options.listedValuesDescription:
7|The default; all references available.
5|A moderate speed gain, little loss on ordinary footage.
4|Faster still; noticeable on repetitive or static content.
3|The minimum.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-5 (default 5) - Depth of the golden-frame pyramid, which sets how many layers of reference nesting are used
options.description:
Frames between golden frames are arranged as a pyramid: a few high-level frames are coded well and the rest predict from them, layer by layer. This is how deep that nesting may go.

A deeper pyramid is more efficient, because the frames nobody predicts from sit at the bottom and can be coded cheaply, and it is also more work and more latency. A shallower one flattens the structure, which costs compression and shortens the dependency chains.

Lowering it is occasionally worth doing on very short clips or high-motion material where deep prediction chains do not pay off, and it is otherwise best left alone.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default; the deepest pyramid.
3|A shallower structure; a little faster, a little worse.
2|Shallow nesting, for short or high-motion clips.
0|Flat; no pyramid at all.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-47 (default 0) - Longest run of frames between golden frames; 0 lets the encoder decide
options.description:
Golden frames are the high-quality anchors the pyramid above is built around, and the encoder normally places them where the content suggests. This caps how far apart two of them may end up.

Forcing them closer together gives more anchors and so more places for prediction to restart cleanly, which helps on material that changes constantly and wastes bits on material that does not. Forcing them further apart is rarely useful, since the encoder was already free to space them out.

0 means no cap, which is the default and almost always the right answer - the encoder's own placement is informed by the lookahead, and a fixed number is not.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the encoder chooses.
16|A firm cap, giving more frequent anchors.
32|A loose cap, rarely binding.
8|Very frequent golden frames; costly, and only for restless content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Whole-frame motion models, which code a pan or a zoom once instead of per block
options.description:
Global motion estimates a single transform describing how the whole frame moved - a pan, a zoom, a rotation - and signals it once, so blocks that simply went along with the camera cost almost nothing to code.

On footage with real camera movement it is a clear win. On a locked-off shot there is no global motion to find and the estimation is time spent for nothing, which is the case for turning it off.

It is on by default and the estimation cost is modest, so switching it off is a speed decision rather than a quality one.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on for anything with camera movement.
0|Off; a small speed gain on static shots.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Locally warped motion, which lets a block rotate or scale rather than only translate
options.description:
Ordinary motion compensation can only shift a block. Warped motion fits a small affine transform per block instead, so a region that is rotating, scaling or shearing - a turning head, an object moving towards the camera - can be predicted properly rather than approximated by a shift and a large residual.

It is one of AV1's more expensive tools on both sides: it costs the encoder search time and the decoder real work. It earns that on footage with rotation and perspective change and earns much less on flat panning.

On by default, and a reasonable thing to turn off if decode complexity on weak hardware is a concern.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on.
0|Off; faster to encode and cheaper to decode.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Overlapped block motion compensation, which blends predictions across block edges
options.description:
OBMC predicts each block using its neighbours' motion vectors as well as its own and blends the results across the boundary, which softens the seams that block-based motion compensation leaves behind.

It removes a class of artefact that is otherwise hard to reach - visible block structure in smooth moving areas - and it costs both encode search time and decode time.

On by default. Turning it off is a speed or decoder-complexity decision, and the picture is measurably worse for it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on.
0|Off; faster, with more visible block structure in motion.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Motion vector cost updates: 0 per superblock, 1 per SB row, 2 per tile, 3 off; higher is faster
options.description:
How often the encoder recalculates the cost tables it uses to price motion vectors during the search. Recomputing them often keeps the prices accurate as the statistics change through a frame; recomputing them rarely saves time.

Higher values update less often and encode faster, at a small cost in decision quality because the search is choosing vectors against slightly stale prices.

It is purely a speed dial and does not change what the format can express.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; most frequent updates and the most accurate decisions.
1|Update per SB row, a reasonable compromise.
2|Less frequent updates, noticeably faster.
3|Least frequent; fastest, with the roughest cost estimates.

options.syntaxDescription: dynamic, 64, 128 (default dynamic) - Superblock size; 64 suits small frames and 128 large ones
options.description:
The superblock is the largest unit the partition search starts from, and everything below it is a subdivision. 128 gives the encoder the option of covering a large flat area with one decision; 64 halves the search space and suits frames where such areas are rare.

dynamic is the default and picks per encode from the frame size and the speed setting, which is the right answer nearly always - it lands on 64 for small frames and considers 128 for large ones.

Pinning it is worth doing only when measuring: 128 on 4K flat-heavy content, 64 when the picture is detailed everywhere and the large-block decisions never win.
options.listedValuesDescription:
dynamic|The default; chosen from the frame size and speed.
64|Smaller superblocks; suits SD and busy, detailed frames.
128|Larger superblocks; suits 4K and flat, uniform frames.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Palette mode, which codes a block as an index into a short colour list
options.description:
Palette mode represents a block as a small list of colours plus an index per pixel, which is dramatically cheaper than transform coding whenever a region really does contain only a handful of distinct colours - text, UI chrome, line art, charts.

It is on by default and the encoder only reaches for it where it pays, so the usual reason to touch this is to turn it off on photographic material where it will never be chosen and the search for it is wasted time.

It is also one of the two tools tune-content=screen exists to emphasise, so on screen capture this is a setting to leave well alone.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on, and especially for screen content.
0|Off; a small speed gain on purely photographic sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or a ratio (default 0) - Minimum compression ratio, capping how large any one frame may be
options.description:
A floor on how much the encoder must compress, expressed as a ratio against the uncompressed frame. Setting it to 20 tells the encoder no frame may exceed a twentieth of its raw size, whatever the rate control would otherwise have spent there.

The reason to want one is a downstream constraint rather than a picture one: a decoder or a delivery pipeline that cannot cope with a single enormous frame, which is what an intra frame on difficult material can become. It is a hard cap and the encoder meets it by raising the quantiser on the frames that would have breached it.

0 is the default and means no constraint. Nothing on this path range-checks the value, so a number chosen carelessly simply binds tighter than intended.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no constraint.
20|A generous cap; only the largest frames are affected.
50|A firm cap, visible on difficult intra frames.
10|A loose constraint that will rarely bind.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or a percentage (default 0) - Ceiling on an intra frame's size, as a percentage of the target frame size
options.description:
Caps what a keyframe or other intra frame may spend, as a percentage of what an average frame at the target bitrate would cost. 300 means an intra frame may be three times the size of an ordinary one.

Intra frames are naturally far larger than inter frames and the rate controller lets them be, which is usually right - a good keyframe pays for itself across everything predicting from it. It stops being right where a peak rate matters: a buffer to fill, a streaming ladder, a device with a bitrate ceiling it will not exceed.

0 is the default and means no limit. It only applies where there is a bitrate target to be a percentage of, so it does nothing in constant quality mode.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; intra frames spend what they need.
800|A generous ceiling, binding only on the worst cases.
400|A moderate cap for constrained delivery.
200|A tight cap; visible softening on keyframes.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or a percentage (default 0) - Ceiling on an inter frame's size, as a percentage of the target frame size
options.description:
The same cap as max-intra-rate applied to predicted frames instead. A value of 200 lets an inter frame reach twice the size of an average one and no further.

Inter frames are already small by comparison, so this binds far less often - it is the setting for the occasional frame after a hard cut or a flash where prediction fails and the encoder codes nearly everything afresh.

0 is the default and means no limit, and like the intra ceiling it needs a bitrate target to mean anything at all.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no ceiling.
400|A generous ceiling for peak-rate control.
200|A moderate cap, binding after hard cuts.
120|A tight cap; the rate stays flat and hard frames suffer.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-10000 (default 0) - Corpus-relative complexity for single-pass VBR; refuses any other rate control mode
options.description:
Single-pass VBR has no second pass to tell it how hard this file is compared with everything else, so it treats every source as average. This supplies that number by hand: a value describing where this content sits against a corpus, which the rate controller then uses to decide whether the file deserves more or fewer bits than its target implies.

It is the one setting here that is worth reaching for only if you already have the number - it comes from measuring a body of similar content, not from taste. Left at 0 the feature is off and the ordinary single-pass behaviour applies.

The constraint is absolute and worth knowing before setting it: libaom accepts this only in single-pass VBR. Set it alongside constant quality, or with two-pass turned on, and the encoder refuses to open at all with "VBR corpus complexity is supported only in the case of single pass VBR mode" - immediately, before any encoding starts, but the run does not happen.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the feature is off.
30|A source below average complexity for its corpus.
60|A source somewhat above average.
100|Well above average; more bits than the target implies.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-5 (default 1) - What it optimises for; 0 visual quality, 1 PSNR, 2 SSIM, 3 image quality, 4 MS-SSIM, 5 VMAF
options.description:
Tune picks the quality model the encoder optimises its internal decisions against, which changes rate-distortion choices, filtering and where bits land rather than just which score gets reported. 0 is visual quality, 1 PSNR, 2 SSIM, 3 still-image quality, 4 MS-SSIM and 5 VMAF.

Tune 1 is the metric-safe default. Tune 0 gives a sharper, more detailed picture for lower scores and more artefacts. Tune 5 applies an unsharp mask to the source before encoding, which the encoder announces as it starts - so it changes the picture rather than only the decisions made about it.

Two of them take other rows away from you. Tune 4 says outright that it overrides sharpness, the variance boost strength and curve, and enable-qm with its min and max levels; tune 3 overrides those plus max-tx-size and scm.

Tune 3 will not encode from this tab at all: it needs an all-intra or low-delay prediction structure, and the encode is refused with "Tune IQ only supports all-intra and low delay" before a frame is written. This is the mainline SVT-AV1 inside ffmpeg, so 5 is VMAF here rather than the film grain bundle the svt-av1-hdr build on the AV1AN tab offers.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default, optimising for PSNR and the safe choice for general video.
0|Live action or animation where visible detail matters more than metric scores.
2|SSIM-driven decisions, a middle ground between 0 and 1.
4|MS-SSIM, which also overrides sharpness, variance boost and the quantisation matrices.
5|VMAF, which sharpens the source with an unsharp mask first.

options.syntaxDescription: 0.0-8.0 (default 0.0) - Psychovisual rate distortion biasing towards texture; raise for grainy, heavily detailed film
options.description:
Adds an energy-preserving term to the encoder's rate-distortion decisions. It compares the visual energy of the source block against the encoded block, so flattening texture is charged as a real cost instead of being rewarded as a reduction in error. This is the same idea as psy-rd in x264 and x265.

The higher the value, the more bits go to grain, noise and fine texture that a plain error metric would happily throw away. Around 1.0 to 1.5 keeps texture and motion acuity intact; 4.0 to 6.0 preserves grain and noise dramatically better, but costs a lot of bitrate and sinks metric scores.

The default here is 0, meaning the bias is off unless you set it - the svt-av1-hdr build on the AV1AN tab ships it at 1.0 instead, so an encode that looked right there needs the number typing in here.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0.0|The default in this build; no energy bias at all.
1.0|A mild bias, retaining texture sharpness across general content.
1.5|Detailed live action and scenes with complex motion.
4.0|Grain retention on film scans, best alongside a lowered tf-strength.
8.0|The maximum, for grain and noise preservation at a heavy bitrate cost.

options.syntaxDescription: -7 to 7 (default 0) - Deblocking sharpness bias, also affecting rate distortion; raise to keep fine detail
options.description:
Sharpness does two things at once. It sets the deblocking loop filter's sharpness level, so the filter smooths less across block edges, and it feeds the coefficient optimisation stage, where a higher value shrinks the rate term and leaves the encoder less willing to zero out small transform coefficients purely to save bits.

Higher values keep fine detail and grain that would otherwise be filtered or quantised away, in exchange for bits and for more visible blocking and ringing where the deblocker no longer cleans up after the quantiser. Lower values give a cleaner, softer picture. Raise it for detailed live action and stills, lower it for animation, flat gradients or low bitrates.

Tunes 3 and 4 override it, so setting both is setting one.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default in this build; neutral behaviour.
-2|Animation or low-bitrate encodes that want the deblocker working harder.
3|Detailed live action where deblocking is visibly softening texture.
7|Maximum detail retention, mostly worthwhile on stills and very high fidelity encodes.
-7|The softest, cleanest end of the range.

options.syntaxDescription: 32 or 64 (default 64) - Caps the largest transform size; 32 holds fine texture better but costs efficiency
options.description:
AV1's 64-point transform has its 32 highest-frequency coefficients zeroed out by design, so any block coded with one loses its finest detail before quantisation even starts. Setting 32 stops the encoder considering 64-point transforms at all, and those coefficients survive.

The cost is speed and some efficiency: more, smaller transforms mean more overhead, and on flat or smooth material the 64-point transform was the right call. The gain shows on camera noise, fine film grain and detailed stills, where PSNR and SSIM do not register the blurring being traded away.

The encoder warns when you set 32, saying it may reduce coding efficiency at low to medium fidelity - which is the same trade read from the other side, and worth heeding if the CRF is high.
options.listedValuesDescription:
64|The default, and the right call on flat or clean sources where efficiency matters more.
32|Camera noise and fine film grain that 64-point transforms visibly blur.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Master switch for variance boost; the strength, octile and curve rows do nothing while it is off
options.description:
Variance boost lowers the quantiser on 64x64 superblocks that measure low variance, so flat and delicately textured regions such as skin, cloud, fog and night interiors receive bits a fixed quantiser would have spent on high-contrast edges.

It is off in this build, which is the difference to know about between the SVT-AV1 compiled into ffmpeg and the svt-av1-hdr build the AV1AN tab drives, where it is on. Measured here, the three rows below - strength, octile and curve - produce a bit-identical file to leaving them alone until this is set to 1, so a value typed into any of them without this is doing nothing at all.

Switching it on costs bitrate and buys visible detail in the flat parts of the frame. It augments adaptive quantisation rather than replacing it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default in this build; variance boost off.
1|Enables it, and with it the strength, octile and curve rows.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-4 (default 2) - How hard low-contrast superblocks are boosted; 1 for smooth animation, 3 for mixed contrast
options.description:
This value selects how large the variance boost grows as measured variance falls. Stronger curves buy visible detail in flat and delicately textured regions but inflate bitrate and can make film grain retention uneven across a shot.

Strength 1 suits flat animation, 2 handles most live action, 3 helps sources that swing between very bright and very dark, and 4 is worth it only when low-contrast detail outranks file size.

It does nothing unless enable-variance-boost is 1, and tunes 3 and 4 override it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|Flat cel animation or screen capture with little texture.
2|The default; live action and animation with detailed texture.
3|Horror and thriller material mixing very dark and very bright scenes.
4|Archival work where low-contrast detail outranks file size.

options.syntaxDescription: 1-8 (default 5) - How much of a superblock must be low-contrast to boost it; higher is stricter, 4-7 advised
options.description:
Where strength decides how hard a superblock is boosted, the octile decides how many superblocks qualify. Each 64x64 superblock is split into 8x8 subblocks, their variances are ranked, and this value picks the point in that ranking which judges the block. At 1 an eighth of the block being low-contrast is enough to boost it; at 8 essentially all of it must be.

Low values spill bits onto high-contrast areas that did not need them and inflate size. High values are stingier and can leave visibly poorer patches inside blocks that are only partly flat. Four to seven is the useful span: move down when detail is lost inside busy frames, up when bitrate climbs without a visible return.

It does nothing unless enable-variance-boost is 1.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|Busy or grainy footage where flat patches hide inside detailed blocks.
4|Slightly broader boosting than default for mixed-contrast live action.
5|The default; balanced selectivity for most sources.
7|Tighter selectivity when bitrate climbs without visible gain.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 0) - Boost curve shape; 1 an alternative allocation, 2 built for still images
options.description:
Selects the formula that converts a superblock's measured variance into a quantiser offset. The curves differ in where boosting starts and how steeply the offset grows, so they change both how bits are distributed and how the result looks. Curves 0 and 1 treat variance below 256 as low; curve 2 raises that threshold to 1024 and so boosts a far larger share of the frame.

Curve 0 is the general-purpose choice and curve 1 shifts the tradeoff without changing the aim. Curve 2 is built for still images and spends noticeably more on flat regions.

This build stops at 2: the PQ HDR curve the svt-av1-hdr build offers as 3 is not here, and asking for it is refused outright. It does nothing unless enable-variance-boost is 1, and tunes 3 and 4 override it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; general-purpose curve.
1|An alternative allocation when curve 0 looks too soft or too costly.
2|Still images, single-frame encodes and very flat material.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-3 (default 0) - Evens quality across temporal layers; raise for consistency at some cost in average score
options.description:
Within a mini-GOP the encoder normally spreads quantisers widely across temporal layers, giving reference frames much lower quantisers than the frames that depend on them. This setting squeezes that spread, so quality varies less from keyframe to leaf frame.

Consistency is bought from average quality: with the layers pulled together, reference frames are relatively less clean and predict less well for their children, so mean scores usually fall even as frame-to-frame variation does. Raise it when pulsing between frame types is what you notice.

At very low CRF the compression can improve fidelity outright rather than trade it. Note the shape of the control here - a whole number from 0 to 3, where the svt-av1-hdr build on the AV1AN tab takes a decimal up to 8.0 and defaults to 1.0, so a value copied across from there is refused or means something else.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default in this build; the widest spread and the best metric scores.
1|A consistency gain at almost no cost, and what svt-av1-hdr defaults to.
2|High-quality encodes where holding the layers together matters more.
3|The maximum; very low CRF or maximum-fidelity work, where it can also aid fidelity.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 0) - Shifts QP by average frame luminance, spending more bits on dark scenes prone to banding
options.description:
Shifts a frame's quantiser according to the average luma of that frame, so dark scenes are coded finer than their measured complexity alone would earn. Dark footage is cheap to code and cheap frames get starved, which is why banding and blocking surface first in night exteriors and shadowed interiors. This value scales how far that shift goes, and 0 disables it.

Bits moved into dark frames come out of the rest of the encode, so on mostly bright material the setting costs size for nothing. It earns its keep on sources with long dark stretches: night cinematography, horror, concert and stage footage, and anything heavily graded down.

The decision is made per frame from a whole-frame average, so a dark object inside a bright frame is not affected.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no luminance-based adjustment.
25|A light lift for material with occasional night scenes.
50|Sustained dark cinematography where shadows band.
100|Maximum bias for very dark sources where shadow detail is the priority.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 2) - Adaptive quantisation; 0 off, 1 segmentation-based, 2 the per-block delta-q the encoder ships with
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation varies the quantiser within a frame rather than coding every block at the same step size, moving bits towards the parts of the picture where they show. Mode 2 is the delta-q path the encoder uses by default; mode 0 turns the variation off entirely and codes the frame flat.

Turning it off is a metric-chasing move and usually a visible loss: the flat and dark regions AQ was protecting are the first things to band. It is worth trying only on material that is uniformly detailed, where there is nothing to move bits towards.

Mode 1 is the older segmentation-based path, and the encoder prints a warning when you select it saying it is supported only for demos, experimentation and further development. Take that at face value rather than as boilerplate.
options.listedValuesDescription:
2|The default; per-block delta quantisation.
0|Off, coding each frame at one quantiser - metric-friendly, usually worse to look at.
1|The segmentation-based mode, which the encoder itself flags as experimental.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Quantisation matrices, which the qm-min, qm-max and chroma-qm rows all depend on
options.description:
Enables quantisation matrices, which weight quantisation by frequency instead of applying one step size across the whole transform block. That lets fine texture and grain be preserved or discarded independently of the underlying structure.

This is the switch the whole matrix family hangs off: qm-min, qm-max, chroma-qm-min and chroma-qm-max all have no effect while it is 0, which was measured here rather than assumed - all four produce a bit-identical file until this is set.

It is off in this build, where the svt-av1-hdr build the AV1AN tab drives has it on, so the four rows below are inert out of the box here. Tunes 3 and 4 override it along with its min and max levels.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default in this build; uniform quantisation.
1|Matrices enabled, and with them the four qm rows.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 8) - Lowest luma quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1
options.description:
The lowest matrix flatness the encoder may select for luma, where lower numbers mean a more aggressively shaped matrix that treats high frequencies very differently from low ones. Level 15 is fully flat.

Allowing a lower floor lets the encoder shape quantisation harder where that helps, keeping fine texture that flat quantisation would round away. It is the luma counterpart to chroma-qm-min, and the more impactful of the two, since luma carries most of the detail.

It requires enable-qm 1 and must not exceed qm-max. The encoder does not range-check this one: 16 and above are accepted at the command line and then produce no output at all, so keep it inside 0 to 15.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default in this build.
6|A slightly wider range, and what svt-av1-hdr defaults to.
4|Allows aggressive shaping, retaining more fine texture.
0|The most aggressive shaping available.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 15) - Highest luma quantisation matrix flatness; needs enable-qm 1
options.description:
The upper end of the luma matrix range. Level 15 is effectively unshaped, so the default lets the encoder fall back to ordinary flat quantisation wherever shaping would not help.

Lowering it forces shaping to be applied more consistently, which holds onto texture across the whole encode at some cost in efficiency.

It requires enable-qm 1 and must not fall below qm-min, and like qm-min it is not range-checked, so stay inside 0 to 15.
options.listedValuesDescription:
15|The default; permits a fully unshaped matrix.
12|A light trim on how flat the matrix may become.
10|A narrower range, and what svt-av1-hdr defaults to.
8|Forces consistent shaping, at a cost in efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 8) - Floor on chroma quantisation matrix flatness; raise to protect chroma when starved
options.description:
This sets the lowest, least flat level the encoder may pick for the chroma planes. Level 15 is fully flat, so lower numbers mean stronger shaping: more fine chroma detail is discarded and the encode gets smaller.

The encoder chooses a level per frame by mapping that frame's quantiser into the span between this floor and chroma-qm-max, so lowering the floor widens how aggressive it is allowed to become. Drop it when chroma consumes bitrate you would rather give to luma; raise it towards 15 on saturated or heavily graded material where colour smearing shows first.

It requires enable-qm 1, and must not exceed chroma-qm-max.
options.listedValuesDescription:
8|The default.
4|Aggressive chroma shaping for bitrate-constrained streaming encodes.
10|Gentler shaping for saturated or heavily graded sources.
15|Pins chroma matrices fully flat, with no frequency shaping on colour.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 15) - Ceiling on chroma quantisation matrix flatness; 15 leaves chroma unshaped at high bitrates
options.description:
The ceiling of the same chroma range: the flattest matrix the encoder may pick. At the default of 15 it can fall back to a fully flat matrix, leaving chroma coefficients unweighted at that end of the range.

Pulling this down forces some frequency shaping on chroma at all times rather than merely permitting it, which trims bitrate but caps how much fine colour detail can survive anywhere in the encode. It is the blunter of the two controls, so reach for it when you want a guaranteed chroma saving instead of a wider span for the encoder to work within.

It requires enable-qm 1, and must be at least chroma-qm-min.
options.listedValuesDescription:
15|The default; permits fully flat chroma matrices.
12|A light trim for sources with noisy or oversampled chroma.
10|A moderate ceiling that still leaves most chroma detail intact.
8|Forces shaping on chroma throughout for a firm bitrate saving.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 0) - The best quantiser allowed; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
options.description:
A floor on the quantiser, capping how many bits any one frame may receive. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody would notice, which shrinks the file without touching the material that actually needs bits.

It must not exceed max-qp, and in constant quality encoding it only bites when the quality target sits below it - which is why a floor typed here can appear to do nothing until the quality box moves.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no floor.
15|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
20|A firmer cap for constrained delivery.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-63 (default 63) - The worst quantiser allowed; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
options.description:
A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality may fall when the encoder runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the smearing and blocking difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates, at the cost of the encoder no longer being able to meet a bitrate target there - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

It is a Target Bitrate setting in practice. In constant quality mode nothing is short of bits, so a ceiling above the chosen quality never comes into play - measured here, 50 and 40 both produced exactly the file the default did at a quality of 32.

It must not fall below min-qp.
options.listedValuesDescription:
63|The default; no ceiling.
50|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
40|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.

options.syntaxDescription: -63 to 63 (default 0) - Shifts the quantiser for the opening GOP, before the usual per-picture derivation
options.description:
Adds an offset to the sequence quantiser for the start-up group of pictures, before the per-picture quantiser is worked out. It exists because the opening of a sequence has no history behind it, so the encoder's estimates there are at their least informed.

A negative offset spends extra bits at the start, which gives everything predicting from those first frames a cleaner foundation and avoids the softness some encodes show for the first second.

A positive one does the opposite, and is only worth it when the opening is a logo or a fade nobody is looking at.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no offset.
-4|Extra quality at the opening, for a cleaner foundation.
-8|A strong start-up boost.
4|Fewer bits at the start, if the opening is unimportant.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 1) - Deblocking loop filter; 2 is a slower, more accurate variant, 0 leaves block edges in place
options.description:
The deblocking loop filter smooths the edges between coded blocks before a frame is stored as a reference, so block boundaries do not persist and propagate into everything predicting from it. Mode 2 is a slower, more accurate variant of the same filter.

Leaving it on is right for almost all encoding. The artefact it removes is the most recognisable failure mode of a block-based codec, and because the filtered frame is what later frames predict from, the benefit compounds.

Grain-preservation setups occasionally turn it off at very high bitrates, where there is little blocking to remove and the filter costs fine detail. The sharpness row is the gentler way to ask for the same thing.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; the standard filter.
2|The slower, more accurate variant for quality-focused encodes.
0|Off; only sensible at very high bitrates, for grain retention.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 4 (default -1, the preset decides) - The ringing filter; 0 off, 1-4 pin how hard it searches, 1 the most thorough
options.description:
CDEF is an in-loop filter that removes ringing by filtering along the direction of an edge rather than across it, so it cleans up the halo around high-contrast detail without smearing the edge itself.

Left at -1 the speed preset picks a level, which is right for normal encoding: the filtered frame is what later frames predict from, so ringing left in place propagates. 0 turns it off, which grain-preserving setups sometimes do because it takes fine noise along with the ringing - though that only makes sense at bitrates high enough that there is little ringing to remove.

1 to 4 pin the search rather than the strength, and the direction is not obvious from the numbers: measured on this build, 1 is the slowest and most thorough of the four and 3 the quickest, with each producing a different result. The preset's own choice came out smaller than all four on the same clip, so there is rarely a reason to override it.

This is not the svt-av1-hdr build's cdef-scaling, which is absent here - there is no way to soften CDEF rather than switch it off.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the speed preset chooses a level.
0|Off, for grain retention at high bitrates.
1|The most thorough search, pinned regardless of preset.
4|A fast fixed level, for a predictable cost.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 1 (default -1, the preset decides) - The loop restoration filter, which repairs coding error after deblocking and CDEF
options.description:
Loop restoration runs after deblocking and CDEF, fitting a correction per region to bring the reconstruction back towards the source. It repairs the general coding error the earlier filters leave behind.

Left at -1 the speed preset decides, and on the clip measured here that came out bit-identical to forcing 1 - so the setting that changes anything is 0, which turns it off.

Like CDEF it cannot distinguish fine noise from artefacts, so grain-preserving setups sometimes disable it. That is worth it only at bitrates high enough that the repair had little to do, since the repaired frame is what everything afterwards predicts from.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the speed preset chooses.
1|Forces it on regardless of preset.
0|Off, for maximum grain retention at high bitrates.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Temporal filtering of alt-ref frames; 0 keeps grain and fine motion detail
options.description:
Temporal filtering builds alternate reference frames by blending several source frames together. The blend cancels noise, producing a clean frame that predicts unusually well, which is a substantial part of where AV1's efficiency comes from.

The cost is that grain and fine motion detail are averaged away in the reference, and everything predicting from it inherits the smoothing. Turning it off is a common move in grain-preserving setups, and it costs bitrate. tf-strength is the finer control and is worth reaching for first.

Only 0 and 1 are settings. Anything above 1 is accepted without complaint and then produces a different bitstream on every run of the same command - measured here, three runs at 2 gave three different files - so those values are not a mode, they are undefined behaviour. The svt-av1-hdr build's adaptive mode 2 does not exist here.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; standard temporal filtering.
0|Off, for maximum grain and motion detail retention.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 3) - Temporal filtering strength; lower keeps grain and fine motion, higher denoises and saves bits
options.description:
How hard the temporal filter blends when it constructs an alternate reference. Where enable-tf decides whether filtering happens at all, this decides how much of each contributing frame survives.

Lower values keep grain and fine motion detail in the reference, at the cost of a noisier reference that predicts less efficiently. Higher values denoise more thoroughly and save bits, flattening texture as they go.

It is the finer control of the two, and worth reaching for before disabling temporal filtering outright. The default here is 3, a good deal stronger than the 1 the svt-av1-hdr build on the AV1AN tab ships - so a grain-preserving encode has further to travel from the starting point on this tab.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default in this build.
0|The weakest setting, keeping the most grain.
1|Light filtering, and what svt-av1-hdr defaults to.
2|A middle ground between grain retention and efficiency.
4|The strongest denoising, for genuinely noisy sources.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Temporal filtering on keyframes only; 0 keeps keyframe grain
options.description:
The same temporal filtering, switched separately for keyframes. Keyframes are treated on their own terms because they anchor everything until the next one, so a clean keyframe pays off across the whole interval.

Because a keyframe is displayed as well as referenced, filtering it too hard is visible directly: the picture softens at the cut and then sharpens as later frames add detail back, which reads as a pulse at every keyframe. Turning this off is what stops that, and it is a cheaper move than disabling temporal filtering across the board.

This build offers the switch only. The svt-av1-hdr build on the AV1AN tab has a kf-tf-strength dial in its place, so there is no way here to soften keyframe filtering without removing it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; keyframes are temporally filtered.
0|No keyframe filtering, for maximum grain retention at cuts.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-50 (default 0) - Denoises by this much and synthesises matching grain at playback; masks banding on flat gradients
options.description:
Synthesises film grain rather than coding it. Real grain is close to random, so it compresses appallingly badly - a grainy source can spend most of its bitrate reproducing noise. The number is the denoising strength used to measure the grain; the encoder then writes a parameter set and the decoder generates matching grain at playback, for almost no bits at all.

The trade is that the grain is statistically similar rather than identical, and it is applied after decoding, so it is not part of the picture anything else can act on.

It is also a practical fix for banding: a little grain on a flat gradient dithers the steps and hides them, which is why small values are worth trying on animation that has no grain to begin with.

The encoder warns that it is expensive above speed preset 6, which is most of the range this tab offers - expect the encode to slow down noticeably.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no synthesis.
6|A light texture, mainly to break up banding on animation and gradients.
15|Moderate grain, close to a lightly grained digital source.
25|Strong grain, for matching a visibly grainy film scan.
50|The maximum this encoder accepts.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Whether the denoised picture is the one encoded, or the denoising is only a measurement
options.description:
film-grain denoises the source in order to measure what grain to synthesise. This decides whether that denoised picture is what gets encoded, or whether the denoising was only a measurement and the original frames go to the encoder.

Left at 0 the grain is still in the picture being coded and the synthetic grain is laid on top of it at playback, which is doubling rather than replacing - the noise is paid for in bitrate exactly as before. Set to 1, the encoder is handed the clean picture, which is the whole point of the exercise and where the bitrate saving comes from.

It has no effect while film-grain is 0, and the encoder says so in a warning as it starts.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; the source is encoded as it is and grain is added on top at playback.
1|Encodes the denoised picture, so the synthetic grain replaces the real grain.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 1) - Scales the grain synthesis block size with resolution; 0 pins it to 32x32 at every size
options.description:
Scales the block size that grain synthesis is applied over with the resolution of the video, so grain on a 4K encode is generated over larger blocks than on a 720p one and ends up looking like the same grain viewed at the same physical size.

Pinned off, synthesis always uses 32x32 blocks regardless of resolution, which makes the grain look progressively finer as resolution rises - the same pattern spread over more pixels.

It is on by default and is generally what you want unless you are matching a reference that was made without it. It only means anything when film-grain is above 0.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; block size scales with resolution.
0|Fixed 32x32 blocks at every resolution.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 off, 1 on, 2 detect (unset matches 0 here) - Palette mode and intra block copy for desktop capture and slides
options.description:
Controls the screen content coding tools - palette mode and intra block copy - which code large flat colour areas and repeated on-screen elements far more cheaply than ordinary prediction. The difference on a desktop capture, a slide deck or a game UI is large.

Mode 2 asks the encoder to detect screen content and switch the tools on when it finds it. Do not rely on that here: measured on four sources including a two-tone synthetic pattern that is nothing but screen content, an encode with this row left blank came out bit-identical to scm=0 every time, at speed presets 2 and 6 alike. Forcing 1 is what actually turns the tools on.

So set 1 for anything synthetic and leave it alone otherwise. Tune 3 overrides it, and out-of-range numbers are not rejected, so a typo here fails quietly.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|Force the tools on - desktop capture, slide decks, game UI, screen recordings.
0|Explicitly off, for ordinary camera footage.
2|Asks for detection, which did not fire on any source measured here.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-2 (default 0) - Avoids the tools that are most expensive to decode, for playback on weak hardware
options.description:
Steers the encoder away from the coding tools that cost a decoder the most, producing a stream that plays back on hardware which would otherwise stutter. AV1 software decoding is demanding, and this is the setting that makes the difference on older machines.

The cost is compression: the tools being avoided are there because they help, so the same quality takes more bits. Only worth setting when you know the target struggles, since it gives up efficiency for a benefit nothing else will show.

It is resolution-gated, which is worth knowing before concluding it did nothing. Measured here, 1 and 2 changed nothing at all at 640x360 across speed presets 4, 6 and 8, and both changed the output at 1280x720 - which is roughly where a weak decoder starts struggling anyway.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no decoder-cost restrictions.
1|A moderate reduction in decoding cost.
2|The strongest reduction, at a real compression cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-1 (default 0) - Inserts overlay pictures as extra references for base-layer frames
options.description:
Allows the encoder to insert overlay pictures, which act as additional reference frames for base layer pictures. They give the prediction stage another, better-matched frame to work from at the points where the reference structure is weakest.

The gain is a modest compression improvement on content with steady motion, and the cost is encoding time and a slightly more complex reference structure.

It is off by default and is one of the cheaper quality options to try on an offline encode.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Enables overlay pictures, a small gain on steady motion.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-120 (default is an automatic depth) - Frames looked ahead beyond the minigop, feeding filtering and rate control
options.description:
How far ahead the encoder looks beyond what the mini-GOP structure, temporal filtering and rate control already require. Lookahead is what lets it place references well and distribute bits across a scene rather than reacting frame by frame.

Left alone the encoder derives a depth from the other settings, which is a sensible choice in most cases. Setting it explicitly is a way to buy better bit distribution at the cost of memory, or to cut it for low delay.

There is no way to ask for the automatic depth back. The standalone encoder spells it -1, and this parameter parser refuses a negative number outright - so a row here with anything in it pins the depth, and clearing the row is the only way to return to automatic.

That automatic depth is already generous, and lowering it is the change that does something. Measured on a 60-frame clip, everything from 32 up produced exactly the file the default did, and 0, 8, 16 and 31 each differed.
options.listedValuesDescription:
120|The maximum; the most information for rate control.
60|A generous fixed depth for offline encoding.
16|A shorter window, trading bit distribution for memory.
0|No additional lookahead, for low delay.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-5 (default 5) - Mini-GOP size as a power of two, so 5 is 32 frames and 3 is 8
options.description:
Sets how deep the pyramid of temporal layers inside a mini-GOP goes, which is the same thing as how long the mini-GOP is: level 5 is 32 frames, 4 is 16, 3 is 8, and so on down.

A deeper pyramid compresses better, because more frames are coded as cheap leaves predicting from a small number of well-spent references. What it costs is latency and memory, and a little responsiveness at scene changes, since the structure spans more of the video before it resets.

The default is the deepest, which is the right call for the offline encoding this tab does. Lower it only for a genuine low-delay requirement, or when a very short source is being swallowed whole by one mini-GOP.
options.listedValuesDescription:
5|The default; 32-frame mini-GOPs and the best compression.
4|16-frame mini-GOPs, a mild step towards responsiveness.
3|8-frame mini-GOPs, for shorter clips or tighter latency.
0|The shallowest structure, for low-delay use.

options.syntaxDescription: good, best or realtime (default good) - How much time the encoder may spend; realtime is a different rate control path entirely
options.description:
Picks which of libvpx's three encoding paths runs. good is the general-purpose one and is where the speed setting the app already sends does its work. best spends considerably longer for a small gain, and libvpx has been folding it back into good for years. realtime is not a slower or faster version of the same thing - it is a separate rate control and speed-feature path written for live encoding.

The realtime path is what makes several other settings on this tab mean anything. Measured here, tune-content screen and static-thresh change nothing at all under good and change the output substantially under realtime, while the alt-ref machinery is unavailable there.

For a file you are encoding once and keeping, leave this alone. best is worth measuring on a short clip before committing hours to it; realtime is for streams and screen capture and costs real quality.
options.listedValuesDescription:
good|The default; the mode offline encoding should stay in.
best|Slower for a small gain; measurably different, rarely worth the time.
realtime|Live and screen capture; the only mode where static-thresh and tune-content screen do anything.

options.syntaxDescription: psnr or ssim (default psnr) - Metric the encoder optimises for; ssim scales RD per block and often looks better
options.description:
Selects the distortion metric the encoder optimises its decisions against. psnr minimises squared error; ssim weights decisions by structural similarity, which changes rate-distortion scaling per block.

ssim generally produces a picture people prefer, because it spends bits on structure rather than on wherever squared error happens to be largest, and it usually scores better on perceptual metrics too.

Neither is a psychovisual setting in the sense x264's psy-rd is; VP9 has no equivalent, which is part of why its output tends to look softer than a comparable x264 encode.
options.listedValuesDescription:
psnr|The default; minimises squared error.
ssim|Structure-weighted decisions; usually the better-looking choice.

options.syntaxDescription: default, screen or film (default default) - Content hint; screen only bites in realtime mode, film only outside it
options.description:
Tells the encoder what kind of material it is coding. screen enables tools for desktop capture and UI recordings, where large flat areas and repeated elements code far more cheaply with the right prediction modes.

film adjusts the encoder's behaviour to retain grain rather than filtering it away. Note this is not the same as the option of the same name in aomenc, which synthesises grain at the decoder - VP9 has no grain synthesis, so here it genuinely means keeping more of the noise that is there.

The two halves reach the encoder through different paths, and measured against this build only one of them is live at a time. screen changed nothing at all under the good deadline and cut a screen capture from 66106 to 51277 bytes under realtime; film did the reverse, moving the output under good and two-pass and doing nothing under realtime. So a screen hint is only worth setting alongside a realtime deadline.
options.listedValuesDescription:
default|Ordinary live action and animation.
screen|Desktop capture, slides and UI recordings - set the deadline to realtime with it.
film|Grainy sources, retaining noise rather than smoothing it.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 to 7 (default 0) - Keeps fine detail by curbing coefficient and skip optimisation, costing PSNR and bitrate
options.description:
Trades measurable accuracy for a sharper-looking picture by curbing the optimisations that quietly smooth the result - the coefficient decisions and skip choices that drop small amounts of detail because they are cheap to lose.

Higher values keep more of that fine detail and cost both PSNR and bitrate. The cost is not small: on a grainy test clip, 7 came out at 333294 bytes against 159216 for the default, more than double, so treat this as a bitrate control as much as a look control.

It also feeds the loop filter level, so raising it reduces deblocking as well. -1 is ffmpeg's way of saying "do not set this", which lands on the same behaviour as 0.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; no bias.
2|A mild sharpening for detailed live action.
5|Strong detail retention, at a real bitrate cost.
7|The maximum, and roughly double the file size on grainy material.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or higher (default 0 off) - Codes low-motion blocks as skip below this distortion; realtime mode only
options.description:
Sets a distortion threshold below which a block is simply coded as skipped rather than searched and coded properly. Anything changing less than the threshold between frames is treated as not changing at all.

The point is speed, and the setting is aimed at real-time encoding of largely static content such as screen sharing, where most of the frame genuinely is identical. Measured against this build that is not just advice: under the good deadline no value of it changed a byte of the output, and only with the deadline on realtime did it start dropping blocks.

Above 0 it will discard real low-amplitude change, including film grain and subtle gradients in motion, so it is a poor fit for offline quality encoding even where it works.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off, and the right setting for quality encoding.
1000|Light skipping for realtime screen content.
20000|Aggressive skipping; visible on anything but static material.

options.syntaxDescription: default or 0 (default 0, off) - Codes frames so a decoder can recover from a lost one, at a bitrate cost
options.description:
Turns on error resilience, which stops the encoder relying on state the decoder may not have - chiefly the backward probability updates that refine the entropy model from the frame just coded. A decoder joining late or losing a frame can then carry on rather than showing corruption until the next keyframe.

It costs bitrate for that, and the cost is measurable rather than theoretical: the same clip came out 3-4% larger with it on. For a file on disk there is nothing to recover from, so it is a loss with no upside.

ffmpeg offers a second flag, partitions, which is a VP8 concept. Measured against VP9 it produces byte-identical output to default, so there is nothing to choose between them here.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off, and the right setting for a file.
default|Resilience against whole lost frames, for lossy transport.

options.syntaxDescription: -1 or a VP9 level such as 4.1 (default -1, off) - Caps the stream to a decoder level, constraining the encode to fit
options.description:
Names a VP9 level the output has to conform to, and the encoder then adjusts its own decisions - frame size, rate, tile and reference limits - to stay inside it. A level is what a hardware decoder advertises support for, so this is the setting that makes a file playable on a device that refuses anything above its ceiling.

Only the levels VP9 actually defines are accepted. Measured, 2.1, 4.1, 5.1, 5.2, 6 and 6.2 all take; a made-up 3.5 is refused with "target_level is invalid" and the encode then simply carries on unconstrained, which is a failure quiet enough to miss.

The loud failures are the ones to plan for, because this is the only row here that can refuse an encode over what another row asked for. A level too small for the frame fails with "The picture size is too large", and a level set alongside multi-layer alt-refs fails with "The alt-ref distance is too small" - measured, level 4.1 with auto-alt-ref 6 and a full lookahead dies part-way into the second pass. If you need a level, expect to give ground on the alt-ref settings.

Leave it off unless a specific decoder demands one; constraining the encoder can only cost quality.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; no level constraint.
4.1|A common ceiling for 1080p hardware decoding.
5.1|Headroom for 4K.
6.2|The highest level VP9 defines.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 0) - Mathematically lossless coding; needs the quality set to CRF 0 or a bitrate mode
options.description:
Codes the video with no quantisation at all, so every frame decodes back to exactly the pixels that went in. It is a real VP9 mode rather than a very high quality setting, and the files are correspondingly large - measured on a test clip, 33035 bytes against 13440 for an ordinary bitrate encode of the same frames.

It clamps the quantiser to zero at both ends, which means it cannot coexist with a constant-quality target of anything but 0. Set it with the quality anywhere else and the encoder refuses to open at all, saying "CQ level N must be between minimum and maximum quantizer value (0-0)" - so if you want this, put the quality slider on 0 or use a bitrate mode.

Worth it for an intermediate or an archival master where the source itself is the thing being kept. For anything that will be watched, a low CRF is a far better use of the space.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; ordinary lossy coding.
1|Lossless; requires CRF 0, and produces very large files.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 1, two-pass only) - Alt reference frames; 2 and above enables multi-layer ARF, usually a quality gain
options.description:
Alternate reference frames are synthetic frames the encoder builds by filtering several source frames together. They are never displayed; other frames predict from them, and because they are denoised they predict very well, which is one of VP9's larger compression wins.

Values above 1 enable multi-layer alt-refs, letting the encoder maintain several at different temporal distances so both slow and fast motion have a good reference available.

Measured against this build the whole alt-ref mechanism is two-pass only, exactly as ffmpeg's own help says: in one-pass encoding, constant quality and bitrate alike, no value of this changed a single byte, while in two-pass 0 and 6 were 15% apart. So this row and the three under it are settings for a two-pass encode and nothing else.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; a single alt-ref layer.
6|The maximum; multi-layer, the usual choice for offline quality.
4|Multi-layer with less encoding cost than the maximum.
0|Disabled; a clear compression loss.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-25 (default 25) - Lookahead depth; more improves alt-ref placement, 0 gives low delay at a quality cost
options.description:
How many frames the encoder buffers before committing decisions, which sets how far ahead it can see. Lookahead is what makes alt-ref frames possible - the encoder needs the frames in hand to filter them together - and it also drives frame type and bit allocation choices.

Lowering it costs compression directly, and dropping it far enough disables alt-refs, taking one of VP9's main advantages with them. Measured, a two-pass encode at 0 came out the same size as one with alt-refs switched off outright.

25 is both the default and the hard ceiling: ffmpeg will accept a larger number and libvpx then refuses to open the encoder over it. Set it to 0 only for genuinely low-delay use; the cost is memory and latency, not encoding speed.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default and the maximum; the right setting for offline encoding.
16|Reduced buffering where memory is constrained.
0|Low delay, giving up alt-ref frames and a lot of efficiency.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-15 (default 0, off) - Frames blended by the alt-ref temporal filter; ffmpeg leaves it off where vpxenc uses 7
options.description:
How many neighbouring frames the alt-ref filter blends together when constructing an alternate reference. The blending is what removes noise and makes the alt-ref such a good prediction source.

More frames give a cleaner reference and better compression, and average away more grain and fine motion detail in the process. Fewer keep the noise but predict less well. Measured on a grainy two-pass encode, 0 gave 143012 bytes, 3 gave 139108 and 7 gave 136223, with 10 and 15 landing on the same figure as 7 - the encoder caps the count from its own group boost, so the top of the range is rarely reached.

The default is the part to know. vpxenc's own default is 7, but ffmpeg carries a second, older spelling of this option whose default of 0 is the one that actually lands, so the temporal filter is off unless you turn it on here. That also means arnr-strength beside it does nothing at all until this is raised.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default in ffmpeg; the filter is off.
7|vpxenc's own default, and a good general setting.
3|Keeps more grain and fine motion detail.
15|The maximum; cleanest references, softest detail.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-6 (default 3) - Alt-ref filter strength; does nothing unless arnr-maxframes is raised above 0
options.description:
How aggressively the alt-ref filter blends the frames it has gathered. Where arnr-maxframes sets how many frames take part, this sets how much of each survives the blend.

Dropping it to 1 or 2 is the usual move on grainy film, keeping noise that would otherwise be averaged out of the reference and therefore out of everything predicting from it. Raising it suits genuinely noisy footage, where the noise is not worth preserving and removing it saves bits.

Because ffmpeg leaves arnr-maxframes at 0, this has no effect out of the box: measured, every value from 0 to 6 produced byte-identical output until the frame count was raised, after which 0, 1 and 2 were all distinct. The encoder also caps the strength it will use from the group boost, so on ordinary material everything from 2 upwards behaves alike. Its own default is 3.
options.listedValuesDescription:
3|The default.
2|Grainy film, preserving noise and texture.
0|No filtering; maximum grain retention.
6|The maximum, for noisy low-light footage.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-24 (default -1, derived from the frame rate) - Shortest gap the encoder may leave between golden/alt-ref frames
options.description:
Golden frames are the long-lived references VP9 keeps around for material that recurs, and alt-refs are placed on the same schedule. Left alone the encoder works out a minimum spacing from the frame rate, which is what -1 means here.

Raising it forces those references further apart, which suits long calm shots where a reference stays useful and there is nothing to gain from refreshing it. Lowering it lets the encoder refresh more often, which helps where the picture keeps changing character.

The ceiling is 24, one less than the lookahead buffer, and libvpx warns and ignores anything above that rather than failing - so a value of 32 leaves an encode running with the setting silently dropped. Like the rest of this group it is a two-pass control; measured, it moved the output in two-pass constant quality and nowhere in one pass.
options.listedValuesDescription:
-1|The default; the encoder derives the spacing from the frame rate.
4|Frequent refreshes for fast-changing material.
16|Widely spaced references for long calm shots.
24|The maximum the lookahead buffer allows.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Frame parallel decodability; 0 allows backward probability updates and compresses better
options.description:
Controls whether the stream is coded so a decoder can work on several frames at once. Frame-parallel mode requires disabling backward probability updates, where the encoder refines its entropy model using statistics gathered from the frame it just coded.

Those backward updates are worth a small but real amount of compression, so turning frame-parallel decoding off makes the file smaller at the same quality. Measured here it is worth around one per cent, and unlike most of this group it works in one-pass encoding as well as two.

Leave it on only if the target decoder needs the parallelism; for file encoding, 0 is the better setting.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; parallel-decodable, slightly larger files.
0|Allows backward probability updates; better compression.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-4 (default 0, off) - Adaptive quantisation: 1 variance, 2 complexity, 3 cyclic refresh, 4 equator360
options.description:
Adaptive quantisation redistributes bits within a frame. Mode 1 distributes by variance, moving bits from busy areas where error is masked to flat ones where banding shows. Mode 2 works from complexity. Mode 3 is cyclic refresh, which refreshes part of each frame in turn and targets low-bitrate streaming. Mode 4 is tuned for equirectangular 360 video, where the poles are massively oversampled and do not deserve equal bits.

It is off by default. Mode 1 is the one to try on sources that band; the others are situational.

ffmpeg accepts the names as well as the numbers - none, variance, complexity, cyclic and equator360 - and unlike most of this tab it takes effect in one-pass encoding too.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off.
1|Variance-based, the usual choice if flat areas band.
2|Complexity-based distribution.
3|Cyclic refresh, for low-bitrate streaming.
4|Equirectangular 360 video.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1, two-pass only) - Temporal dependency model; improves bit allocation between frames
options.description:
The temporal dependency model looks ahead to work out which blocks later frames will predict from, then spends bits on those blocks in proportion to how much depends on them. A block that fifty later frames refer to is worth more than one that is never referenced again.

This is one of the larger quality-per-bit wins available in VP9 and it is on by default. Disabling it only makes sense to save encoding time.

It needs lookahead to work, so lowering lag-in-frames weakens it, and measured against this build it is two-pass only - in one pass, switching it off changed nothing at all.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; leave it on.
0|Disables the model to save encoding time, at a real quality cost.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-10000 (default 0, off) - Corpus VBR complexity midpoint; holds quality steady across a library of clips
options.description:
Sets a fixed complexity midpoint for corpus VBR, a rate control mode intended for encoding a whole library of clips to a consistent quality rather than each clip to its own target.

Normally the encoder judges difficulty relative to the clip in front of it, so an easy clip and a hard one both end up looking average. Giving a shared midpoint across the library means an easy clip is allowed to come out small and good, and a hard one to spend more.

It only applies to two-pass bitrate encoding - in constant quality it does nothing whatever - and its effect there is enormous rather than a tweak: the same clip at a 250 kbps target came out at 276382 bytes with a midpoint of 100 and 31195 with one of 10000. Only meaningful when the same value is used across a set; 0 disables it.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; ordinary per-clip rate control.
1000|A shared midpoint across a library of mostly easy content.
3000|A higher midpoint for a more demanding corpus.
10000|The maximum; treats almost everything as easier than the target.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far under target rate a section may run; higher lets easy scenes save more bits
options.description:
How far below the target rate the encoder is allowed to run over a section, as a percentage. It gives the rate controller permission to spend less than the target where the content does not need it.

Raising it lets easy passages come in well under target and bank the difference, which suits a varied source where some scenes genuinely need very little.

Lowering it forces the encoder to keep pace with the target even when there is nothing to spend bits on, which mostly wastes them. It applies to bitrate-targeted encoding; in constant quality there is no target to undershoot.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Lets easy scenes save considerably more.
100|Maximum freedom to undershoot.
0|Holds the rate at target regardless of content.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 25) - How far over target rate a section may run; higher lets hard scenes spend more bits
options.description:
How far above the target rate the encoder is allowed to run over a section, as a percentage. It is the permission a difficult scene needs to spend beyond its share rather than degrade.

Raising it protects hard scenes at the cost of a less predictable size and a higher peak rate, which matters if the result has to fit a buffer or a delivery constraint. Lowering it holds the rate down and lets quality drop on the material that most needs bits.

Watch the ceiling here: ffmpeg's own range for this option runs to 1000, and libvpx then refuses to open the encoder for anything above 100, failing the encode with "rc_overshoot_pct out of range". 100 is the real maximum. It applies to bitrate-targeted encoding rather than constant quality.
options.listedValuesDescription:
25|The default.
50|Gives difficult scenes more room to spend.
0|Holds hard to the target, at a visible cost on hard scenes.
100|The real maximum, whatever ffmpeg's range says.

options.syntaxDescription: Percentage of target, 0 for unlimited (default 0) - Caps what a single keyframe may spend
options.description:
Limits how many bits one intra frame may take, as a percentage of the average frame's share of the target bitrate. A keyframe is by far the most expensive frame in a stream, and left alone the encoder will spend whatever it takes to make the first one good.

That is right for a file and wrong for a stream, where a fat keyframe is a buffer stall. Capping it holds the peak down at the cost of a visibly softer keyframe, and everything predicting from it inherits some of that.

It applies to bitrate-targeted encoding, and the effect is large - the same realtime clip came out at 192486 bytes unlimited, 143875 at 900% and 104139 at 100%. Leave it at 0 unless something downstream has a peak rate it cannot exceed.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; unlimited, and the right setting for a file.
900|A generous cap that still bounds the peak.
300|A firm cap for streaming.
100|Very tight; the keyframe gets no more than an average frame's share.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-100 (default 0, off) - Drops frames rather than let quality collapse when the buffer runs dry
options.description:
Lets the rate controller throw frames away when it cannot meet the target rate, as a percentage of how full the decoder buffer has to get before it starts. A dropped frame costs almost nothing to code and the previous one simply stays on screen for longer.

This is a live streaming control. It keeps a constant-bitrate stream inside its channel by sacrificing smoothness instead of picture quality, which for a video call or a screen share is the right trade. For a file it is the wrong one - the result plays with visible stutter and there was no channel to protect in the first place.

It needs a constant bitrate to do anything: measured, it changed nothing under an ordinary VBR target and dropped roughly a third of the bits once minimum and maximum rate were pinned together. The range libvpx accepts is 0 to 100, and anything outside that fails the encode outright.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0|The default; off, and the right setting for a file.
25|Light dropping when the buffer runs low.
50|Moderate; noticeable stutter on hard scenes.
100|Drops as freely as it needs to hold the rate.

options.syntaxDescription: 1 to 6.2, including 1b (default auto) - Decoder level written to the stream; x264 only warns, it clamps nothing
options.description:
The decoder level written into the stream header. Levels bound resolution, frame rate, bitrate and how many reference frames may be buffered, and hardware decoders advertise the highest level they implement.

x264 works out a suitable level on its own, so this is only worth setting when a target demands a specific one - Blu-ray at 4.1, or a device that refuses anything higher.

Be aware that x264 only warns when your other settings exceed the level you asked for; it does not reduce ref frames or anything else to fit. Getting a conformant stream means setting those yourself.
options.listedValuesDescription:
4.1|Blu-ray, and a very common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
3.0|Older mobile devices at standard definition.
1b|The lowest level there is, for legacy handset profiles.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Entropy coder: 1 is CABAC, 0 the older CAVLC that only very limited decoders need
options.description:
H.264 has two entropy coders. CABAC is arithmetic coding and is worth something on the order of ten percent of the bitrate at the same quality; CAVLC is the variable-length coder the Baseline profile is limited to, and it is cheaper to decode.

There is no quality reason to turn CABAC off. The reasons are compatibility - a Baseline-only decoder cannot read it - and decode cost, since CABAC is inherently serial and is the first thing to give way on hardware that cannot keep up.

It is one of the tools any decode-cost tuning drops for exactly that reason. Leave it on for anything a current device will play.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; CABAC, and worth around ten percent of the bitrate.
0|CAVLC, for Baseline decoders and very weak playback hardware.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - The High profile 8x8 transform; off drops the stream to Main profile and costs efficiency
options.description:
Allows the 8x8 integer transform alongside the 4x4 one, so flat and smoothly varying areas can be coded as one larger block instead of four small ones. It is a High profile tool and one of the larger single wins H.264 has over what came before it.

Turning it off restricts the encoder to 4x4 transforms and drops the stream to Main profile. That costs a few percent of the bitrate and softens large smooth areas, and the only reason to do it is a decoder that implements Main and nothing above.

It takes i8x8 out of the partition set with it, so a partitions list naming i8x8 will not get it while this is off.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; the 8x8 transform on, as every current decoder expects.
0|Main profile output, for a decoder that cannot do High.

options.syntaxDescription: alpha,beta each -6 to 6 (default 0,0) - Loop filter strength; negative keeps grain, positive hides blocking
options.description:
Offsets for the in-loop deblocking filter, which smooths the edges between coded blocks before the frame is used as a reference. The first number shifts the filter's strength and the second the threshold at which an edge is considered worth filtering.

Negative values filter less, so grain and fine texture survive the loop instead of being averaged away - at the cost of visible block edges if the bitrate is not there to support them. Positive values filter more, which hides blocking at low bitrates and costs detail.

Write the two numbers separated by a comma. x264's own documentation spells this alpha:beta, and a colon is what separates one parameter from the next in the string this grid builds - so a colon here ends the value early, and what that costs depends on what comes after it. With another row filled in below, the half past the colon is read as that row's name instead: this one keeps the first number only and the next row is dropped. With nothing after it, ffmpeg refuses to open the encoder at all and the encode never starts. A single number sets both.
options.listedValuesDescription:
0,0|The default, neutral filtering.
-1,-1|A mild sharpening, common for detailed live action.
-3,-3|Strongly preserves grain; needs a generous bitrate or it blocks.
1,1|Smooths more, for low bitrate encodes where blocking shows.

options.syntaxDescription: 0 or 1 (default 1) - Master switch for the psychovisual optimisations; off raises PSNR and looks worse
options.description:
Turns x264's psychovisual optimisations on or off as a group - psy-rd, psy-trellis, and the small chroma quantiser bias that goes with them. On, the encoder prefers a block that keeps the same amount of visual energy as the source over one that measures closer to it; off, it takes the lowest measurable error every time.

Off is a benchmarking setting. It raises PSNR and SSIM, which is exactly why it is not something to ship: those metrics reward the smoothing psy exists to stop.

The chroma bias is worth knowing about because nothing else mentions it. With psy on, x264 applies a chroma-qp-offset of -2 of its own on top of whatever you set, so a stream encoded at the defaults reports -2 rather than 0; turning psy off removes it and the same stream reports 0.

None of this does anything below subme 6, which is where rate-distortion optimisation starts.
options.listedValuesDescription:
1|The default; psychovisual optimisations on.
0|Off, for PSNR and SSIM benchmarking only.

options.syntaxDescription: 0-16 (default 3) - B-frames between I and P frames; more helps low-motion and animated sources, costs latency
options.description:
The longest run of consecutive B-frames the encoder may insert. B-frames predict from both earlier and later frames, which makes them by far the cheapest frames to code, so allowing longer runs lets static and slow material spend its bits where something is actually happening.

Returns fall off past five or so on live action, and beyond about eight almost nothing is gained on any source. Animation and static footage benefit the most because long stretches genuinely do not change.

Every B-frame adds encoding latency and a frame of decode delay, which is why low-latency settings put this at 0.
